before. Much of that debt has been incurred in buying houses from each other or buying
consumer goods, none of which generates a re turn to the econom y. New Zealanders are
now being careful with their spending and are trying to pay off debt, but we have barely
16598 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
made a dent in that $107,000. In the meantime, the people who lent the money to us still
want us to pay interest, and we have to keep going back to them through the banks to
roll over that debt.
If we thought that $61,000 was enough debt per household, then every household in
New Zealand would have to pay off $40,000 of  debt. That would have an enormous
impact on this economy, because it is money that would not be going into the job-rich
areas such as the retail sector, or into building new houses. Even if we think $107,000 is
about the right amount of debt, that figure sti ll represents a lot of constraint in this
economy. The burden of debt that households  have built up has now become quite a
considerable drag on economic growth. Until households believe that they have their
debt at the right level and th at they can cover the risks of interest rates rising on that
debt as the economy recovers, they will not go out and spend up.
In the agricultural sector it is worse. The ag ricultural sector debt per farm more than
doubled over the period from 2003 to 2008. De spite the fact that we have record
commodity prices, we are not seeing that money flowing into the shops in Hamilton and
Invercargill, because people in the farming community have to pay down the debt that
they ran up, some on productive investment , but mostly on bidding up the prices of
farms and buying them from each other.  Again, although conditions are favourable,
with very high commodity pric es, it will take some time for those conditions to filter
back into the economy because the debt hole on our farms is so large. They will be
pouring their profits into that hole for some time yet.
The same kind of scale of rebalancing is evident when it comes to job growth. We
can think of the economy as being 80 percen t non-tradable—that is, domestic, which is
not competing with the rest of the world—and about 20 percent making up the export
sector and the tradable economy. The non-trad able sector was delivering a lot of new
jobs over the last decade. But far too many of  them were funded by the debt that I have
just talked about and by big increases in Government spending. That spending simply
cannot continue, and it is not continuing. New Zealanders have decided that it will not
continue. The Government has been a bit slower, and we are deciding  that we will have
to tighten up.
Substantial job growth will not come from  that 80 percent of the economy. There
will be some growth, and there has been. In the last 15 months there have been 35,000
new jobs in the non-tradable sector, but that is 80 percent of the economy. The
sustainable job growth has to occur in the ot her 20 percent. In the export sector in the 5
years to 2009 the number of jobs shrank by 55,000. We had 55,000 fewer people in the
export sector 5 years on from 2003. That tren d has just turned round, and with high
commodity prices it should keep turning r ound. So 20 percent of the economy needs to
grow very fast to offset the fact that the other 80 percent of the economy, which
generated all the jobs, is now heavily constrained by debt and will not be growing
nearly as many jobs as it used to grow. There is a long road ahead of us to get a vibrant,
job-generating export sector up and going when it has been on its knees  for a fair bit of
the last decade, shrinking in production and shrinking in jobs.
That brings me to the issue of the public  sector, which the Prime Minister addressed
in his speech. We are very keen to see an  enthusiastic, profe ssional, and innovative
public sector. Not only are we keen to see it; it is an absolute necessity. New
Zealanders’ demands and expectations for pub lic services have not shrunk because of a
recession; those demands and expectations have continued to grow. In fact, those
expectations are probably lifti ng: people expect better health  care, they expect better
education, and they expect more effective law and order from the police and prison
system. So the Government is focusing on producing more and bette r public services,
knowing that it will have to do so for less.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16599
I expect Opposition members will rant on about cuts, as they usually do, but in the
time since they left office we have reprioritised $4 billion—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Cuts.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: He means cuts.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There we go: they ca ll it cuts. Any dollar spent in the public
sector under Labour is a dollar that cannot go anywhere else . They are the only people
in New Zealand who think that. Every household and every business in New Zealand
has had to reorganise its affairs, and the public sector will need to be reorganised in
order to produce more and better services. We are determined to do that.
The Government will go about this task as it has so far: in a very considered and
thoughtful manner. We have already initiated quite a lot of change  across the public
sector. Increasingly the public sector is taki ng leadership of that change because its
members can see that to have satisfying professional lives, and to meet their strong ethic
of public service, things will need to be done a bit differently. It will be the
Government’s role to support them in that  task. They are aware of the financial
constraints; they have heard that message  for a couple of years. The rest of the
community is aware of the financial constrai nts, which is why pe ople take no notice of
Labour’s ranting about cuts. Th ey know, actually, that Labour oversaw a pretty bloated
public sector, which is now being brought into line.
I, along with the team in the National-led Government, look forward to participating
in a process that sees improvements in publ ic services at the same time as we get
Government finances into line, reduce our record-breaking liabilities to overseas
lenders, and get this economy up and running and producing more jobs.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Yesterday when John
Key spoke in Parliament he told us that a society is judged on how it protects the
vulnerable. It perhaps will not surprise memb ers in the House that he did not get the
quote quite right. The quote comes from an American politician named Hubert
Humphrey, who said that the test of the morality of a society was the way in which it
looked after those in the dawn of life, the tw ilight of life, and the shadows of life. If we
put the National Government’s record to that test in just one sector of our society, the
health sector, we can see a total failure by the National Government. We can look at
those in the dawn of life, the young. Today in question time I raised with Tony Ryall
whether it is acceptable for someone living on the Kapiti coast to have to spend 20
percent of the weekly family grocery bill on a visit for after-hour s treatment for their
daughter’s cut lip. Is that acceptable?

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Twenty percent of that family’s weekly grocery bill was
spent on one visit for after-hour s care, and this was from a Government that said that
under-sixes and the treatment of our young children would be a priority. So those in the
dawn of life are not receiving the kind of trea tment in the health sector that we would
expect.
Research last year told us that there were 2,000 more admissi ons of children to
hospital in 2009 than there we re in 2007. That is 2,000 extra admissions to hospital for
diseases of which many would have been pr eventable if the Government were prepared
to invest in primary health care, if the Gove rnment were prepared to invest in the well-
being of our young people. The fact that we have rheumatic fever in New Zealand, at
all, is a disgrace. We need investment in t hose who are in the dawn  of life because that
is a test of the morality of the Government, but we have seen that this Government is
failing that test. Again, we see it with the cuts to ea rly childhood education as well.
Young people are being left behind in the hea lth  system because Mr Ryall is obsessed
by his focus on elective surgery. He is obse ssed by looking good in front of this House
16600 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
when it comes to the health sector, but th e reality for some, like that young family on
the Kapiti coast, is that the health cost s they are facing end up putting them and other
families in a situation where it is a choice between food on the table or health treatment.
Well, in this country we do have choices. That Government  has choices, and it has
chosen to give tax cuts weighted towards the top 10 percent of earners. The Government
could have made a choice to invest in health  and education and to ensure that care for
under-sixes could be free for people all ar ound New Zealand, but it made a choice to
give those tax cuts to the highest-income earners.
If we take Hubert Humphrey’s quote furthe r, we may consider those in the twilight
of life, the elderly. The record on elder care in the health sector from this Government is
appalling. I could not believe that in a country like New Zealand I would have a
constituent come to me about her 92-year-o ld father, a World War II veteran, who had
had his home-help hours cut over the phone. Th is man has hearing difficulties and sight
difficulties, but his home-help hours were cut over the phone. That is not the kind of
New Zealand I want to live in. I want to live in a New Zealand where we look after each
other and where we make a priority of look ing after one another,  not a priority of
rewarding the top 10 percent of earners with a tax cut that they did not need. So those in
the twilight of life have not been treated well by this Government.
What about those in the shadows of life? I take that to mean people, for instance,
who are receiving care under the mental hea lth system. What kind of treatment have
they seen from this Government? There ha ve been cuts to funding right around New
Zealand for mental health. Here in my own area, the Capital and Coast District Health
Board in Wellington has cut mental health funding over the last 2 years. That means
that two community clinics in  Wellington city will close this year—two mental health
community clinics will close this year. It m eans that right across th e health sector, non-
governmental organisations that provide vita l support to people in our community are
losing money.
An organisation like the Phobic Trust of  New Zealand, run by a wonderful woman
named Marcia Read, who has been lauded by parties on both sides of this House, is
losing a funding contract here in Wellington to support people with phobic disorders. Is
that the kind of country that has a good morality? That is the kind of message the
Government is sending. It is failing the test of looking after the vulnerable. It is failing
the moral test of a Government to look after its  citizens in the dawn of life, the twilight
of life, and the shadows of lif e. That is a shame upon this Government, and it is more
evident in the health sector than anywhere else. It is a question of priorities.
The Government has already said that it will cut the spending allowance in the next
Budget down to $800 million of extra spending.  If the health budget stands still, it will
take up $600 million of that $800 million—if it st ands still. Actually, that is still not
enough. In fact, over the 4-year Budget cycle that the Government likes to do its Budget
on, there will be a $750 million hole in the h ealth budget. One whol e year’s worth of
new health spending will have gone, across thos e 4 years. That will inevitably lead to
more service cuts. It will inevitably lead to more pressure on distri ct health boards not
to provide those services to the young, to th e elderly, and to those patients in mental
health. That is not good enough, because the kind of country that I want to live in is one
where we invest in health and education. It is one where we  actually m ake the choice to
say that we will look after our fellow citizens to enable them to achieve their potential,
whoever they are and wherever they are from.
Instead, we have a message from John Key that he cares more about the private
insurers who will benefit from  the privatisation of accide nt compensation, the top 10
percent of income earners, and the foreign investors who will get hold of our State
assets than he does about or dinary New Zealanders. The me ssage to New Zealanders is
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16601
that John Key does not care about them. He cares about all of those other people—the
foreign investors and the overseas-run insura nce companies—because that is where the
value is going in New Zealand today. That is the value that has been put on this. It is the
accountant’s view: the cost of everything and the value of nothing. That is the message
that is coming out of John Key.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Hey!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Not all accountants, I tell Mr Mallard.
From a Labour point of view , we want to focus on invest ing in our future in this
term, because it is vitally important when  the people of New Zealand see the choices
being made by the National Government that they know there are other choices that can
be made and that they know it is possible to  invest in our future through a relentless
focus on children. I totally reject what Heat her Roy said in this  House today. Annette
King is bringing forward a programme on inves ting in the early years that will make a
fundamental difference to the future of New Zealand. It is not about putting an
ambulance at the bottom of the cliff as the Government have done with boot camps; it is
about building those fences at the top to allow young children to flourish, wherever they
are and whatever families they are born into. That is an investment in our future, and,
yes, it will take resources to do that. It will absolutely take resources to do that, but
resources are better spent there than on tax cu ts to the top 10 percent of income earners.
Resources are far better spent on investing in health and education.
If we want to invest in our future, then  we need a fairer tax system. We need a
system where people pay their fair share. It is not about punishing people for success; it
is about encouraging success for everybody by ensuring ever ybody pays a fair share as
part of a fair tax system. It is about having a monetary poli cy that supports exporters,
and that actually says we want export growth. Where was the message on export growth
in the Prime Minister’s speech yesterday? It was just words and no action on that issue.
On this side of the House we know that when the Prime Minister comes here to make
a statement he should be setting out a vision. He should be setting out his vision for the
future of New Zealand. What we got yesterday was a directionless statement. The Prime
Minister is all map and no compass. He ha s all the polling and all the focus groups, but
he has no idea where he wants to take New Zealand. He has no vision for the future of
this country. This year Labour will be presenting a positive vision about investing in our
future and investing in our young people, in contrast with National members, who see
the cost of everything and the value of nothing.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: This political year got off
to a decisive start with Prime Minister John Key setting out a very ambitious and
focused plan for how we can shift this economy and secure the sort of future we want
for New Zealanders, by getting out of the debt and consumption cycle and moving to an
economy that is based on productive investment  and exports. In contrast, what we have
heard from Phil Goff and from Labour’s most  recent speaker, Grant Robertson, is all
that stuff about big spending and about th e borrow-and-hope policies that actually got
New Zealand into the pretty fragile position we are in today. It is noteworthy that in the
month of January Labour s pokespeople promised over $5 billion of new spending. The
cash register was ticking over in bulk as Gran t Robertson just gave that speech. I will
give an example. Mr Robertson has said: “Free after-hours care for all New
Zealanders.” I have a simple question fo r Grant: where is the money coming from?
Where is the money coming from? Can Mr Ro bertson and Mr Goff tell us where their
money tree is? Where is their money tree? Ther e is absolutely no fiscal credibility in
where the money is coming from to fund th e extravagant and unsustainable spending
comm
itments we are seeing from Labour members, across the board.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Do you not believe in free care for under-sixes?
16602 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: You see, during Labour’s years in office, I remind Mr
Robertson, sure, Labour doubled the amount of money it spent on health, yet there were
negligible additional services. Labour members can go on about the care of children, but
the reality is that Labour had an appalling record on something as basic and important
as immunisation. I congratulate my coll eague and benchmate Tony Ryall on achieving
the highest-ever level of imm unisation of children in this  country, and particularly on
the high levels for Pacific Island and Mā ori children. They are the things that count and
that show that this John Key Government is serious about getting good-quality public
services, but not a bloated Public Service.
The biggest growth in health during Labour’s years was in the number of bureaucrats
in the health ministry. I make no apologies for being part of a National Government that
wants to focus our public services on the front line, on our police, on our nurses, on our
doctors, and on our teachers. That  actually will make a materi al difference, rather than
the bureaucrats whom Mr Robertson always wants to see getting a bigger slice of the
funding.
I will focus also on some of the issues re levant to my portfolios that expose the
contradictions in Labour’s a pproach. Let me take employ ment. In 2009 we had the Job
Summit. A big concern for a large number of employers and councils around this
country was the ridiculous air-quality rule s the previous Labour Government put in
place that would see 17,000 New Zealanders—17,000 New Zealanders—lose their jobs.
Let me tell members why. Despite  the fact that our biggest problem with air quality is
actually households and cars, the only people to be punished  under Labour’s air-quality
policy were going to be those in industry. You see, it is very simple for Labour; they are
anti-business. It does not matter what the problem is. If there will be punishment, it has
to be businesses that pay. Wh at they do not understand is that those businesses employ
the very New Zealanders whom it is more important than ever we keep in jobs. I was
pleased to announce at the Bluegreen conf erence in Akaroa the new air-quality
standards that will save 17,000 jobs—a policy change that is backed by the
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Enviro nment, who said that Labour’s policy
unfairly targeted business. I say to members opposite: “Don’t stand on your feet and
talk about jobs, when the very regulations that you passed and you continue to support
to this day would see thousands of New Zeal anders, in cities all over this country, lose
their jobs.”
Then there was the other contradiction. I heard members opposite crying crocodile
tears about the cost of living. Let me take just one example. On 24 December Labour
made an announcement on climate change policy. Labour said it wants to move the
emissions trading scheme to full obliga tion immediately—immediately! Let us be
honest about what that means for the cost of  living. It means that  it will put 3.5c on the
price of both petrol and diesel  immediately. It means an ex tra 5 percent on the price of
power. So I say to members opposite: “Don’t cry crocodile tears about the cost of living
when you are, at the same time, announcing policies that will push up costs for ordinary
New Zealand families.” I make no apologies for members on this side of the House
having a sensible, balanced emissions tradi ng scheme that has reduced the costs that
Labour’s scheme would have imposed on families and on businesses.
Let me take another area. I was interested  today to get advice about what sorts of
things would happen to the cost of living for families, under Labour’s ACC policies. Let
me put it simply. For the first time in years this National Government said: “We’re not
going to put the ACC levies up  on motor vehicles, on earn ers, and on businesses.” We
have been able to do that because we, as a Government, have been able to get on top of
the costs that were occurring in ACC. T hose costs were going up by 12 percent every
single year from 2003 to 2008. If there is a 12 percent increase each year in claim costs,
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16603
who pays that? It is ordinary New Zealande rs. When they register their vehicle, and
every week when they receive their pay, thos e ACC levies are taken out. If we had let
those costs continue to grow, those levies  would have had to rise by $200 per New
Zealand family. In other words, every singl e New Zealand family would have had to
pay another 30 bucks when they registered their car, if we had allowed Labour’s
policies to continue.
Every New Zealander on the average wage  would have been up for another $150 a
year—another $3 a week—in terms of the earners levy, if we had allowed those costs to
continue to rise at 12 percent per year. Members oppos ite talk as though they are
concerned about costs on New Zealanders, but  during their period in Government over
and over again they had policies that simply  drove up costs. Those costs end up falling
on households and businesses. The changes that this Government has made are
consistent.
I make one further important point. The Prime Minister started this year with a very
bold call on the mixed-ownership policy in re spect of State-owned enterprises. That
policy will extend the investment opportuni ties for New Zealanders who are being
burned off the finance companies. They do not  want them investing more and more in
residential property. We will provide opportunities for them to invest in good New
Zealand companies. But I want to expose the double standards of that. I quote David
Cunliffe, the Opposition finance spokesperson, from 25 November 2010, who said, in a
very important speech at Victoria Un iversity: “We can unleash State-owned
enterprises—”

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Unleash!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Unleash—“to create and grow new businesses with private
partners and private shareholders.” That was from the speech made by Mr David
Cunliffe, the finance spokesperson for Labour members opposite.
I have a simple challenge for Phil Goff and the other members of Labour’s team who
have ranted and raved agains t this policy. Well, why did th ey not rant and rave in
November? I will tell members why. It is because they are absolutely hollow in their
vision for New Zealand. They want to play pol itics with the issues that are so important
to this country: getting efficient public services, reorienting our economy towards
exports, getting quality educ ation services, and making su re that our environment
policies are supporting the growth and the jobs  that New Zealand needs, as well as in
areas like agriculture where my colleague s have made big announcements about the
Primary Growth Partnership.
This Government has a positive plan for New Zealand, whether it is for jobs, whether
it is for the cost of living, or whether it  is for mixed ownership for State-owned
enterprises. The mixed signals, the confused policy, and the straight  pure politics that
we see from the Labour Opposition show that  Labour is into opportunism, but it has
absolutely no idea what is required to make New Zealand strong.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Yesterday when the Prime Minister gave his statement
to the House it was confirmed once and for all, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that that
Government has no plan to lift this country’s economy. The Pr ime Minister told us last
year that he was going to aggr essively bring the country out of recession. By the end of
the year he had the country pretty much convi nced that things were going pretty well,
economically speaking. Then suddenly this year, it has gone to hell in a basket—New
Zealand has become a basket case, according to the Government this year. I do not
know what happened over Christmas, but ev erything was ticking over, and now this
year the Prime Minister is out there saying “Sorry, everyone, we’re actually a basket
case.”
16604 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
If this country is a basket case, then it must be the Government that we have to
blame. This Government inherited one of the lowest Government debts in the OECD
when it took office, but suddenly it is now trying to convince other New Zealanders that
the country is a basket case. It is such a basket case that I ask members to guess what
the solution is from this National Government. Surprise, surprise! It is exactly the same
solution every National Government has had in  my living history. It  is to flog off the
family business and sell off the State assets. It is the same old theory that National has
always had; it has not worked in the past, and it will not work now.
The second thing that a National Govern ment has always done in every single
situation is to give tax cuts to favour the wealthy in this country. So that is the formula
to get us out of this situation. The Prime Mi nister said yesterday that he was sorry he
had led folks down the garden path, but that the country was actually a basket case. He
said to forget what National told people la st year, but New Zealand is a basket case
under National, so it will have to sell off th e family silver and fl og off our State assets.
New Zealanders already own them, but Nationa l will flog them off. It will have to do
that because the Government has borrowed to pay for tax cuts that favour the wealthy—
that is the situation we are in.
But then the Prime Minister said something else that wa s interesting. He said only
about three or four things that were intere sting. The next thing he said was that we
should judge his Government’s performance on how the vulnerable are treated in our
society. That is what he said. If that is  how we are going to judge his Government’s
performance, then I am afraid it is an epic fail. It is a fail on all counts, because the
vulnerable in this society are struggling more  and more as every single day of this
National Government goes on.
I will talk about both ends of the spectrum, from the cradle to the grave. If we look at
how our children are faring in this country under this Government, we know that one of
the first areas it has taken the funding-cut knife to has been ea rly childhood education.
Those funding cuts are ringing out as we speak, because they only came in on 1
February this year. On 1 February many, ma ny thousands of families in this country
learnt that they will have to pay more to take their children to early childhood education,
and some of those families, quite frankly, cannot afford it. They cannot afford it because
that Government has put up GST on everythi ng that moves. They cannot afford it
because that Government has let doctors’ fees keep increasing for families. But National
is now saying to those families that they w ill have to pay more for early childhood
education. We have heard Government memb er after Government member get up and
wreck their own credibility by claiming that there are no funding cuts in early childhood
education. Kate Wilkinson is one who said that in her electorate alone—

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: She doesn’t have one.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: —oh, not her electorate; the elec torate where she happens to
live—there was going to be only $29,500 lost from her entire area  in early childhood
education funding cuts, the cuts that her Mini ster and her Prime Minister have told her
do not exist. I am sorry to tell her, but if she just wanders down the road a little bit to
Swannanoa Preschool centre, which I understand is not 50 metres from where she lives,
she will find out that that centre alone  has had a budget funding cut from her
Government of $100,000.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is $100,000 for just one centre, which is not 50 metres down
the road from where a Minister of this G overnment lives, a Minister who was trying to
tell her community that the funding cuts did no t exist, and that if they did they were
going to be only $29,500. So I think those me mbers opposite have to be very, very
careful that they do not keep undermining their own personal credibility every time they
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16605
step out on the street and try to convince voters  in their electorates that there have been
no funding cuts to early ch ildhood education. They have  only to go and visit any
kindergarten, or visit most of the early childhood education centres in their areas, to find
out that those funding cuts ar e real. The cuts have not been made up by the Labour
Party and they have not been made up by the sector.
Why is it that families are now facing increased fees of between $2 and $80 per child
per week? That is the effect of that Gove rnment’s funding cuts, yet the Prime Minister
had the gall to go on national TV and tell th e nation that on 1 February fees would not
be going up for families because of his funding cuts. That is what he told the nation.
Well, I would like him to go and speak to a fe w of the people in th at sector. He should
get out and speak to some of the families. Has he spoken to Debra Bullock, for
example? Debra Bullock is from Wanganui. She has two preschoolers who attend Durie
Hill’s Polson Park Kindergarten. Her fees are going up by $35 a week. In fact, they are
doubling. She was initially paying $35 for her two children to attend kindergarten up
until the time that the Government took th e knife to early chil dhood education, the
sector with the most vulnerable children in our society, and caused her fees to go up to
$70 a week. That is a 100 per cent increase in early childho od education fees for that
family alone. But she is not alone. About 100,000 children and their families are
affected by these early childhood education fu nding cuts in New Zealand, right across
the board. Has the Prime Minister spoken with Lisa Kingsford? I challenge him to speak
with Lisa Kingsford, because she has a child going to the Newlands Childcare centre in
this region, here in Wellington. She has said that she has had a fee increase of an extra
$25 a week for her 4-year-old daughter, Caitlin, to attend  preschool. Yet the Prime
Minister is on national TV trying to convince the country that his funding cuts to early
childhood education will not increase costs to families. Well, that is absolute rubbish.
That is our Prime Minister, getting up on TV  and telling the nation something that is
blatantly untrue. It represents a broken pr omise from his National Government. He is
embarrassed about it, and he should be. Not only have fees gone up but also his promise
that 20 hours’ free early childhood education would stay in place, that the subsidies
would stay the same, and that the rules woul d stay the same has been completely and
utterly broken. In fact, the Mi nister of Education was caught out this week writing to a
kindergarten specifically to recommend that it increase the fee for 20 hours’ free early
childhood education. She recommended that th at was the way the kindergarten should
deal with that funding cut. Anne Tolley wr ote to it and asked whether it had thought
about increasing fees for 20 hours’ free early childhood edu cation care; that was the
way out of it.
We cannot believe anything this Govern ment has to say about early childhood
education. We cannot believe those members when they say that those funding cuts
have not occurred, because anyone who goes out and about in the community and visits
early childhood education centres knows diffe rently. I am starting to wonder whether
the National whips have issued an instruction that no National MPs are to go out to the
early childhood education sector. I certainly  have not seen one at the many early
childhood education centres that I have visited. I challenge Government members, the
Minister of Education, and particularly the Prime Minister to talk to those families who
face increased fees, and to go to the early childhood education sector and dare to front
up and tell them there has been no funding cut in  their sector, because they are living it,
day in, day out.
Those families now have to find that extra m oney out of their very tight budgets just
to make sure that their children can get a preschool education—a preschool education
that is their right; it is an investment in their future. Labour will restore that funding cut
from that unkind Government.
16606 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.role: Minister for So cial Development and Employment
items.text: I
am going to stand up today and have a bit of a chat about unemployment and
employment in New Zealand, an d where we are at. I would love to talk about welfare
and the Prime Minister’s statements on that, and also about vulnerable children,
protection, and where we can go further there.  However, I cannot help but respond to
the previous speaker, Sue Moroney. Really, if we cut down to it, we are talking about
some fundamental differences. This side of the House legitimately feels that to have a
teacher-led early childhood education centre wh ere 80 percent of teachers are qualified
is fair and reasonable in the early childhood sector. Eight out of 10 teachers being fully
qualified and two not being qualified is OK.  The way we were heading under Labour
was that pretty soon parents themselves woul d have to get degrees  to look after their
own children. To have eight out of 10 early childhood teachers with a degree at an early
childhood centre for under-5-year-olds is OK by most New Zealanders. Under-5-year-
olds are different. There is the word “play”, and there is the word “love”, which is very,
very seldom used by Labour when we talk about those children. For those children to be
nurtured and loved by teachers, a small percentage of whom are unqualified, is perfectly
acceptable. I will stand up and advocate that  on behalf of the National Government
every time, and I think parents see the sense of that.
Unemployment has increased in a recession, and that is a fact. January numbers for
the unemployment benefit, and for benefits overall, have just been released. The number
of people on the unemployment benefit went  up by just over 1,000 for the month of
January. That is the smallest increase we ha ve seen for the month of January for more
than 3 years. We have also seen the lowest increase for the month of December that we
have seen for 3 years, as well. Those figures are not sa ying that more people are not
going on the benefit and that there is not a lo t more work to be done; they are saying
that we are seeing some changes in the labou r market, and that jobs are coming on line.
We have also recently seen reports of more  jobs being on line. At Work and Income
alone we saw more than 6,000 jobs come in for the month of January.
Because the member of Parliament Jacinda Ardern is in the Chamber, I will mention
the issue of youth, because I know that issue is very dear to her heart, as well. One thing
that I am particularly proud of from last year is that of the 56,000-odd young people that
came into Work and Income to go on a benefit, 45.5 percent of them did not go on,
because they either found work or they went into training. So we actually managed to
triage off 45.5 percent of th em by steering them in the right direction. There are a
number of reasons why and how that has worked. Some of that has been around job
opportunities—that is, making sure we linked in better with employers, and giving a
subsidy for those young people. So far abou t 13,000 places have b een taken up in both
Job Ops and Community Max. Of those 13,000 places, the Job Ops component is about
9,500 places. So the $5,000 goes to an employer for 6 months, paying around half of the
young person’s wage, and making a big difference.
Industry relations have been strengthened between Work and Income and employers.
We are also able to direct young people into training more quickly, and, as a
consequence, we see fewer of them go on to benefits. There is no doubt about it, that
has been a huge bonus.
We also have to consider benefit numbers,  and my colleagues will appreciate this.
During the 2000s we saw the number on the sickness benefit incr ease by nearly 50
percent, and the number on the invalids bene fit increase by over 50 percent. So while
the number on the unemployment benefit was going dow n, the number on the other
benefits was going up; Labour was transferri ng people from the unemployment benefit
to the sickness benefit and the invalids benefit. Actually, we were not getting a heck of a
lot sicker. We certainly were not getting 50 percent sicker, a nd that is for sure. In what
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16607
were supposedly the best of times, whic h were completely squandered under the
previous Government, we saw beneficiaries just moving from one benefit to another.
In the last 2 years, we have seen the lowest percentage increase between those
benefits since the early 1990s. We have b een honest about the numbers on benefits,
about what is happening, and about the type of benefits they should be on. We are not
seeing the transfer from the unemployment benefit to the si ckness benefit and on to the
invalids benefit, from where, quite fra nkly, someone’s chances of going into work
would be very poor. Under the mechanisms put in place by the previous Labour
Government, people were more likely to go on to superannuation than into work when
on the invalids benefit. We want to turn some of that stuff round.
We believe that people are worth more than  a lifetime on welfare, and, yes, that will
mean some changes. I personally understand some of the concern that comes from the
sector that depends on welfare. I understand some of the frustration and the fear that
comes from the possibility of coming change s. I also understand the way that Labour
has chosen to absolutely scaremonger and play on that fear. Labour would like people to
stay victimised and stay on welfare, because, quite frankly, it thinks that keeping people
down is the way to do it. We are saying that we believe in people being worth more. We
believe in backing people to get themselves either into work or ready for work.
It is about recognising that 85,000 people are on the invalids benefit for 10 years or
more—which is the likelihood and which is certainly what we have seen in the last 10
to 15 years—and that is not the place for them to be. So we are going to back those
people, and it will mean some changes. We have already made some changes to welfare
around obligations and incentives and evenin g that up. Changes were made to the
domestic purposes benefit in October last  year, and we have seen 1,800 people go off
the domestic purposes benefit and into work in that period. As tough as times are, one
must say that that is a great achievement. I can take no credit for it, though, because it is
the people themselves who have got the j obs, and it is those w ho have worked with
them who have made that happen for them.
I want to talk about issue of teen parents, which is dear to my heart and drove me to
get into Parliament in the first place. There is no doubt that I am now in a position to be
able to do some stuff. Budget 2010 introduced  a $14.9 million spend in this area. It was
the biggest spend ever in one lump on this  group of young people. I was in Rotorua on
Monday night and opened one of the supported teen houses. It was absolutely cool to be
there. This is voluntary housing. It is not one of the tough kinds of housing for teens
who are having lots of troubles and are being made to go there to sort themselves out or
else there might be dire consequences. This  is a housing situation for teens who have
said that they would like a bit of help and th at they do not quite have the family and the
whānau support around them. They ask to live in the house for a while, bond with baby,
learn how to run a house, learn how to mana ge a budget, learn how to be a mum, and
learn a bit about relationships—all of those things are often what our own parents would
do for us if we were young and a bit scared. I reckon having a new baby is terrifying, no
matter what age one is. It is putting teens into supported housing like that. Te Arawa
were predominantly there, a nd they will do a fantastic jo b of running this house. We
have put money into helping teen parents, we have certainly supported teen dads, and
we have also put in more intensive caseworkers, and there are heaps of positive stories
arising from that. But we do need to look again at  the issue, and that will be part of this
Government’s work. The Prime Minister t ouched on this issue ye sterday. I say that
4,670 babies were born to teen parents last y ear. There are definitely spots where there
are predominantly more teen births, such as Gisborne and Kawerau, and Rotorua is
certainly on
e of those areas.
16608 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
We cannot talk about teen parents without  talking about some prevention measures,
as we want to see teen birth numbers come  down. The statistics are pretty daunting. I
hate doing the statistics, but teen mothers are nine times more likely to have no
qualifications, twice as likely to suffer from depression, tw ice as likely to  be substance
dependent, and three times more likely to be suicidal at times. Those statistics are pretty
ugly and pretty awful. So we need to put in resources, provide support, and introduce
prevention measures. Teen mothers will al so, on average, spend 7.1 years out of 10
years on a benefit, and stay on a benefit for longer. They are also almost 30 percent
likely to have another baby while on a benef it. We can do better. We can do better for
them, we can do better for their children, and, quite frankly, we can do better for New
Zealand, because they are ours. We will look at  what we can do, as far as front-loading
that support, getting it in plac e, and then making sure that we back them. That is what I
think it is about. I am so proud to think a bout where we are going th is year with this
vision, under this Government. I am so proud to be a Minister in the John Key - led
National Government.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to follow the Minister for Social
Development and Employment, and it is quite timely, given that th e issues I wish to
focus on also sit around unemployment and wi ll touch on youth unemployment as well.
The Minister said at the be ginning of her speech that she was not playing politics, and
implied that Labour was. She then went on to say that we did not have enough love for
the people whom we are here to represent.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: That’s not actually what I said. If you’re going to quote me, do
it properly.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I summarise what the Minister said, because that is certainly
what was implied. All I point out to the Minister is that if that is not playing politics,
then I do not know what is.
I also point out a couple of i ssues that I have with quoting some of the st atistics that
the Minister has around young people going into Work and Income offices and not
moving on to benefits. Young people, of c ourse, do not become eligible for the
unemployment benefit until they are 18, a nd as we know, the NEET figures—those
youth not in employment, education, or training—in New Zealand, which I am happy to
go through later on in my speech, are incredibly high. A number of the young people
who will be presenting to Work and Income w ill not be eligible for a benefit, because
the Government has also made it very hard for young people to go on to an independent
youth benefit, which is the only other benefit they would be eligible for.
I have also heard anecdotal evidence of young people being told that they will not be
put on to a benefit, even if they are 18, unless they go on a Limited Service Volunteers
programme, even if it is held several hours away from where they live. They see that as
a barrier to their getting furt her support. There are issues with quoting statistics willy-
nilly, and if the Minister is happy to provide more evidence I would be happy to see it.
In the Prime Minister’s speech yesterday I think all of us were looking for a vision,
some hope, and a plan. The Minister may cl aim that Labour is scaremongering. What
scaremongering is there in asking the Prime Minister to present a plan as to how we will
stimulate the economy and grow jobs for Kiwis?  That is not scaremongering; that is our
responsibility as the Opposition. The fear comes in when there is a blank answer from
the Government as to what its plan is. That is scary. It is absolutely frightening that after
2 years of recession the Government still does not  have a plan to bring us out of it, and
to start creating jobs for the 6.8 percent of Kiwis who are currently unemployed.
That is not just a statistic. On 3 February, when we found out that unem
ployment had
increased, that statistic re presented 158,000 Kiwis who are currently unemployed. That
is 52,000 more than when the Government t ook office. We know, as we always do, that
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16609
with these kinds of figures there will alwa ys be some who are overrepresented in the
statistics, and in this case it is young people.  Twenty-five percent of 15 to 19-year-olds
are looking for work—25 percent. The last time the figure was as high as that was
decades ago. I also point out that the last time it was as high as that we had a youth
minimum wage. That is a message for the ACT Party. It should stop trying to bring
back policies of the past that did not work.

items.speaker: Hon Heather Roy
items.text: It works.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I say to Ms Roy that it di d not work. The last time youth
unemployment was as high as that was when  we had a youth minimum wage. There is
no robust evidence to suggest a correlation between lowering unemployment and giving
youth a lower wage for doing the same job as an adult.
What about the figures for youth not in em ployment, education, or training? There
are 34,000 fifteen to 19-yea r-olds not in employment, education, or training—34,000.
That is the figure that frightens me. The Mini ster is content to talk about unemployment
benefit numbers, but those numbers do not include those young people. Predominantly
the young people in that category are not having  any contact with Government services,
training, education, or anything that will give them a long-term future. They are the
young people we should be most concerned about.
In the 20 to 24-year-old ra nge 11.2 percent are unemployed,  according to the latest
household labour force survey, which is 39, 000 not in employment, education, or
training in that category. These represent a group of young people who often have come
out of training or education and have faile d to find work. Again, the longer that those
young people are unemployed, the more difficult it becomes for them to find work. The
Minister should have addressed that issue in  her speech today when she told Parliament
and New Zealand that an extra 1,000 peopl e are drawing benefits. She should have
given us a plan. If she did not  give us a plan, the Prime Mi nister should have. But we
have heard nothing from either of them.
Instead, we have heard excuses. Of the five times that the Prime Minister mentioned
employment in his speech, once was in refere nce to employment fo r people who are in
prison and once was in terms of employme nt law and removing people’s employment
rights as a way, apparently, to get them into work. That leaves three times. In those
three times did we actually hear anything concrete? Well, across the range of statements
we heard from Paula Bennett and the Prime Minister about unemployment figures, we
have heard that the figures ar e volatile. We have heard statements that there are not
enough jobs. We have heard statements from Minister Bennett that job seekers just need
to keep a positive attitude. Kiwis do not want  to be told that th eir attitude needs to
change in order to find work; they need to be told there are jobs. They are looking. We
know they are looking, but if the jobs are not there it is a futile exercise.
Labour has always said that things can be  done to stimulate the economy in order to
create employment. We have talked about  a systematic change to the way the
Government intervenes in the economy. Of  course, this falls on deaf ears because
ideologically we perceive these things very  differently. We have asked the Government
for a plan around economic growth. Instead, what have we seen from the Government? I
am willing to acknowledge that the Government threw up Job Ops very early on. So far,
almost the entirety of the Government’s plan  is Job Ops. The New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research gave the Government a C on youth unemployment, stating that Job
Ops, at best, would hit about 8 percent of  young people who were in need of work. For
those who were affected by the scheme, most of the jobs turned out  to be short term,
because there were only short-term incentiv es for em ployers to take on subsidised
young people, and the jobs were not necessa rily long-term opportunities that would
16610 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
exist beyond 6 months. Essentially, that is wh at we have seen from the Government in
terms of a plan: Job Ops. Beyond that, we have seen very little.
What about the second area that the Govern ment could have contributed in: skills
and education? The Government has not in vested in skills and education as the
Australian Government has done, and which now has unemployment in Australia at a
level of 5 percent. The last time we saw a level of 5 percent unemployment was when
the Government decided to have its Job Summit, since which time we have been
hurtling towards higher unemployment, so obviously it has not had the outcome that
was intended.
Instead of investing in skills and education, what did we see? In real terms, we saw
cuts to tertiary education. There is less funding, so un iversities are now unable to
provide the number of placements to  meet the demand among young people. The
Government has also made it difficult to stay  in tertiary educa tion by tightening up
student loan requirements, and it has essentially cut $50 million out of skills and trade
training, which is the exact opposite of what most sensible Governments have done in
the face of a recession and unemployment.
What about job creation? We saw the 9-day working fortnight, but that was a
preventative; it had nothing to do with creati ng work. The one thing we are left with at
the end of the day is the cycleway. Labour ne ver said the cycleway was a bad idea, but
we said that if it is the on ly idea, it is a shocker. It has created about 200 jobs. When we
have 158,000 people out of work, 200 jobs is not a plan.
I will be happy to come back  to the issue of the 90-day trial period, because there is
much more to be said on that issue.
As an alternative, Labour has said all along that we must  make systemic change. We
need a Government that will take an ac tive role in the economy through monetary
policy. It is not enough  to talk about trade deals if our  exporters are st ruggling to deal
with our volatile New Zealand dollar. It is about a fairer tax system , and about bringing
back incentives for research and development, rather than cutting $620 million out of
tax credits and $700 million out of the Fast  Forward Fund. PricewaterhouseCoopers has
told us there are billions to be made in cleantech, if only New Zealand would capitalise
on that opportunity. If there are no jobs there, where are they?
Turning to skills and trade training, La bour has always had a plan for youth
transition; it is just a shame that the Govern ment came in and cut it. We have also said
that we need to invest in apprenticeships, and we need to deal with the 70,000 young
people who are not in employme nt, education, or training. But instead of hearing a plan
from the Government we have heard the cons equences of not having  a plan, with just
this afternoon 1,000 more people joining the dole queue. Enough is enough. If Kiwis
want a plan, Labour will deliver it.

items.speaker: RAHUI KATENE
items.text: For the average New Zealander
the world of politics must be really hard to fathom. Over recent months the news that
has captivated the headlines has been about whether particular politicians have dyed
their hair, whether the Prime Minister shoul d have minced on the catwalk or admitted
that Liz Hurley is “hot”, and what sort of behaviour is befitting of MPs.
What seems to have slipped below the radar is the fact that a crisis is occurring in our
hospital admissions. It is a fact that medical conditions, which occur more frequently for
tamariki living in poverty, have been increas ing over recent years, particularly for our
Māori and Pasifika mokopuna. Close to 250,000 ta mariki are living in homes reliant on
the benefit for their income.
My colleague Te Ururoa Flavell last night  sp elt out some of the consequences for
families living in severe or significant ha rdship: families who go without fruit and
vegetables, put up with the cold to save on heating costs, delay going to the doctor or
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16611
the dentist, live in cramped conditions, or tell their children that the opportunity to go on
a school trip or play sport is a privilege that they can ill afford. Is this a nation fit for our
tamariki? We need to heed the research that  shows us there can be a different life for
our babies, if we make it a priority.
Last year I spoke at the launch in Dunedin of The New Zealand Children’s Social
Health Monitor Report 2010 . That report revealed th e inevitable, showing that
economic recessions have affected children’s health in other countries. We have seen
research showing the close correlation be tween recessions and high hospital admissions
for children here in New Zealand. However, the report also reported on the experience
of Sweden in the 1990s when, despite large numbers of children living in low-income
families, there were no significant increas es in childhood hospitalisations for poverty-
related illnesses.
I remind the House of the question I asked th e Minister of Health earlier today. In
question time I noted that in 2010, 2,000 more children were admitted to hospital with
poverty-related illnesses th an during 2007-08. We are talking about admissions for
respiratory problems, infectious diseases, and other conditions with links to poor
housing and economic hardship. Those are a ll diseases of poverty, which could have
been prevented if children had been taken to see a doctor earlier. The Prime Minister
said earlier in this debate , when talking about those ve ry children, the children who
suffer the consequences of long-term dependency, that the “Government is not prepared
to leave those people behind.” Th at was welcome news for the M āori Party, but
statements are at risk of becoming platitude s without a plan being put in place. Slogans
and placards are great for the cameras, but where is the strategy to put the words into
action?
I tell the House that it is  in the relationship and in  the confidence and supply
agreement between National and the M āori Party. In that document we spelt it out in
black and white: “The Maori Party seeks sign ificant outcomes in whanau ora, through
eliminating poverty”. Not content with that, we then made child poverty a key platform
in our economic policy. In our policy appro ach to end child poverty by 2020 we stated
that successive Governments and their policies have created policy problems in our land
of plenty. We put the time and effort into investing in the promise of prosperity. We
called for seven simple solu tions to support children, whānau, and families. We will set
a deadline to eliminate child poverty by 2020. We will designate an official poverty line
at 60 percent of the median household dispos able income after housing costs, and set
net income for those on benefits at this measure to prevent poverty. We will increase the
minimum wage to at least $15 an hour. We will raise core benefit levels, including
superannuation and veterans pensions. We  will simplify Working for Families,
including extending the in-work payment to  all families. We will investigate the
reintroduction of a universal child benefit. We will esta blish a neighbourhood renewal
fund, which may include incentives to encour age people to live more collectively by,
for example, encouraging the use of community gardens, after-school care, and post-
natal support for parents.
There were other cross-sector priorities that we have brough t to the attention of this
Government. We have talked about the adop tion of the genuine progress index, rather
than the continuing reliance on GDP as the onl y measure of the health of a nation. We
proposed the establishment of an “every chil d matters” fund, which would be a targeted
and time-limited grant to ensure, among other things, that no child starts school without
shoes or a raincoat. We have put pressure  on the Government to expand retrofit
programmes in order to ensure houses can meet the achievable warm house standards
target.
16612 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
I would love to say that we have achieved in all of those areas, and that life for our
children has improved. There have been some big gains, which have come directly from
our relationship with the G overnment. One of the most si gnificant things we have
achieved has been the investment of $320 milli on in retrofitting to insulate and heat
homes built before 2000. We were pleased to  know that priority would be given to
homes with families suffering poor health, a disproportionate number of whom will be
whānau Māori. The opportunity for community servic es cardholders to be eligible for a
grant of up to $3,000 was also really importa nt. Eighteen months ago the Government
put $320,000 into the KidsCan StandTall food in schools programme, which will make
a difference for something like 7,500 childre n. The minimum wage did increase, but
only by a mere 25c an hour. Yes, benefit a nd superannuation payments did increase by
some 1.96 percent, but it was an April Fool ’s Day increase, which just kept pace with
the cost of living. But as for any substantia l, meaningful difference made in terms of
addressing child poverty, we are still waiting.
But the M āori Party is not a party that sits and waits for a nother day, nor is it our
party’s policy to wail and weep if we do not have a strategy in mind. Our policy
approach has always been to face the risk, take a step forward, and do all that we can to
make gains and create a positive difference. Just before Christmas members will have
noted that I wrote to every one of the members of the House seeking their support to
hold parliamentary cross-party ta lks on child poverty. It was not just my bright idea; at
the Children’s Social Health Monitor launch last year, members of the audience asked
whether politicians could work together to el iminate that disgrace. It is the opportunity
we all need to turn round the public percep tion of politicians and to work together
collectively on the things that really matter.
We know that by investing in  education, social services , and access to free health
care, the impacts of poverty and recession on children can be dram atically reduced. I
have a raft of ideas, I have the enthusiasm  to match, and I have been following matters
up with individual members. Now, all I am  waiting for are the remaining responses
from right across the House declaring our collective concern about the well-being of our
mokopuna.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.role: Minist er for Building and Construction
items.text: I
will start today with what I think is one of life’s most delicious ironies. It is just
dripping in the most delicious irony. It is to do with the nom ination of candidates in the
Botany by-election. In Botany, which is next to my electorate of Pakuranga, as some
people will know, a debate has been raging for many years about the need for better
roading networks. We do not have the luxury of a rail network like west Auckland does,
or a dedicated bus lane like No rth Shore does; we in east Auckland do not have those.
But the Greens, in particular, and also others from the green movement, have absolutely
railed—and I used that word guardedly—again st the building of the eastern motorway.
They say we do not need it, it is not necessary, people should use public transport, and
we do not need new roading in east Auckland, especially in Botany.
Yesterday, if people listened carefully, they  could hear the sound of flapping wings
as the chickens came home to roost. Yest erday the Green candida te got caught in a
dreadful traffic jam on Ti Rakau Drive and did  not make it to the returning officer in
time to get his nomination registered. Now, sadly, there is no Green candidate standing
in the Botany by-election. Why is that? B ecause, as people who know the area will
know, one can go out there and get stuck in unbelievable traffic jams.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Was he not bicycling, then?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, he was not bicycling—that is true. Someone
else asked why he did not take the train. Ther e is no train out in east Auckland to take. I
thought that if there is someth ing in the world called deliciou s irony, then it has to be
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16613
when the Greens fail to even register thei r candidate. I do not understand why they did
not get him to go the day before, or the day before that. It was not as if he was told he
had 10 seconds to get there—ready, set, go; no, stop—and that is it. The Greens decided
to leave it until the very last minute, and th eir candidate actually did not get there at the
last minute because the traffic jam cut him out . That is a shame, because it would have
been good to have had a Green candidate in th e race, but he could not even get there to
register. It is more proof that in the easte rn suburbs of Auckland, more investment will
be required in roading.
One of the most fabulous quotes I ever heard from Maggie Thatcher—and she was
my favourite politician—was when she said that the Good Samaritan did not do what he
did just because he was good; he also had the money. I thi nk that is so important for
people to get their heads around when we are debating—

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Twyford doesn’t get it.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, Twyford does not get it. But any other
family in this country other than Mr Twyford’s understands that if they spend more than
they are earning, then the day of reckoning must come. Eventually, if they are spending
more than they are earning, the day of reckoning will come.
What Labour members who have spoken today have never, never brought into their
equations is the fact that something ghastly  happened to the world a couple of years
ago. [Interruption] It was not their world; something ghastly happened to their world a
long time before 2 years ago, but 2 years ag o something ghastly called the global
financial crisis happened to the world. Just  like any family who has a plan, maybe, to
upgrade their house, change their car, or spe nd some money on a holiday would have to
change all those plans if, say, the breadwinner in the family became unemployed and
there was no income, so this nation has to  relook at absolutely everything being done
and consider, first of all, how we buffer our citizens from the really harsh, sharp edges
of the global financial crisis. Bill English deserves unbelievable credit for what he has
done as Minister of Finance to make that happen.
Secondly, we have to ask how we cut our cloth accordingly so that we can still keep
spending money on essential services and also  try to get some ec onomic growth going
in the market place. The socialists on the other side of the House—and this is how
socialists think—say that what we should do is tax the rich. They say the rich have lots
of money, so let us tax them.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: What rich?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, that is their attitude . What they do not get is
that once we go past a certain level of taxation, we actually get less money, because any
people worth their salt when it comes to th e financial markets know they have green
screens with keyboards. They can move money out of this country, and they can change
their circumstances accordingly. We cannot ju st tax the rich until the cows come home,
and say make it 60c in the dollar, make it 70c  in the dollar, or how about 80c in the
dollar. That is what the socialists would do. All I can say is that the old definition of
socialist—somebody who has nothing and wants to share it with everybody—rings true
to me, because that is what we are heari ng from members on that side. They say we
should put up taxes. It does not matter that doing that will stifle economic growth; they
say we should just keep taxing people.
What this Government did, which should be applauded as far as I am concerned, was
the whole tax shift that occurred last year. We said that we should move away from
taxing the good things in life, like earning income, as quickly as we can and tax some of
the not-so-good things in life, like spending. Consumers can still buy a plasma screen,
they can still spend money on certain things if  they wish, but at least the Government is
16614 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
giving them the chance now to keep more money in their pockets. They can decide what
to do with that: invest it, save it, or be taxed by spending it.
I was gobsmacked again while listening to some speeches in this debate from Labour
members, because one of their mantras ha s been to ask where the Government is
creating all the jobs. I have real news for that lot: the only place where jobs were created
under their Government was in government. I agree. The bureauc racies of health,
education, and just about everyt hing else went through the r oof. In fact, I saw a figure
that in 2008, the increase in floor space for core Public Service offices here in
Wellington—core Public Service office space—was 14.5 hectares. That was the
increase in floor space.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Bob Jones will be happy.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Yes, Bob Jones would have loved that
Government. Accompanying that 14.5 hectares of floor space came all of the
bureaucrats, with their desks,  their computers, and so on. That is where job creation
occurred under Labour. Well, I have sorry news for those members: that does not add
wealth to the economy, and it does not make the place function well. Yes, there is a core
Public Service that is vital.  That is the front-line service: teachers, nurses, doctors,
health services are all at the very front end, doing jobs.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What about Biosecurity New Zealand? Customs officers—what
about customs officers?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Customs officers—gotcha! Absolutely gotcha.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Biosecurity officers?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Yes, biosecurity. But growing the bureaucracy
of the head office and having more desk space fo r all of the dead weight that is added is
just not good enough.
The real generator of jobs in this country is the priv ate sector. If we get the
fundamentals of the economy right and privat e sector companies feel that they can
begin to employ and invest again, they will, and the benefits will flow. Kate Wilkinson
gave a fantastic example of that today at question time, when she talked about the 90-
day probation period. The jury is already in on that measure, because the survey results
show that that has a created substantial num ber of new jobs. It has given employers the
safety to go ahead and hire someone and to ta ke the risk that that person will work out
to be a good employee. So they have and it has worked. The dreadful old, trade union -
driven Labour Party mantra is that the 90-day probation period is evil and we cannot
have it. Well, it has worked, and a lot more people are in work because of it.
One of my other personal favour ites that has come to light in the area where I live is
what Judith Collins has done in the area of  police. Counties-Manukau was in crisis.
Counties-Manukau had more robberies, more  burglaries, and more beatings than
anywhere else in the country on a per capita basis, and Judi th Collins, our Minister of
Police, saw that. She comes from the area, so she knew it firsthand. I can tell members
that the 300 extra police that this Government has delivered into my patch in Counties-
Manukau have made a huge difference.
Our candidate in the Botany by-election is  Jami-Lee Ross. By th e way, he did get
there on time. He got his paperwork in a nd signed up. Jami-Lee Ross—I will repeat his
name, because members will hear it a lot in this Parliament over the coming years—is a
fantastic young man. He is already basking in the glow of things like the 300 extra
police. I went out with him into the Botany shopping centre on the weekend, and a
number of people commented that one of th e best things our Government has done in
the last 2 years is putting the 300 extra police into this area. It has made those people
feel safer; it has made them feel well. Jami-Lee Ross will win the Botany by-election. I
tell members one person who will not even come in third place: the Green candidate.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16615

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: After National’s 9 years
in Opposition and 2 years in Government, that speech by Maurice Williamson is as
good as it gets. It absolutely  shows that National did no  thinking, after 9 years in
Opposition and 2 years in Government, as to what will take this country forward. In
fact, the Prime Minister’s speech given yesterday was lacklustre. It failed to show
leadership on the real issues facing ever yday Kiwis throughout New Zealand. It was a
case of great spin, a lot of mincing, but more smoke and mirrors. The thing about
listening to this debate is that although Government members have used the recession to
hide some of their most blatant objectives, such as selling off State assets, they really do
not have any new ideas to address the real issues affecting New Zealanders throughout
the country: no plan to grow the econom y, no new jobs, and no response to lift young
children out of poverty. Of everything that I have listened to throughout this whole
debate, the failure to articulate that res ponse clearly is the most disappointing. One
would have thought that a Government leadi ng the charge, or so it says, on a brighter
future would be able to spell it out quite clearly—quite clearly.
On this side of the House we have raised  issues that have affected those everyday

items.speaker: New Zealanders
items.text: the rising cost of living, and things like petrol prices, food prices,
power prices, rent increases, rates increases , and mortgages. Those types of things are
affecting real families, and those families are starting to feel the pinch. Every member
of the Opposition will be able to dive into their electorate and give members numerous
examples of where people are starting to feel the difficulties under a recession and a
jobless recovery. The Government cannot articulate clearly enough to the people in
those communities how it will lift their sights above the parapet.
I point to some examples. Rents, for exam ple, have increased in some areas by 9.5
percent. In my electorate in Ng āruawāhia, which would be seen as a very humble
community, we are seeing an average rental of about $320 for a three-bedroom home. In
Hamilton that figure is up to about $350, so there is not much difference. In Raglan, in
Kāwhia, in Whitianga, and in Whangamata people will tell you—and pensioners will
tell you—how much their rates have increased ov er this period of time, how much their
power bill is, and that as a result of their limited fixed in come they are struggling to
make payments. Those are the stories I hear when I go out and about, and I am
concerned. In a recession people generally understand that in difficult times people have
to pull their belts in. I think that is well understood across the House. But when we have
a jobless recovery where those pensioners are starting to see their kids put out of a job,
having to take redundancy, and with no job prospects in their immediate community,
the whole whānau starts to become a little bit stressed.
General practitioner fees, for example, ar e going up, sadly. I got an example in the
weekend where an elderly pe rson who is over 80 is paying  $35 to go to her general
practitioner—$35. It is unbelievable. Grant Robertson, our spokesperson on health, is
absolutely right that the amount of money one pays to go to after-hou rs care just does
not stack up, and people put it off until they can afford it. It costs $69 to go to accident
and emergency if one accesses services after hours. People will wait, and sometimes
waiting makes all the difference between bei ng in hospital and having something more
critical wrong. That is the type of choice people are making.
I will read a real-life story from a consti tuent; she will not mind that I am reading
this. Ann Newland, who lives in Taupiri—I do not know her—talks about the pressures
on her family about the cost of living. She sa ys: “The health system has become a joke.
Engari, we are not la ughing. To make a decision to go to the doctors has become a
burden. Knowing you have to go to the doctor s but there are other things you have to
buy like kai, pay bills like the power, have petrol in the car, and trying to m eet the needs
and wants of your children, going to the doctors  gets moved right down the list. Due to
16616 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
the price of the doctors, one puts their own well-being last. I have  experienced in the
last year that if you have money, people wi ll jump to help you, but if you don’t have
any money or not enough, nobody really want s to know, except the Salvation Army,
may God bless them. And when it comes to our  young people, well, that is a really sad
reality of what is happening. Unskilled, la ck of motivation, some have no dreams for
their future, and some of this is to do with  the education system. There seems to be no
solution or methods to help whā nau with their young people, who are already feeling
the burden by society.”
We hear the Minister for So cial Development and Employ ment talking about all the
good things that are happening in the area of youth employment. Yes, Job Ops and
Community Max are short-term opportunities,  but they are just that—short-term
responses to some very challenging needs of  our young people. We need to invest in
their skills. We increased the investment in Modern Apprenticeships training, which
was a long-term investment to ensure that we  were lifting the skil led workforce of the
next generation. Under this Government th at is not happening. Community Max is a
short-term response to the long-term challenge  of making sure that we invest in the
skills of our young people. Quite frankly, on the youth unemployment front we are
sadly lacking in the wa y we are meeting the needs of many young people—M āori,
Pacific, and Kiwis alike—throughout the whol e country. We have to do better on that
front. I was quite dismayed at the fact that the Minister did not s how any lead on what
the opportunities might be in terms of pathways beyond Community Max into further
training and tertiary study. In fact, in the tertiary sector we see many universities having
to turn students away, and polytechs as well are under pressure in terms of their
enrolments because of the policies put forward by this Government.
In early childhood education we heard a number of representations from the
Government that 80 percent teacher-led services are OK—they are OK—and that
parents would understand that. That is a dire ct quote from the Hon Paula Bennett. But I
tell you what. If National had campaigned on cuts in the early childhood education
sector and parents had a real choice between quality, 100 percent t eacher-led education
and 80 percent teacher-led education, I bet members that every time parents would have
chosen 100 percent teac her-led quality education for thei r kids. Every pa rent wants to
know that they are putting their young peopl e in the hands of people who are qualified
to look after them. Paul Qu inn went on to ask about k ōhanga reo. If he had visited
kōhanga reo they would have told him that they struggle to reach 80 percent M āori
language teachers in their kōhanga, so actually they are not doing too badly by this. But
they will always, always want to try to lift investment to increase the number of
qualified Māori language teachers into kōhanga.
We need to set the record straight becau se, quite frankly, we  have not heard the
Government members articulate its plan to grow the economy, to grow new jobs, and to
stop people getting into the dole queue. One hundred and ten people were released by
AFFCO in Horotiu today. That is not good enough. They are seasonal workers who will
be hurting as a result of a recession that has a jobless recovery, and there has been no
response by the Government to try to address the real needs of real families out there.
Tim
e and time again, Labour has been putting t hose issues in front of the Government,
because, quite frankly, the Prime Minister’s st atement has fallen short of identifying the
Government’s plan. If privat isation is the Government’s answer and National members
are saying that Māori will be the big investors and will cash up their relativity clauses to
be able to invest in State-owned enterprise s, they can think again. Those issues will
have to go back to iwi before any decision like that is made. It is all huff, all puff, more
smoke, and more mirrors. The Government has failed good, working New Zealanders
