and good families in our country because it has not shown a clear plan for the future.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16617

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Here we go: members on the
other side are once again showi ng that they have not learnt  the lessons of the last 2
years. It is interesting to listen to Labour members in this Chamber. They constantly put
the cart before the horse. They keep thinki ng up new ways to spend more money that as
a country we do not have. That is Labour’s solution. It was Labour’s  solution for the 9
years it was in Government, it was the solution that got us into this mess, and it would
be the solution Labour adopts at the end of th is year if it gets back into Government.
That would be a disastrous situation for th is country. In fact, it would be economic
vandalism.
Let us look back in history to the so-cal led boom times of the previous Government,
when we had runaway consumption, governme nt spending, and property speculation.
We had a tradable sector th at was in reverse for 5 years. Labour members never talk
about that situation, but that is actually what was going on. Inflation hit 5 percent just
before Labour left office. We were in r ecession in this country before the global
financial crisis came, and when the global financial crisis came, the tide went out. As
Warren Buffett is fond of saying, when the tide goes out, we see who is swimming
naked. The previous Labour G overnment was swimming naked and it was not a pretty
sight. As well as that terrible thought, when  we became the Government we inherited a
decade of deficits projected forward for 10 years because of Labour’s horrible increase
in spending. In the last 5 years of the Labour Government, it increased spending by $2.8
billion more every year. So it was $2.8 billi on the first year, then $2.8 billion plus $2.8
billion the second year, and then $2.8 billion plus $2.8 billion plus $2.8 billion the third
year. That is correct; Labour managed to push up Government spending by 50 percent
in 6 years. Labour Government members were economic vandals then and they are
economic vandals now.
The National Government has come up with a very strong plan to build for stronger
growth in this country. It is interesting that Labour members cannot decide whether they
do not like the plan or that National does not have a plan. They are still flip-flopping
between those particular lines of Opposition argu ment. It is either that they do not have
a plan or that they do not like the plan, but  they cannot make up their minds. We have a
very strong plan. Let us be blunt; Labour  members do not like it because it is the
solution for real growth in our economy. They do not have those solutions. They
ignored them for 9 years when they were in  Government, and they want to ignore them
again and to go back. They talk about foreign ownership. They want to go back and
hock themselves off to the foreign banks so they can spend some more money and make
themselves more popular in the short term—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How much are you borrowing?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —in exactly the same way they did when Mr Robertson
was in the Prime Minister’s office. They  were spending money like there was no
tomorrow. Labour members just want to go back and do that again at the end of this
year. Thank goodness there is no sign that the people of this country will fall for that a
second time. There is absolutely no sign of  that. Members on the Labour benches will
have to come up with a new songbook, because there is no sign that the people of this
country will fall for that rubbish twice.
We have a plan to build for stronger gr owth, and it starts w ith building stronger
Government accounts. We have to have tighter  fiscal control, which will stabilise and
reduce our Government debt and which will le ad to lower exchange rates and interest
rates over the cycle. Opposition members will  not do that by having a little group get-
together and saying it is terrible that the exchange rates are high; it is actually done with
practical economics, which takes the pressure off the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates
and for exchange rates to rise. Those guys in Labour do not understand that.
16618 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
The second thing is that we have to build exports in this country. We are a trading
nation. Members opposite forgot about trading for 5 years. We have to get back to
focusing on building exports. How do we do th at? We cannot just magic companies out
of thin air with a task force, which is basically what Labour tried to do over 9 years. We
have to send out talented Ministers like Mc Cully and Groser to lead our discussions on
free-trade agreements, which we are doing. As I said, we have to get the exchange rates
right, and we have to encourage business and give business confidence. How do we do
that? We have to show we understand business. We have to build  business confidence
by controlling the costs of doing business and by reducing red tape in the business
sector, like with the Resour ce Management Act, the Building Act, and some of the
things that have been done in local government in Auckland . We have to deliver more
competition in the utilities market, like el ectricity, which Mr Brownlee has been
working on. We also have to deliver things that provide flexibility in the labour market,
encourage employers to employ, and give pe ople the opportunity to  have those jobs.
People will look back on the debate about the 90-day probationary period and ask what
all the fuss was about, because it created great jobs in this  country. People will not be
interested in the ideological rubbish from the Opposition.
We have to build infrastructure for growt h. I heard the pending leader of the Labour
Party, Mr Andrew Little, on Radio New Zealand last week.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: He’s got to get into Parliament first.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, he is on Radio New Zealand, so I suppose he is
almost there. He was saying that the Government should build some infrastructure.
Hallelujah! Hallelujah to Mr Little! The Government is investing massive amounts in
the national electricity grid and massive amounts in the roads of national significance—
indeed, according to the Greens, way too mu ch. We are investing in the KiwiRail turn-
round plan and in ultra-fast broadband and rural broadband—a whole range of things. In
fact, we have ring-fenced some spend—alt hough past Governments have said they
could not afford to spend on infrastructure—to commit to that infrastructure so that
when we come out and get str onger growth, we do not have the bottlenecks that we had
going in. That is the foresightedness of this Government.
We also have to build skill s for growth. This is where Labour members really are
telling porkies with all this rubbish about the Government cutting this and cutting that.
The Government is spending more on early  childhood education than has ever been
spent before in this country. That is a simple  fact. It is a simple  fact, and no matter how
many times Labour members say that it canno t be true and that the Government is
cutting it, all they have to do is look at the books. We have more places in tertiary
education in this country than we have ever had. We will have 16,000 or more places
than there were 3 years ago. Who was in Government 3 years ago? It was Labour.
Labour was in Government 3 years a go, and there were 16,000 fewer places at
universities than we have today.
We are building skills for growth and we are building savings and investment. The
plan is to lift minority stakes in State-ow ned enterprises. Labour is against that too.
Labour members think that somehow the St ate-owned enterprises will be sold off
overseas. They have a little problem there wi th percentages, for a kick-off, because 51
percent in Government ownership is more th an half—at least, it was when I went to
school. It really is time they sorted out their maths in that respect. At least 51 percent is
being held by the Government of the day. As the Prime Minister says, priority will be
given to New Zealand investor s so that New Zealand mums and dads can share in the
upside for these companies. It gives these co m panies the opportunity to invest overseas,
which they cannot do now. It  really is a win-win for all parties, except for the
ideologically bound members over there on the Labour benches.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16619
We have a plan. Labour does not like the plan. Labour wo uld rather we went away
and did not have the plan. Labour’s plan is to spend more money. Labour’s plan is to
find a money tree and to just keep cutting the money off the money tree. That is the
extent of its plan. It is economic vandalism.
In the first month of this year—this elec tion year—the leader of the Labour Party
shot right through the roof on the economic desperation inde x with a couple of billion
dollars of promises for more spending. This  was before the end of January. He is
making promises worth over a couple of bill ion dollars yet he has no idea where it is
coming from. He has some plan to soak the ri ch or something like that. Of course, he
does not realise that labour mobility was anot her thing that killed the economy through
the 2000s, with the 39c tax rate that sent a whole bunch of people overseas. But that is
OK; he is proposing something like a 50c tax rate  for the top earners in  this country, so
we would lose all the people we need fo r our hospitals and sc hools. We would send
them all overseas. This is remarkably reminiscent of Labour in the 2000s. There is no
surprise there, because those members from  the previous Labour Government are all
still over there and are all running the same song. In fact, they are fighting the wrong
war. They were fighting the war when they  all had money to burn in 2005. They were
fighting not the last war but the one before it, and now they have to wake up and get
into the second decade of the 21st century. They are acting like economic vandals.
Labour members are also being xenophobic. I heard the Leader of the Opposition say
yesterday that it was outrageous that some Germans had bought a little bit of rural land
in the South Island. That shows the desperation of this Opposition. Those members have
to work out that New Zealand is interested  in how we grow the economy, and we have
to do that before we start working out how to spend the money that we do not have.
This Government has a plan to build stronger growth. This Government has a plan to
build a brighter future for this country. Ne w Zealanders support th e plan, and that is
what we will be focusing on this year.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: He mihi nui ki a koutou katoa. Today I will
talk about education; something the Prime Minister mentioned several times in his
opening speech yesterday. He probably did not want to talk about education, as his
Government has such a woeful track record, but he had to, because, in a country with
nearly 25 percent of young people unemployed and high rates of illi teracy and poverty,
we cannot ignore education. What  did the Prime Minister talk about? He talked about
cuts to early childhood education, he talk ed about the shambolic national standards
policy, and he talked about opening up our schools to corporate management in the
form of public-private partne rships. This Government’s education policies are failing
our young people.
Let us start with early childhood education. All the evidence shows that nothing
could be more important than investing in early childhood education. Overseas evidence
shows that for every $1 we spend on early ch ildhood health and education, we save up
to $3 immediately and up to $17 by the time the child enters adulthood in reduced
health, justice, and other spending. We do not  get that kind of cost-benefit ratio from
any roads of national significance; in fact, we get negative returns. But the Government
is not interested in making a meaningful investment in our children’s future. This
Government has cut funding to early childhood centres with the most qualified teachers,
actively discouraging the goal of having all our  children taught by qua lified teachers in
the early years, and we w ould never get away with th at in schools—never. Those
members can bandy around the $1.4 billion figure for funding all they like, but the
reality is that parents are already pulli ng their kids out of early childhood centres
because John Key’s Government’s cuts mean they can no longer afford the fees. I know
this because centres are ema iling and calling me every day. This Government’s cuts to
16620 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
early childhood education are failing our chil dren, they are failing our families, and we
will all pay the price in the long term. Early childhood education cuts do not heal.
I will also talk about national standards. John Key is still clinging to this flawed
policy, despite all the evidence against it. Never mind the international experts who say
that national standards do not produce the best educational outco mes for our children.
Never mind the 38,000 parents who signed a petition expressing concern about the
impact of national standards on their ch ildren. Never mind the more than 200 schools
that have refused to implement the standa rds because they are concerned about the
rushed way they have been developed and rolled out. Never mind the New Zealand
principals who have formed a campaign ag ainst national standard s because of their
concerns about what they will do to schools and kids. Never mind the voices of children
and young people and what they want out of education.
It is too easy for politicians, and even parent s and teachers, to forget that those most
affected—young people—have strong opinions and valuable ideas about what they need
from a real education. I have always valued the opinion of students as much as that of
parents and teachers. That is why I starte d a high school students’ union when I was 15
years old. Even now I cannot forget the bored om and frustration of being a high school
student in some of my classes, and I was a relatively privileged P ākehā girl whose
family ate Western literature for breakfa st. The education system was designed for
people like me, but many thousands of young people going through it are not like me,
and their voices are important.
That is why when I came into Parliament  in 2008 I set out to  find out what young
people need from a real education. I called this the real education project. Over the
course of 2 years, I have visited 17 school s and learning centres around the country and
have spoken with young people directly. I aske d the same questions at every meeting:
what young people love about school, what they hate about school, what they need to
know, and what a real education would be lik e. I launched the findings of this project
last week in my report What is a Real Education?. Strangely, nobody raised the issues
of National Certificate of Educational Achievement versus the University of Cambridge
International Examinations, or national st andards. Nobody saw assessment as being the
central issue for their learning. All the young people from all kinds of cultural
backgrounds, no matter how alienated from school, wanted to learn and wanted literacy.
They were crystal clear about what the barr iers were to their learning, and they knew
what they needed from teachers to help them progress.
The young people I spoke with stressed the importance of the three Rs, but they were
not reading on its own, or writing, or ar ithmetic. They talked about respect,
relationships, and relevance. They wanted  their opinions and th eir culture to be
respected. They wanted good relationships w ith teachers and other students. They
wanted an education that is relevant to th em in terms of both content and methods of
learning. Recognition of their culture, language, and identity were particularly important
to Mā ori and Pasifika students. Also, the four th R that many of them brought up was
resources. I will never forget students at a public school asking me whether it was true
that some schools had swimming pools. There are vast disparities in the levels of
resources available to students at different schools. These kids were amazed to hear
about a private school I had visited in Auckland that had a heated swimming pool so
that students in new wetsuits could learn kayaking on warm water.
The idea of a free education was very important to the young people I spoke to. They
were not preoccupied with our aspirational jargon and m easuring methods. They were
preoccupied with what it feels like to have someone teach them respectfully and with
passion, and they identified some great teachers in their lives. However, I will never
forget the boy who said to me: “How can I learn if the teacher hates me?”. We might
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16621
well ask John Key how our kids can learn if  the Government does not value them—and
a few Aspire Scholarships to private schools will do nothing to change that.
But it is not our kids the Government values; it is big business and it is narrow
ideology. Instead of listening to the views of young people, John Key’s Government is
preoccupied with a privatisation agenda , or, to use the new euphemism, a mixed-
ownership model, which can be applied to schools. The Ministry of Education did a
cost-benefit analysis of public -private partnerships in ed ucation that showed it would
cost up to $6 million to set up the public-pri vate partnership model and would save just
$800,000 over 30 years, which is hardly a grea t investment. The business case has been
found wanting, yet we can expect the tenders fo r the first public-private partnerships in
our schools to start in the ne xt few months because this Government values free-market
ideology over all else. The Green Party ha s consistently opposed any moves towards
public-private partnerships in our schools a nd, for that matter, in other key areas—
unlike the Labour Party—and we will continue  to do that. The international evidence
and the Government’s own business case show that public-private partnerships have no
place in our schools. Of course, this could all be moot if we sign up to the Trans-Pacific
Partnership and find that we have to allow overseas contractors access to all kinds of
public contracts, or risk being sued.
These education policies are failing our young people. Combined with the signalled
attacks on welfare, the failure to make th e minimum wage a livi ng wage, and the move
to restrict university access, they will widen the gap between those who have the most
and those who need the most. But what di d we expect from a National Government?
We should not be surprised by these policie s, but we should not pretend, as John Key
does, that he has the underclass in mind. Let us be honest and just admit that increasing
inequality is seen by this Government as the natural or der. Much could be done in the
area of education to close these gaps. I think particularly of students with what they call
special needs, children with disabilities, fi ghting for inclusion. I think of the children
whom I met on my discussions around the c ountry talking about bullying, homophobia,
and racism, and calling for a respectful envi ronment—an environment where they felt
that it was safe to call for a real educati on. They are not obsessed with employment, but
they want practical skills for a real world, taught in a respectful manner.
We could start with a Te Tiriti - based analysis of our education system, because
there are issues to resolve there, and then we should also commit to universality of
access for everyone. From early childhood th rough to high school and university,
universality is better at targeting the vulnerable than particular niche policies that sound
nice in the media but do nothing for the ove rall vulnerability of more and more poor
families in need. But, in fact, if we were to do that, we would have to admit something
very fundamental—that it would have to matter more to spend that money in education
than to build roadways of national significan ce, and it would have to matter more than
tax cuts for our mates. Kia ora koutou.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: On reading a children’s book over
the Christmas holidays I came across a fantastic  quote: “It is our choices, Harry, that
show what we truly are, far more than our ab ilities.” It is our choices that show who we
really are; this Government has made the choice to invest in e ducation. We will not
tolerate one in five children leaving school unable to read, write, or do maths anywhere
near the level they need to succeed, both as  individuals and in employment, as the
previous Labour Government did for 9 long years. The 2009 Programme for
International Student Assessment results that  w ere released before Christmas showed
that our top 5 percent of stude nts are up with the best in th e world. As a matter of fact,
they showed that our top 25 percent of stude nts are up with the best in the world. But
the gap between our top 5 percent and our bottom 5 percent is the worst of the top-
16622 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
performing countries, and the gap between  our top 25 percent and our bottom 25
percent is also the worst of those top-pe rforming countries. The reading achievements
of our 15-year-olds have remained unchange d for 10 years, and maths achievement has
remained unchanged for 6 years.
There is no doubt that we have a very good education system, but this John Key - led
National Government has made the choice to ensure that it becomes a great education
system. We can do that only by addressing the needs of those children who are being
failed by the system, and who have been failed consistently by the previous Labour

items.speaker: Government
items.text: the one-in-five kids who do not learn to read and write and do maths, the
50 percent of young M āori who leave school without even  passing National Certificate
of Educational Achievement le vel 2, and the 37 percent of Pasifika children who also
leave without that same qualif ication. It is the very qualification that we know is the
minimum they need out in the wider world if  they want to go on to further training,
become an apprentice, or go on to furthe r employment. This Government, under John
Key, has said that that is simply not good enough. We have made the choice to make
changes.
The Labour Government actually knew it needed to make some changes, and I refer
to comments from Labour education spokesm an Trevor Mallard in  1998, who said “A
national system of benchmark testing was needed so principals and teachers could
significantly raise standards in schools and he lp New Zealand to regain its status as a
world leader in education.” In 2000 that same person, who was then Minister of
Education, said “This Government is going to make a difference. We want high
standards, not low standards. We want tests that occur week by week and are reported to
parents regularly, rather than the 4-year approaches taken by the previous Government.”
That sounds familiar—it sounds familiar. So what happened? Well, that Government
backed down. It made the choice to kowtow to its union mates instead of toughing it out
for the sake of the kids. It made the choice instead to put quite a lot of money into a
programme for just a few schools. It was a very effective programme, but it was so
expensive there was just no way that it coul d ever reach enough schools to truly make a
difference.
Well, this Government has made the c hoice to introduce national standards in
reading, writing, and maths, and to get system -wide change so that children right across
New Zealand will benefit. Amongst my Ch ristmas correspondence were a couple of
comments from principals. One says “We had been working with the staff on
moderation of writing for the last three years and we used that experience to provide
guidance for staff in all three standards. It was still a challenge for some but we do need
to move out of our comfort zone to raise the standards of teaching.”—a fabulous
principal! Another one said “We have reported against the National Standards twice this
year and the achievement of students in the second part of the year was exponential and
amazing—almost unbelievable. These benchmarks actually focus teachers on deliberate
and targeted teaching which leads to improvement.”
As the economic crisis bit hard on our comm unity, this Government made the choice
to stop funding middle-class a dults to learn Moroccan cook ing, gardening in the wind,
wine tasting, and the like; instead, we funded places for the growing number of
disengaged youth. Two thousand Youth Guarant ee places last year were provided at
tertiary institutions around the country, and we added another 500 this year. In fact, it is
almost 700. These places provide school-l evel qualifications for young people in a
tertiary setting. They  include some pastoral support,  and we are seeing some great
results. We are re-engaging young people for whom school seemed irrelevant. The
Government made the choice to go out to the education sector for ideas to provide better
training opportunities for those kids who work  better when they are working practic ally
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16623
with their hands, making something. We call th em trades academies. We promised five,
but we made the choice to fund eight, which are opening this year, and another four are
lined up to open next year. They bring th e resources and the expertise of schools,
tertiary institutions, industry training, a nd workplaces together to meet the needs of
students—not of the system but of the students.
Finally, this Government made the choice to address behaviour and truancy. Students
cannot learn if they are queued up for most of the day outside the principal’s office, or if
they are wagging downtown. The Positive Behaviour for Learning: action plan ,
designed and overseen by the education sector itself, was originally given $45 million,
but in the last Budget I added another $15 m illion to that. It focuses on a few effective
programmes that work with parents, teachers, and schools. There are currently 119
programmes running around the country for pare nts; almost 2,000 parents will take part
this year. We are targeting 7,000 teachers, w ith a third of them coming from the early
childhood sector, and almost 200 schools are cu rrently participating in the school-wide
training.
Truancy—well, this Government made the choice to face the problem. The first thing
we did was reinstate the survey that the previous Labour Government had cancelled
because it did not want to know—it did not want to know. What did we find? We found
that 30,000 kids were missing on any one  day from school—30,000. That is the
population of my home town, Gisborne. For goodness’ sake! Students cannot learn if
they are not at school, so this Governme nt made the choice to double the funding to
fight truancy. We are building capacity in sc hools to track and monitor students. We
have funded a determ ined reduction in the number of kids who are completely
disengaged from school, and we are working to get them back into the system. We are
trialling several initiatives around the count ry and evaluating their results. We are
working closely with the sector and social services to build our knowledge of what
actually works, and we have given the district truancy services a pay rise. I think that is
the first one they have had since Labour came into power 10 long years ago. We have
also started to lift the quality of alternativ e education to get bette r results for students.
That sector got extra money for the first time in 9 years.
So this Government will work with the education sector, unions, business, the
community—with anybody who is in terested in getting better results for kids to make
our education system great. And Dumbledore, whom I quoted at the beginning, was
right, because it is our choices that show who we are, who we  really are, and this John
Key - led Government’s choice is to get better results for kids.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: As the newest member in Parliament, I must
admit to having had a sense of expectation about the Prime Minister’s speech yesterday.
Yes, I did have a sense of expectation. As it was the first of what will be many Prime
Minister’s speeches I will si t through, I thought I might not  agree with everything, or
anything, of what the Prime Minister had to sa y but that I might finally get an idea of
where this Government is taki ng us and what cour se it will take to try to improve the
lives of New Zealanders. But what a di sappointment. It was a huge disappointment,
which would have been shared around New Ze aland by Kiwis in th eir homes, because
we got nothing. We got absolutely nothing. Yesterday Phil Goff got it 100 percent
right—2 years on and this Government has no ideas. It has run out of ideas. It has no
ideas and no plans and has created no jobs. What a disappointment it was that it took 22
pages for John Key to tell us nothing. Twen ty-two pages—what a waste of 11 pages of
A4 paper.
National has reverted to the tired old policie s of old. It has gone back to the vault,
pried it open, and what do we have? We have  State asset sales, cuts, and slashes.
National has reverted to those, because it has no ideas and no plan.
16624 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
The fact that this Government has no ideas  and no plan just shows how out of touch
it is with normal Kiwis—with the people w hom I see at the Porirua markets, who go
down there to make sure they can get the best  deal because they are struggling to make
ends meet, and with the parents whom I saw at the early child hood centres who are
worried about their kids’ educ ation. The Government is ou t of touch with the people
whom I saw at the league, who all came up to me and said that they are really worried
about what is happening with prices rising faster than wages.  This Government is out of
touch.
Those people are worried about simple thi ngs, such as their power prices going up,
which will only get worse when this Government sells off our State-owned power
companies, and rising petrol prices, which ha ve gone up to nearly $2 a litre thanks to
John Key’s increase in GST to 15 percent.  Their grocery bills are going up, because
John Key broke his promise not to raise GST. Those people are also worried about early
childhood centres, and what the cuts mean fo r them. Some parents in my electorate will
be forced to pay $25 more a week for each child, and some of those parents have three
children in early childhood centr es. I wonder where the Minister  will tell those families
to get that money from.
Yesterday we all sat here, hoping for a bit of  help and a bit of hope for the people in
our electorates, but what did we get? We  got nothing. What did the people who were
sitting around the kitchen table, looking at  the bills piling up and wondering how they
will pay them, get from John Key? Well, they got no ideas, no plan, and, for lots of
them, they have no jobs, because this Gove rnment does not care about them. It cares
about the 42 percent of tax cuts it gave to the top 10 percent of earners. The
Government does not care about the people who are sitting at the kitchen table,
wondering how they are going to pay the bills. Those families are struggling because
this Government has done nothing about jobs. It has no ideas and no plans to create
them.
Members of the Government sit over there thinking they are the great guardians of
the economy. Well, great; last week unemplo yment went up to 6.4 percent. There are
158,000 Kiwis now without jobs—158,000 breadwinners who cannot support
themselves or their families. There were 1,700 more unemployed in the last quarter just
in Wellington alone, and, unfortunately, I am su re that plenty of those people are in
Mana. They have become unemployed because  this Government has no ideas and no
plans to create jobs.

items.speaker: Government members will sit over there and say
items.text: “Hey, we have done heaps.” What
have we had? We have had a cycleway, la unched at the hastily arranged Job Summit in
early 2009.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: The big idea.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It was to be a huge idea, with thousands of jobs. Well, excuse me,
but I do not think I have seen thousands of tourists riding around on any cycleway, and I
have not seen any jobs created by that scheme, which John Key was praising to the hills
in early 2009. National has done nothing but window dressing.
What does that mean in the community? It  means plenty of hurt, but no hope. On
Monday I visited a number of community serv ices in Porirua that are picking up the
pieces of this Government’s lack of plan and lack of ideas. I travelled up to Family
Budgeting Services, which is flat tack. The people there told me they are seeing more
single men—the kind of people that Mr Key is trying to attract when he goes on Radio
Sport. He is doing nothing for them. The budge ting service told me it is seeing more
breadwinners, and more couples where both people are without jobs. There is no end in
sight for those people, because there are no jobs to go to because this Government has
not created any.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16625
If we pop up to the citizen’s advice burea u, it tells us that people are getting more
desperate. When a factory closes in my electorate, there are deluges of people asking for
help, but what can we do for people when there are no jobs to go to? Not one thing. We
say: “Hey, just sit around and wait for a job to come.”, but this Government is not doing
anything about it. It has no ideas and no plans to create jobs.
What the Government should be doing is investing in education, training, and
innovation, and giving tax cuts to people who need them by stimulating the economy
and feeding that money into the economy so that the people who need help are
stimulating the economy and creating more jobs. Did we get that? No; we got 42
percent going to the top 10 percent. This Government is not he lping those Kiwis who
are struggling at the moment.
This Government also does not care about gi ving our kids the best  start in life. The
Minister of Education’s example of early  childhood education cuts is the perfect
example of that—$400 million is being taken out of early childhood education. I tell the
Minister that those kids mi ght not have voices, but thei r parents do. We have been
visiting those early childhood centres, and we know that the pa rents are unhappy. I am
not surprised the Minister is not visiting those centres at the moment . In my electorate,
as I said, one centre is increasing its fees by $25 a week. One family has three kids, so
that is 75 bucks a week.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: That’s outrageous.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It is outrageous, and that Minister  is doing that. It is outrageous,
and the penny has finally dropped for the Minist er. It is outrageous that early childhood
education fees are going up, and she is doing that. That family has three kids at the
centre, which will cost $75 mo re a week. I ask where they will they get that money
from. What goes? Will it be the food or the clothes? I ask which bills pile up on the
kitchen table at the end of the week so that  those parents can give  their kids the best
start in life—so that those kids can go to early childhood education between the ages of
2 and 5 and have the best start in life. What  is going to go? What is going to go? Those
are the questions I am facing in my electorat e because of the decision this Government
is making.
Some early childhood centres need to be congratulated, because they will not be
increasing their fees. The kindergarten association needs to be congratulated, because it
will not increase its fees. But the kids are indi rectly affected, because we must ask what
else will go. Cuts in staff mean teacher to student ratios will go through the roof. We
can kiss goodbye the trips for the kids, because they are not happening any more. We
can kiss goodbye the building maintenance for the kids, because that is not happening
any more. We can kiss goodbye the resources. What will we have? Will we have early
childhood centres with no crayons and paint be cause this Government is so stingy and
does not want to invest in early childhood education? That is the reality of what is going
on.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What was the investment, Kris—what was the investment this year?

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: This is about priorities, and we will make early childhood
education a priority because we care about th e future of our kids. Government members
know the cost of everything but the value of nothing, as many of my colleagues have
said today. Those centres will be cut ting staff, cutting resources, and deferring
maintenance for our children in the earliest stage of their lives.
The Kapi-Mana News got it right this week with its headline “ECE cuts a ‘backwards
step’,”. What did we get from the National list member for our ar ea? She stated that
“more effective spending in the tough economic times will benefit in the long run.”
What a load of rubbish. We know that fo r every dollar we spend on early childhood
education we save $17 down the line, and I think that is a great investm ent.
16626 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
On this side of the House we care about our kids. This Government has no ideas and
no plan to create jobs. This Government has no ideas and no plan to  give our kids the
best start in life. This Gove rnment has no ideas and no pl an to help struggling Kiwis.
But we do.

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: I think there is at least one
thing on which I agree with the previous speak er this evening, Kris Faafoi, and that is
the importance of education. He is absolutely right. He is Pacific, I am M āori, and we
come from a tradition where so me of our people have not gained the best out of the
education system in the past. Also, we are from families who value education. That is
hugely important, but it is also why it is a great shame that he has joined a party that
went out of Government in 2008 with one in five M āori leaving school without literacy
and numeracy. Over 50 percent of Mā ori boys were leaving school without National
Certificate of Educational Achievement leve l 1 after 9 years of a Labour Government.
So, yes, I can identify with the previous sp eaker, absolutely. He is Polynesian; I am
Polynesian. Our families put great store on educ ation, but he has joined a party that put
nothing, absolutely nothing, into the edu cation of young Pacific Islanders and M āori. If
it had, we would not have inherited the results it bequeathed to us in 2008.
When I say that Labour did that, I like n it to committing a crime. Labour committed
a crime because it ran surpluses and it was in a position to invest more in the education
of young Pacific Islanders and M āori and it did not. It is  no wonder that when the
recession came 2 years ago, young Māori and Pacific Islanders were hit hard by the loss
of jobs and by the inab ility to get new jobs. Where were those young M āori and Pacific
Islanders 9 years previously? They were coming through a school system that Labour
was in charge of, and Labour refused to use the surpluses to build the knowledge, the
learning, and the skills of young Pacific Islanders and Māori.
National has a plan. It is important to have a plan—absolutely. Our country can do so
much better, and it will do so much better pursuing the plan that John Key, leader and
Prime Minister, unveiled last week and which he presented to this House earlier in the
week. The plan is not rocket science.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It definitely isn’t that.

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: No, no. It is easy to u nderstand and I will tell
members why it is easy to understand. Thousands of New Zealand families have to
manage their household budgets daily. That is what they have to do. In the same way,
this Government will grow and manage our eco nomy so that we can get the best out of
it for those young Pacific Island and M āori children who missed out—many are young
adults now—when that member’s party was in  power. The plan is this: people cannot
spend what they do not earn, we cannot live o ff the borrowings of others, and we have
to pay our way in the world. That is what hous eholds have to do, and that is what we as
a country have to do. Interestingly, up at Waitangi, where one would expect Māori to be
saying “W
ell, Georgina, what are you guys do ing?”, many of them understood the plan
we outlined. We must save. We will build savings, we will boost investment, and we
will boost exports.
The other thing I found interesting is the way the previous speaker talked about jobs.
He said that there were no jobs, as if we can just grab jobs out of the air. The economy
has to be rebalanced to make sure there are permanent jobs, so businesses will invest in
jobs. To do that, we have to  support businesses. They shoul d not be loaded up with red
tape and regulation. National has cleared a lo t of that. We do not get more jobs by
creating a bloated public service and that is  what that party did in Government. It
created a bloated—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What would you cut?
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16627

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: We will not cut anything—and we have not,
particularly in areas where we have return ed value for money to taxpayers. There will
be no cuts where we can see that front- line services are hugely important to New
Zealanders. They deserve to have services where value ca n be extracted, and not to
have, as under the previous Government, a pub lic sector that grew just willy-nilly to
create jobs, and New Zealanders were liv ing on a whim. Labour had New Zealanders
living on an idea that  they were doing well when actua lly the country was going down.
That was 9 years of a Labour Government. So basically we build  a stronger economy.
We build the conditions that will get growth in the economy—something that that party
does not know anything about. Without growth we cannot get the jobs—there you are.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Where is your plan for growth?

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: New Zealanders understand what we are doing.
We will encourage and build savings. We will spend only what we earn. Sue Moroney
can shake her head. She does not understand the basics. We will build the skills and the
knowledge of our youngsters.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: How?

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: By investing in education—members heard the
Minister of Education previously—by bu ilding the skills and knowledge of young
people, young New Zealanders. They are our future.
The member Kris Faafoi know s that within 25 years one out of every second baby
born in New Zealand will be either M āori or a Pacific Islander.  That is why we have
invested $91 million—nearly $100 million—t o specially make sure that the
participation of young Māori and Pacific Island children in early childhood education is
increased. They are the future workforce of  New Zealand, and unless we want to see
them have a wasted life, then we have to inve st in their future. That is what National is
doing. That is what National has done. We have put more money into early childhood
education. Anybody who says that we do not care about a good start for young children
needs their head read. That is so untrue. No matter how many times those members say
that this has been cut or that has been cut,  it is not true. I am l ooking at those who want
their Pacific Island and Māori children to have a decent start in life—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Go and visit them.

items.speaker: Hon GEORGINA TE HEUHEU
items.text: Yes, members can go out to some of the church-
based early childhood education centres, whic h know exactly the im portance of this
plan. We will support them. We will build on what is happening in that sector.
I turn to national standards. Teachers ask why we are forcing national standards on
them. I ask what the composition of M āori children is in their school, how they are
doing, and whether they are succeeding. The teachers cannot tell me whether they are
succeeding. So I say that our national standards will make sure that children do not
leave school without literacy, numeracy, and the learning they need to come out of
college with qualifications and to go on to tertiary education.
There is a plan. It is a very simple plan, but it is a very important plan. People cannot
spend what they do not earn. We must en courage savings. We will build savings, we
will encourage investment, and we will build assets that grow the economy. That is
what we are doing. In my 2 years as Minist er for Pacific Island Affairs I have been
hugely, hugely impressed by the willingness and the understanding of parents, mums
and dads, who want to work with our Govern ment to make sure that their children do
well. Of 60,000 children who started school 2 weeks ago, 12,000 of them will leave
school without basic literacy and nume racy unless we do something pretty
determined—those are the children we are aiming for. We are doing that right
throughout all sectors: education, health, a nd the justice system . Our Addressing the
Drivers of Crime programme is  in order to ensu re that we stop th e flow of youngsters
16628 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
into the courts—and as Minister for Courts that is of huge interest to me. We are
growing initiatives that will make sure that we cut the numbers of youngsters who enter
the court system, and cut the number of youngsters who end up in prison.
National is doing a lot. We have more to do. The potential for New Zealand is huge,
and we can realise that potential only through our young people.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: During this debate a lot
of members of the House have focused on what  the Prime Minister said. Of course, that
is appropriate; it is the debate on the Prim e Minister’s statement. But I will not focus on
the Prime Minister, because, as my colleague Kris Faafoi said, the statement was 22
pages that said absolutely nothing whatsoever.
I will focus on one of the tr ue acolytes of the National Party, David Bennett, because
last night David Bennett managed to say in 10 words what the Prime Minister could not
bring himself to say in 22  pages. Members can check Hansard and have a look at what

items.speaker: David Bennett said. He said this
items.text: “The Govern ment is not there to make your life better
…”. That is what David Bennett said. It is fantastic that we finally have a National Party
member who is prepared to tell the truth a bout this Government’s agenda. I will say it
again: Mr Bennett said: “The Government is  not there to make your life better …”.
Ain’t that the truth, because we have seen cuts to front-line health services, and we have
seen cuts to early childhood education. I will pause on that for a moment.
The Minister of Education says that if parents are not happy, they should change
centres. If the early childhood centre where parents send their kids is putting its fees up
because the Government has cut its funding, then they should change centres. Well,
guess what! The parents of kids who are going to kindy, to early childhood centres, send
their kids to a particular centr e because it is part of thei r community, or because it is
close to where they work. They do not want to have to change centres; they should not
have to go to the other side of town. The Mi nister just shook her head nonchalantly, as
if it is no big deal, no problem . The Minister is saying th at she is not there for the
parents of children in kindy or early childhood ce ntres. She would prefer that they go to
the other side of town if their centre has to put its charges up because she has decided to
cut the funding.
We have seen increased GST. We have seen the Government let unemployment go
through the roof. It has no plan  to grow the economy. It ha s no plan for jobs. It has no
plan for manufacturing. It has no plan for clean technology. It has no plan for New
Zealand’s future. Why? Because David Bennett is right: the Government is not there to
make people’s lives better. What the Government has done is create public debt. Net
public debt was zero when the Government came into office. It has let that skyrocket,
too. Why has it done that? Because it wants to  sell our State-owned assets. That is why
it has let that debt get out of control. This  Government wants to sell off assets that
belong to every New Zealander. John Key got up and said the reason he was doing that
is that we need to take ownership of our future. I think the Prime Minister has been
hanging out with Prince William a bit too much. He is clearly using the royal “we”,
because it is only people like John Key who will be able to take ownership of New
Zealand’s future if we continue to sell off our State assets.
John Key’s message to hard-working New Zealanders is simply this: “The National-
led Government is not working for you.” Whom  is it working for? Well, it is working
for the tiny number of people who have the most—those with millions of dollars in the
bank who receive interest hand-over-fist—becau se they got the tax cuts. John Key got
$1,000 a week in tax cuts. Natio nal is working for the foreign banks and the finance
companies. They will be the ones that get to  buy shares in our State-owned assets; they
will be the ones that take over ACC. They will be the ones that sell us health insurance
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16629
because this Government will not take its responsibility seriously and will refuse to
provide proper health care.
This Government is certainl y not there for people who need proper health care. It
should not cost a parent in Ne w Zealand 20 percent of their weekly budget just to take
their child to the doctor after hours. But t hose parents are not a priority to this
Government. The cost of going to one’s general practitioner, no matter what time of day
it is, should not be going up—but it is. That means it is harder for everybody to see their
doctor—everyone except, of course, the very  few whom this Government is working
for. Wages went up 1.7 percen t last year, and general prac titioner fees increased by 6.5
percent in 2009. They went up again in Octo ber last year when National’s GST hike
kicked in. But that does not matter, because this Government is “not there to make
people’s lives better”—David Bennett said so.
Hard-working Kiwi families know that the Government is not working for them.
This Government is working for someone else. The Government is planning to cut $750
million from health over the next 4 years. Th at means cuts to the services hard-working
Kiwis rely on. It means hard-working New Zeal anders will not get the treatment they
need. What will National say then, if it is still in  charge? It will say that health care is in
crisis and that we need to privatise, priva tise, privatise. The insurance industry will be
licking its lips at that idea, just as it was when Merrill Lynch told it to expect a $200-
million-a-year windfall when National privatis es ACC. That is whom this Government
is working for.
In health care there is a test coming up very soon for this Government. We are
negotiating a free-trade agreement, the Tr ans-Pacific Partnership, and a number of
American pharmaceutical companies are putting the pressure on to make sure the cost
of medicines in New Zealand goes up. Who will the Government go into bat for? Will it
be New Zealanders? Will it be hard-worki ng Kiwis who appreciate the fact that
pharmaceuticals in this country are inexpe nsive? Pharmac has provided the cheapest
medicines anywhere in the world. Or will it be the overseas corporations? Will it be
“Big Pharma”? Is that who the Governme nt will go into bat for? That is a huge
question, and people will be asking that as we get closer to those negotiations.
The track record of this Government is no t good. If someone is in need of health
care, that person’s costs have gone up and hi s or her services have been depleted. If
someone is a parent who has a child in early childhood education, that person’s costs
have gone up and the quality is going down. Those people are facing higher prices at the
supermarket. There is a greater  chance that they have lost their job. There is no plan—
there is no plan.
That is why constituents are coming into my office, such as the two who came in last
week. One has just completed her teaching qualifications. She has applied for 25
teaching jobs and has been turned down for every single one. She is not lazy, and she is
not sitting on her backside at home. She is out there working extremely hard to try to
find a job, but there are none. What is the Gove rnment’s message for her? It is: “We are
not working for you. You are lazy. That is why you do not have a job.” That is the
Government’s message for people like her. I met a gentleman who was made redundant
last year. He gets no support from the Govern ment. He is out there working hard to try
to find a job, but he feels labelled and stig matised by this Government, because it is not
working for him, either.
This Government is not working for New Zealanders; it is working for someone else,
and it is about time that it came clean. It is about time that we heard more people like
David Bennett get up and tell it like it re ally is. Here are his words again: “The
Government is not there to make your life be tter …”. That is true; the Government is
working for foreign finance companies, for foreign landowners, for insurance
16630 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
companies, and for people who have the ver y, very most—the tiny, tiny percentage in
this country who have the very, very most. National is working for its mates.
This Government needs, maybe, to take a leaf out of the Opposition’s book, because
we will invest in skills development. We will support New Zealanders to make the most
of themselves. We will invest in early chil dhood education. We will make sure health
care services are available for everybody, accessible for everybody, and of the very
highest quality.
New Zealanders need to know that the Na tional-led Government is not working for
them; it is working for someone else. New Zealanders need a Government that is
working for them, and that is a Labour Government.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Happy New Year, Mr Deputy Speaker. I
just say how much the member for Palmerst on North is looking more and more like my
colleague Tim Macindoe with every passing day.  Perhaps he wants to have a chat with
his leader about some strategies to remedy that.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Or Murray McCully.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Perhaps Murray as well—and many others in the
House, I have no doubt.
As I was gathering my thoughts and myse lf to come from the office to the
Chamber—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Where do you get your Grecian from, Michael?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Being such a young fella, I do not have to worry
about these things yet. I was thinking as I left my office to come to the Chamber that the
last thing I wanted to do was to leave my speech notes behind, which happened to be
the last thing I did do before I came to the Chamber, but there is just such fertile ground
on which to build an election year speech.
I really did think that I was parachuted into some parallel universe a couple of weeks
ago when I heard—
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker Bark er, I know you have been
waiting with bated breath through the adjournment to hear what happened to me a
couple of weeks ago.
I had the distinct feeling that I had transferred into some parallel universe following
Labour’s announcement of tax cuts, which it  would borrow heavily to fund. That is
right—a tax-free zone of $5,000 for every sing le New Zealander, including the very
rich, the spouses of the very rich who work part time, and the middle-income earners
whom Labour claims it wants to help. Labour  will have to plunge New Zealand more
deeply into debt to fund it. It will cost in  the region of $1.55 billion to fund that and the
dropping of GST on fruit and vegetables.

items.speaker: Mr Goff said in his speech
items.text: “I won’t make any promises that I can’t keep or that the
country can’t afford.” Then he mumbled something about loopholes and taxing the rich.
He said that Labour would deal with the l oophole in respect of th e ability to offset
unrelated income from salary, through loss attributing qualifying companies I presume,
from rental property losses. I have news for the Labour Pa rty. That loophole was closed
in Budget 2010. The tax losses that were ge nerated are largely fr om non-cash offsets
through depreciation. What happened to depreci ation? It has disappeared. So there is
nearly no help there.
The other so-called tax loophole that will be  closed is in resp ect of high-income
taxpayers who, according to Labour, are not paying their way. We will be returning to
Labour taxing the rich, but Labour members cannot have read the Tax Working Group
report very closely. The report said the prob lem with the tax system was that it was
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16631
distorted and misaligned—that the top rate of income tax of 39 percent and the trust rate
of 33 percent created arbitrage. So National has fixed the loophole, but Labour wants to
bring back the loophole—an envy tax.
But this time Labour says it will not tax the rich, it will tax the really rich. Who the
really rich are and what rate of tax Labour  will charge them, heaven only knows, but it
would have to be around 60c in the dollar or more. Last time Labour’s envy taxes hit
the uber-rich, like teacher s, the police, doctors, and nurses, the really rich went to their
tax accountants, but the docto rs and nurses went to trav el agents and booked their
tickets to Australia. It would happen again if Labour got the chance. At this rate the $1.5
billion tax cuts would be funded out of pie- in-the-sky loophole closures that do not bear
up to close scrutiny and raise very little offset revenue to fund it.
So if there are no cuts to spending, there is only one other way to fund those cuts and
that is to borrow. The Labour Party is prom ising to borrow to pay for tax cuts. Voters
will have a choice at the end of this year—more envy taxes, more spending on
bureaucracy, and more debt to be repaid by futu re generations, or fisc al discipline, less
bureaucracy, a plan for growth, and a determination to reduce debt, not to grow it.
I will paraphrase from a recent speech where one leader said we need to “freeze
annual domestic spending for the next five years … this would reduce the deficit …
This freeze will require painful cuts. Already, we’ve frozen the salaries of hardworking
federal employees for the next two years. I’ ve proposed cuts to things I care deeply
about, like community action programs.” Who said this? Was it some extreme, right-
wing leader, hell-bent on destroying social  policy? No. It was Barack Obama in his
State of the Union message. So if Mr Obama gets it, if countries  with similar debt
profiles, like Ireland, Greece, Spain, and Port ugal, get it—left-wing administrations
proposing austerity measures far beyond anything this Government is proposing—what
is up that the Labour Party completely failed to get it? The spending frenzy went on for
the last 3 years of Labour’s administration, and if Labour gets back on to the Treasury
benches, God forbid, Labour proposes to continue it. But it simply cannot continue.
Whatever the policy question is, the answer  cannot be to burden this country with
more debt. When we are talking about how to improve the quality and volume of our
health services, the answer cannot be more debt. It is a l azy approach—a tax-and-spend
approach that is past, populist policy. We need to think smarter about it, and that means
looking at quality control, looking at systems and processes, looking at new
technologies, and avoiding waste and error.  I know that is possible in our health
services. They are actually do ing it. The results of the last  couple of years of excellent
progress in elective surgery discharges and reductions in waiting times for emergency
treatment and cancer treatment is evidence of it. But there is plenty of scope for more. It
needs to be done because the answer to th e question cannot be to burden this country
with more debt.
Our early childhood education funding change s are a very sensible example of not
doing that. But Ms Moroney, Labour, and their union mates are running around like
Chicken Little, saying that the sky is going to fall in because of a small change to the
staffing model that the Government is prepar ed to fund in these st raitened times. At the
same time they are ignoring those very positive contributions for our Māori and Pasifika
kids—Mr Davis knows exactly what I am talking about—some of whom around the
country have no more than about 60 per cent access to early ch ildhood education. He
will sit by while his party promises to send about 1,000 early childhood educators to the
wall, for the sake of an ideology that says an experienced parent or grandparent, or an
experienced teacher aide or caregiver, cannot possibly look after a child under the age
of 5. It absolutely beggars belief. They insult those parents and grandparents. It is stupid
and it is ide
ological.
16632 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
But nowhere more does this ideology get in  the way of doing the right thing than in
the belief that the only way for a business to  run is if the Government is the only one
running it. The best example of that is ACC. We have waited nearly 2½ years for
Labour to apologise for the $7.2 billion hole it left in the accident compensation
scheme. But the public should not hold its breath. I am very proud of the scheme, but it
is not a sacred cow. It is not something that can be hermetically sealed for all time.
Choice is a good thing. It will re duce costs, and levy payers will have the choice to stay
with ACC if they wish.
On Monday night I attended a function in Hamilton when the city’s economic
development agency launched the various  TechNZ research and development
investment programmes. It was a great night.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: What were you doing there?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I happened to have been in Cambridge that day. The
Government has invested more than $320 millio n in those programmes. They are a hell
of a lot more effective than a lazy research  and development tax credit programme that
benefits tax accountants more than it be nefits the economy. Mr Goff trumpeted the
release of Labour’s action plan for jobs and growth, and the only thing he could think of
to announce was the return of the research and development tax cr edit. It was the one
lazy lever that Labour could think of.
But there is not just one lever to pull.  Real, meaningful growth comes from
innovation funds. The 90-day probation period  was recently found to have had a very
positive impact on small businesses. We have kept Hobbit jobs in New Zealand, we
have committed billions of dollars to infrastructure development, we have reduced the
barriers to doing business by unwinding red tape, and we ha ve built on the free-trade
agreements we had already developed to drive the export-led recovery we need. We will
campaign on competition and partial floats. Ther e is a plan. It is a really good plan on
many fronts, and I will put up that plan against the tax, spend, and borrow promises of
the Labour Opposition, any day.

items.speaker: Hon DARREN HUGHES
items.text: I rise to speak against the confidence motion
that was moved by the Prime Minister yest erday. Now, more than  ever, New Zealand
needs a Government for the many, not a Government for the few. The speech we heard
yesterday from John Key was all about governing for the few in our country, at the
expense of the many. We need a Labour-led Government in New Zealand that can make
sure there is a plan for the future in our country, not just a gimmick for tomorrow
morning’s New Zealand Herald or Dominion Post. We need leaders in this country who
understand that prices are going up faster than wages, whatever statistics, dodgy as they
may be, the Government chooses to put forward. Families in this country know that
when their wages come in every week, they are being outstripped by the prices that are
going up at the supermarket, the petrol st ation, and in so many other areas where
families need to be able to spend money.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: Hon DARREN HUGHES
items.text: When the member for North Shore says that that is not
true, we know how far out of touch Gove rnment members have become when they
believe that prices are not going up faster than wages. They are, and if we ask anyone in
a supermarket they will tell us that that is true. It is absolutely true. [ Interruption] Hekia
Parata stood in the Mana by-election and was all in favour of low and middle income
families just last November, but within 6 w eeks of being in Cabinet she now says it is
untrue that prices are going up faster than wages. But people listening to this debate
know that instinctively. It is true in thei r eftpos accounts, it is true in their cheque
accounts, and it is true as they struggle to pay off the cr edit card they ar e having to put
their groceries on. It is staggering how out of touch this Government has become.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16633
We need higher incomes and better jobs in New Zealand, and we need to put
children at the centre of our social policy. Th e re-election of the Prime Minister should
not be at the centre of what Government policy is about. We do not need a Government
that is cutting the social wage as this Government is, and making a mockery of the Kiwi
idea that we should all be able to get a fair  go. What is clear from this debate, and from
the Prime Minister’s speech ye sterday, is that after 9 year s in Opposition and 2 years in
Government, the party opposite has no plan fo r what to do with, and for, New Zealand.
The results are in; having no plan has faile d. On the key social and economic indicators
that people know are real for their lives—not on opinion poll results—indicators such as
unemployment figures, wage-increase figures, and cost of living pr essures, having no
plan has failed our country and it is fa iling our people. Stumbling from gimmick to
gimmick might have got the Government thr ough the first 2 years, but it will not get it
through this year. We need a Government for all the people.
The only ideas that were in the Government’s plan yesterday were either more
gimmicks or ideas that went back to the cryp t, back to the idea th at we should sell off
our assets one more time, just in case we we re not totally convinced  of the failure of
doing that the first time around. It pays to have a memory like an elephant when it
comes to our country’s assets, and members opposite have forgotten just what a disaster
those things were.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: All you’ve got is memories.

items.speaker: Hon DARREN HUGHES
items.text: I hear Dr Mapp speak up. It is no wonder he is retiring,
because he is embarrassed about being part of a Government without a plan. He thinks
it is a disaster.
I listened to the Prime Minister tell us  why asset sales would be a good idea.
Apparently Kiwi mums and dads could then own the assets. I thought every single Kiwi
mum and dad did own them, along with every brother, sister, aunty, uncle, grandma,
grandpa, and cousin—every single person in this country owns them. But there was the
killer: John Key said that the Air New Zealand model wa s what we should base our
asset ownership on, because that gave us the best of both worlds. But which party
opposed the buy-back of Air New Zealand? It was National, wh ich here in this
Parliament fought tooth and nail against the buy-back of Air New Zealand. But it turns
out that if we are prepared to wait just 7 years, National can tell us whether it is in
favour of buying back an asset. The problem is  that we have to check in for our flights
slightly before 7 years; we have to check  in for our flights 15 minutes before we go.
Being in Government is about making tough  decisions, and when that tough decision
was there National opposed the buy-back of Air New Zealand. Today, of course—just
stop and wait—7 years is how long it takes th e conservative forces in New Zealand to
catch up and say that the Air New Zealand model gives us the best of both worlds.
We are now told by the Government, wh ich has spent 2 years making appalling
choices for our country and our people, that we are back to  “tina”, which means “there
is no alternative”. Speaker after speaker from the Government is standing up and saying
that the Government is having to do things because it is borrowing money, it has made
all those bad decisions, the economy is in the cart, and it has to carry on now with its
economic and social decisions. National MPs sa y “tina”; well, this is New Zealand, this
is Aotearoa, and in this election campai gn Labour members say “tama”, which means
“there are many alternatives”. The alternatives being put up by Phil Goff, Annette King,
and the Labour team are the sorts of things that can make a major difference to the lives
of New Zealanders up and down this countr y. We can now see the effect of having no
plan at all.
First of all, we were going to be the international hub for financial services. That was
the first thing we were going to be, but that sort of fell apart. In fact, the last time we
16634 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
heard John Key talking about Ireland, he was saying we should model New Zealand
after Ireland. That is what he said. He went up and down the country saying we should
be the “Celtic tiger of the South Pacific”, and of course National MPs got up, as they
do, unthinkingly, and repeated all those lines from the research unit that John Key had
said. We were challenged, as a Labour Govern ment, to make sure we were like Ireland
and that we were following the Irish model. No w I sit here in this debate and listen to
the same MPs—or to a few new ones, who know nothing about political history—get up
and say that we cannot run New Zealand like Ireland because that would be a disaster,
and that we would go to hell in a handcart if we followed Ireland. But that was exactly
what National members had said should happen.
Then there was going to be a cycleway; we were going to cycle our way to success.
Well, that has been a complete disaster, so  now our economic recovery is based on the
brand new idea of privatisation, an idea that has never been  heard of before. We will
privatise our way to success. That will stop all the problems that we have in our
country, and power bills will go down because  we will sell power companies. Yeah,
right! There is not a single pe rson who can honestly say that power prices will be lower
for families and pensioners as a result of privatising our power companies. What the
Government is saying is absolutely ridiculous.
We are listening to members opposite say that taxes are a major issue for the
campaign. In fact, that party opposite reduced the entire economic debate in our country
to one that was simply about ta xes. It cut taxes more than we could afford as a country,
and now we are borrowing money because of its decisions. Eighteen months ago I used
to listen to the same speech 58 times over, when members opposite complained about
borrowing $250 million a week. That was a terr ible figure, and nothing more could be
done in New Zealand because we were borrowing $250 million a week. Now the figure
is $300 million a week, which is $2.5 billion extr a a year. What is the difference? It is
the tax cuts that the Nationa l Government put in place an d that we could not afford.
Now the Government is saying that $300 milli on a week is the ceiling, and that we
cannot afford any more than that. As this  economy continues to go down the gurgler we
will have to borrow more because of that Government’s decisions, and because having
no plan has not worked for our people. It  is like saying that we should extend the
mortgage, buy more new items, put more on the credit card, and get more hire-purchase
agreements, then go and ask the boss to pay us less in salaries and wages to pay for
those things.
Members opposite inherited a Government net debt of zero. Do members know when
that had last happened in New Zealand? Ne ver! From 1854, when we  started having a
Government, to the time of the Clark-Culle n Government, there had never been a net
debt of zero, but that is what National inherited. Those memb ers on the other side of the
House also inherited the lowest unemployment rate in the world, but they have ruined
both figures. Yet they get up in this Chamber and try to argue that nothing else can be
done, that there is no alternative, and that although 68,000 people are out of work it is
their fault. They say that Labour created j obs only by hiring people in the public sector.
Is that how 68,000 people have been added to the dole queue  since the last election?
Have 68,000 extra people all come from the public sector? I do not think so; I do not
think the National Government is aware of what it is doing.
It is in education that we see the party opposite making bad choices for our country.
Education is in a mess. Cuts in early childhood education have been hitting families this
week and last week, with families having to pay more per week per child. The best
single start we can give any young New Zealander is a quality public education that
invests in our people to make sure they can reach their potential, and unleashes them for
a big, brave world in which they can, as indi viduals, achieve and be  the best they can
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16635
be. Members opposite have a timid view; they believe in cuts, and they believe that
early childhood education is baby-sitting. I tell National members something: parents
are involved as volunteers at primary schoo l as well, so under th e logic that we are
hearing from National members, which states  that because parents and grandparents are
involved as volunteers in early childhood edu cation we need to have only 80 percent
qualified staff, we might as well have only 80 percent qualified staff in primary schools.
When the Rugby World Cup comes along later this year we would never say let us have
only 12 qualified professional All Blacks and three really interested and avid fans of
rugby to help them out and make up the full 15. We want 100 percent qualified All
Blacks to win the Rugby World Cup later th is year, and we should have 100 percent
qualified staff working with parents and grandp arents to start making sure that kids get
the best start at ages 3 and 4, if we want to make this country the cleverest it can be. But
members opposite are not interested in that; they see early childhood education as baby-
sitting.
The Government is putting costs on families, prices are going up faster than wages
possibly can, and the social wage is being br oken. Education will be a big issue in this
campaign, because Labour has a vision for a bright future.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: There was a huge amount of fuss and
bluster from the previous speaker, Darren H ughes, a person who had a bit of a cheek in
saying that my colleague Wayne Mapp shoul d feel embarrassed about being in this
House because he is retiring. I think th at Darren Hughes should feel very, very
embarrassed about being in this House—his electorate voted him out, yet he is still here.
I tell him to explain that to his people. He was full of criticism of the Government, but
he was a member of the Cabinet that co st this country $700 million in the failed
purchase of Tranz Rail. That is how smart he is!
Then what did that man’s Government do? It  left us, I say to Mr Hughes, with a $2.5
billion underfunding problem in the ACC account. There was a shortfall there, and in 9
years of that man’s Government what did he do as a Cabinet Minister? He increased the
number of Public Service employees by 50 percent. What an absolutely appalling
Cabinet Minister he was! That  speaker has, this evening, fo llowed a long line of other
Labour speakers who have—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: Communists.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Yes, they are communists, as Dr Mapp says, and basically their
plan for this country is to borrow and hope. That man, his party, and his colleagues are
about borrowing and hoping. As  my Prime Minister, John Key, said 2 days ago, the
annual cost of Labour’s spending promises is  $5 billion and clim bing. A succession of
Labour speakers, followed by Mr Hughes today,  could explain to one person in this
country how they are going to pay for this plan.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: We are going to cut your Public Service pension.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: I say to Mr Hughes that his lead er spent 7 hours in a beauty salon
over the summer and that was just to get th e estimate for colouring his hair. Every time
Phil Goff opens his mouth in this House he  confirms Labour’s borrow-and-hope recipe,
but it will add hundreds of millions of dollars to Government borrowing.
This man, Darren Hughes—Mr “Whatever He  Is”; a list MP in Levin—and his
leader would saddle New Zealand with more de bt to foreigners, who would have to be
paid back—guess what—with interest. That is Labour’s plan. They borrow m
ore, and
then New Zealand gets a credit downgrade.  What will that do? That will push up
interest rates for Kiwi families, it will push up interest rates for business, and it will cost
jobs. How dumb is that!
In a state of the nation speech last month, Phil Goff announced a $1.3 billion promise
to make the first $5,000 of annual income free of tax, including for the wealthiest New
16636 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
Zealanders, like me and like every person in th is House. He wants to give us all a tax
cut. It is the most expensive way of providi ng a benefit in this c ountry. It is totally
dumb, I say to Mr Hughes. It is totally  dumb, I say to Mr Goff. Although many New
Zealand families are careful with their money and pay their own debts, Labour is
promising to do the exact opposite. But they  will not do it with their money. Oh, no!
They will do it with taxpayers’ money.
At least Mr Goff has done New Zealanders a service early in the electoral year. He
has contrasted Labour’s lack of a plan, l oose spending, more borrowing, and high taxes
with National’s responsible plan to bring debt under control and to get this economy
growing faster.
