Darren Hughes lives over the hill from me. My community suffered for 9 long years
under Georgina Beyer and Hele n Clark, and we are in a r ecession now because they
squandered the good times. [ Interruption] They squandered their money in the good
times. Why are our businesses in recession? I say thank you to Georgina Beyer, Helen
Clark, and Cabinet Minister Darren Hughes—they did a w onderful job squandering our
taxes.
The farmers in my electorate, and the manu facturers in Dannevirke, like Metalform,
and the Fonterra milk powder plant in Pahīatua need world-class infrastructure to ensure
that they can compete efficiently and pr oductively on the global ma rket. I am really
supportive of Minister Joyce and his efforts to  ensure that our schools in Porangahau,
Eketāhuna, and Pirinoa can get on board the broadband train and make the most of this
great technology. Minister Joyce has ensured that the work gets done.
I heard Georgina Beyer promise for 9 year s that the Labour Government would fix
the Rimutaka hill road, and what did it deliver with Helen Clark? It delivered nothing.
What did Mr Hughes deliver  in Cabinet? He deliver ed nothing—absolutely nothing.
Steven Joyce has not only fixed the Rimutaka hill road, as everybody can see when they
drive by, but is also working on the highway  between Woodville and Dannevirke in my
electorate. Furthermore, he is working ve ry hard to help KiwiRail become more
competitive, and I know from the Greater Wellington Regional Council that the
Wairarapa train service is the most profitabl e in New Zealand. In my electorate we are
also providing help to people with leaky homes. Why? Well, what did Labour leave
behind?
The Wairarapa and Hawke’s Bay farmers in my electorate, who earn this country’s
foreign exchange, were left, after 9 long year s of poor governance, with dial-up Internet
compromised by electric fence interfer ence and no plan. Industry paid the
telecommunications levy for improving rural broadband but there was no accountability
about how it was spent.
Labour set up a $325 million broadband investment fund, which was all about giving
piecemeal grants to operators. It was not about building a solid broadband network.
Labour called for tenders before the 2008 elec tion. Did I see anything come of it in my
first term in this House? Not a jot. Th is country’s Prime Minister, John Key, is
swapping a $325 million grant scheme for a $1.8 billion investment.
When one looks at science and innova tion, with my good friend Wayne Mapp, we
see that a new ministry, the Ministry of Science and Innovation, has been established. It
will be a far more effective bridge between sc ience and industry in helping to turn great
ideas into export successes. Wh at did Mr Mapp inherit when he became the Minister in
this area? He inherited a system that  was overly complex and bureaucratic, and
businesses were not investing enough in rese arch and development. Tax credits were
open slather for accountants, with no guarant ee that the money would be used for
research.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Dr Mapp is on to it.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16637

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Absolutely, he is on to it.
In the last 12 months, through the work efforts of Murray McCully and my colleague
Tim Groser, this country has signed a trade agreement with China, which has generated
about $850 million of new exports to China. Th at is the same as finding a market the
size of Indonesia, and who does that help? It helps every farmer.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Labour started it.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Labour started it, but Labour did not finish it, did it?
I was particularly pleased to be on the G overnment select committee that dealt with
the Rugby World Cup legislation. As we ha ve seen in the last 2 months in the
Wairarapa, the air show run by Tom Williams  brought in about $8 million to our area,
and the La De Da concert brought in huge amounts of money and saved the Masterton
south area from total economic devastati on over the summer period. The Rugby World
Cup will do the same for the Wairarapa when we host the Georgian team. This
Government has a plan. The plan  is to increase the accountab ility and the efficiency of
the bureaucracy, grow the economy, promote exports, and get rid of waste.
This afternoon I heard a lot of comment s from Opposition members about cutting
early childhood education. I can tell members that that budget has actually been
increased by $400 million and that although there are some readjustments, we are trying
to help the people at the bottom of the pile, no t at the top. I can tell members that in my
electorate fewer than 40 percent of child care centres are actually impacted by that
change. When I have written about it in the paper—

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: So that’s all right, is it? That’s great for parents.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: I can tell the member that it ha s strong community support. I have
had only complimentary comments, except fr om two people in the Labour Party who
are busy writing to the local newspaper on that  issue. This Government has a plan and
this plan is going to be implemented over the next 6 years. Thank you.

items.speaker: JO GOODHEW
items.text: The constituents in the Rangitata
electorate have already real ised that 2011 will be a big year for New Zealand, and not
just because of the Rugby Worl d Cup. It will also be a big year because decisions will
be made that will have a big impact on our  economy, our prosperity as a country, our
health, our safety, and the future for today’ s job seekers, for tertiary, secondary, and
primary students, and even for those who are younger than that. This year will be a year
of stark contrasts.
This year the National Government—led by popular, hard-working, pragmatic real
person John Key—will need to pull out all th e stops to prevent New Zealand heading
for, at best, a mediocre future, and, at worst, a similar fate to countries such as Spain,
Greece, Portugal, and Ireland—those countries  with very high foreign indebtedness.
This year the National Government will tr y to improve our economic performance in
order to get the books back in order, b ecause continuing to borrow $300 million a week
and then gifting that debt to our children is not OK. We have had to borrow to blunt the
sharp edges of the recession, but now is the time to get the books back in order.
I send out a warning to the Labour Opposition: New Zealanders are far from stupid.
They knew when they had had enough of th e nanny State and the arrogant Clark era.
New Zealanders knew that we enjoyed economic golden weather for 9 years under
Labour, but only now are New Zealanders rea lising how hard it is to climb out of
recession when so much of Labour’s legacy—and it is not a case of no plan; this is
about Labour’s legacy, I say to Mr Darren Hughes—is economy-sapping, unproductive,
and promotes dependency on the State. That is what Labour left us. Labour spent way
too much time on calculating how to spend money to create a culture where the voters
depended on the Government’s largesse, but New Zealanders saw through that in
November 2008.
16638 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
Unfortunately, we hear the same clap trap now over the fiscally prudent
announcement to raise the minimum wage by 2 percent to $13 an hour. Labour tells us
it should be higher; even the Greens are tell ing us it should be higher. Guess what! We
wish it was higher too, but  the trade-off for a $15-an- hour minimum wage would be
almost 6,000 jobs lost. Labour’s rhetoric is si mply an endless promise to spend, without
an admission that to spend more than Na tional is doing now simply means borrowing
more—more than $300 million a week.
While I am on the subject of promises to  spend lots of dosh, let us look at the
borrow-and-hope Phil Goff and his Labour spendt hrifts. Phil Goff’s state of the nation
speech revealed two things. Th e first of these was a decide dly unrealistic sense of the
challenges facing New Zealand, and the genesis role that his party actually played in
creating those challenges. The second was a staggering $1.3 billion promise to make the
first $5,000 of annual income tax-free. I have  a message from my constituents for Phil

items.speaker: Goff
items.text: my constituents just love that polic y. The students who work in the holidays say
thank you for thinking of them. The part-time workers whose partners are on really high
incomes say thank you very much to Mr Goff  for thinking of them. The kids who work
in their parents’ businesses say thank you for thinking of them. But I have a question for

items.speaker: Phil Goff
items.text: are they really the people he meant this policy to help? It is not the way he
talks about it, anyway. It is  yet another stunning example of Labour throwing a dart at
the dartboard of vote-catcher ideas without any thought of targets or of what a policy
should actually achieve. Since that speech, Labour’s interim leader has promised
another $400 million for early childhood education—but more about that soon.
Last year Labour promised to take GST off mangoes, ras pberries, bok choy,
boysenberries, and peas and carr ots—as long as they are not frozen. That was at a cost
of $250 million a year. Added to that is  a whopping $2 billion a year on the
Superannuation Fund, so this temporary Labour leader has amassed more than $5
billion a year in promised extra expenditu re. But New Zealanders  are not dopey; they
know we cannot afford that. If we venture down that track, then we are assured of worse
than negative watch from Standard and P oor’s. So maybe we need to remind Labour
that a downgrade means paying higher interest rates in return for all of that. I tell the
spendthrift Labourites to explain that to New Zealanders.
While I am on that thread, there is anothe r woeful example of chucking buckets of
money at a sector without analysing whethe r it really, truly im proves the lot of New
Zealanders who really need Government assistance. National is spending the most
money ever—$1.4 billion—on early childhood edu cation, but we are actually targeting
projects to markedly improve participation in  it. That is a far cry from the ill-targeted
Government policy under Labour that would have seen 1,000 early childhood education
centres close because they could not meet the mandated 80 percent registered teachers.
That was going to be a whole lot of kids who would have been out of luck, was it not?
In my electorate some centres face choices as to how they will have to tighten their
belts, but many are unaffected by National’ s policy change to fund only up to 80
percent of a centre’s teachers being registered teachers. Some centres are actually
nowhere near the 80 percent; some have a mix of qualified and unqualified staff, or
qualified and training teachers.
The public should also get their heads around the thought that quality staff is really
important, but the children attending the cent res are aged 0 to 5 years, so a mix of
education and childcare is what happens in t hose places. Surely there is a role for those
who are trained in childcare as well as registered teachers. A mixture of skills—

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Jo, this is about our children.

items.speaker: JO GOODHEW
items.text: Well, childcare is very important—very important, I say to Ms
Chadwick. A m
ix of skills and qualifications can still mean there is quality early
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16639
childhood education. What is wrong with re gistered nurses working alongside nurse
assistants and enrolled nurses, or lawyers working alongside law cl erks and interns? I
can think of many examples of groups of pe ople who have different skill sets working
together to complement each other’s skills. So Labour should just quit the slogans and
admit that its focus was never on maximising participation in early childhood education,
but that National’s actually is.
I mentioned at the beginning of my contribution this evening that there will be a stark
contrast between the offerings to voters on 26 November. On one hand we have a
National Government that knows that bui lding a brighter future will entail
determination and some tough calls. Nati onal’s vision is for stronger Government
accounts, where we will move away fro m the debt-fuelled consumption and
Government spending towards savings, investme nt, and exports. This vision is in stark
contrast to recent proclamations from Labour  spokespeople, which in effect add up to
massive job losses, and all for the sake of  Labour Party ideology. Without the 90-day
trial period 13,000 New Zealanders would not  have had the opportunity of a job.
Labour’s unrealistic time frames for clean ai r would have seen thousands of job losses
in industry, as industry was penalised for dom estic polluters who were not meeting the
deadlines.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: So you’ll kill 500 people instead?

items.speaker: JO GOODHEW
items.text: Mr Chauvel needs to remember that failure to meet a deadline
certainly does not save any lives. Hello? Wa ke up! As I have already said, had the
minimum wage been raised to $15 an hour it would have resulted in 6,000 job losses.
When we add to that more than $5 billion worth of promises, under Labour ideology we
would have increased debt, increased taxes,  and higher unemployment. Is that what
New Zealanders want? I think not.
National is taking significant steps to alter the environment in which New Zealand’s
businesses exist, to allow them, and therefore our economy, to grow. What does it mean
when the economy grows? It means more money for healt h, more money for welfare,
more money for education, and more jobs. It also means more money to spend on safety
and law and order. We are building world-class infrastructure to help businesses
compete. We are building skills and knowledge  for future-proof jobs. We are helping
exporters to produce more valu able products more efficien tly, and to sell those goods
for a higher price. We are giving businesses c onfidence and certainty so they can invest
in new businesses, take on more workers, and pay them more. What a stark contrast this
is to the borrow, promise, and hope approach from the spendthrift Labour Party.
The National Government plans to address all the reasons that New Zealand is not as
productive, as healthy, as wealthy, or as safe as we aspire to be. We have the guts and
determination to tackle the hard issues, li ke a bloated Public Service that grew like
Topsy under Labour at the expense of front-lin e services. New Zealanders instinctively
know that if the biggest business in town is the Government, we  will never build
ourselves a brighter future. In Rangitata a nd around the rest of the country the question
will be about which political parties have the ability and the courage to build a brighter
future for New Zealand, and which political parties will try to buy a brighter future for
only themselves.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: Nothing in the Prime Minister’s speech yesterday gave
me any confidence that John Key, the National Government, its Māori Party supporters,
or ACT have any plan whatsoever for the future , to create jobs, or to ease the cost of
living. In fact, in the time it took for Jo Goodhew to finish her speech, the National
Government borrowed an extra $300,000. It  is borrowing $30,000 a minute. It is
borrowing $500 a second. The borrowing is all to  pay for the tax cuts that this country
cannot afford.
16640 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
We heard Jo Goodhew ask what is wrong with enrolled nurses  working alongside
registered nurses. Well, why do we not just  have volunteer nurses?  National expects us
to have volunteers in early childhood education centres. Why do we not all just go up to
the local hospital and start administering injections? Let us start dishing out pills. Let us
start doing all that sort of stuff. It is the stupidest thing I have ev er heard in this House
to ask what is wrong with having volunt eer nurses going up and administering
medicine.
I also heard in John Key’s speech that he wants to help solve social problems and
improve the prospects of the next generation. I ask John Key how on earth he expects to
improve the prospects of the next generation when he is cutting hundreds of millions of
dollars from early childhood education. For Anne Tolley to stand in the House tonight
and say that that is not happening is a disg race. Anne Tolley needs to crawl out of the
cave she has been hiding in, come up north with me to Kait āia, and visit the early
childhood education centres I visited last w eek on 1 February when their funding cuts
kicked in. She should hear from the peopl e themselves on the gr ound that the funding
cuts are hurting them.
One early childhood education centre up in the far north is losing $160,000 a year—
$160,000. That is being taken from the kids of that particular early childhood education
centre up in Kait āia. We are talking about Tai Toke rau here. We are talking about
Northland, one of the most socioeconomica lly deprived areas in New Zealand. The
Government thinks it can cut $160,000 from that early childhood education centre.
What will happen? That early childhood education centre has two choices. I heard
the Minister Anne Tolley ta lking today about c hoices; this early childhood education
centre has two choices. The first choice is to reduce the education op tions it is offering
the kids. I ask Mr Key how it will improve th e prospects of the ne xt generation if the
Government reduces the education options of those kids. The second choice is to charge
the parents to make up the shortfall in the funding. The parents in one of the most
socioeconomically deprived areas in New Zealand can expect to pay an extra $20 or $40
a week to have their kids go to an early childhood education centre.

items.speaker: Those parents also have choices
items.text: they can c hoose to pay to have their child attend an
early childhood education centre, or they can choose to feed their kids that week. Those
are the choices that parents are being forced to make: food, shelter, and clothing over
early childhood education. Yet the Prime Minister  said in his speech  that he wants to
improve the prospects of the next generation.
It is just ridiculous. The research is adaman t that if we give children the best start in
the years from birth through to age 6, then  we will see improved outcomes throughout
their life at 10 years of age, 12 years of age, 16 years of age,  and through into adult life.
But the Government is cutting the support. Na tional members sit there and defend cuts
to the kids—the little kids in early ch ildhood education, who are the most vulnerable
sector of our society.
The Prime Minister minced up to the marae at Waitangi on the weekend and told
Māori that they have to set aside grievance and take hold of education. Those are the
exact sentiments that I have. We as M āori need to set aside grievance and focus on
education. In my maiden statement I said that  we can achieve more with one generation
of fully educated M āori than we can from another 171 y ears of grievance. I still hold to
that view, and I am glad to hear that the Prim e Minister supports my sentiments.
The problem is that we have seen the Government actually entrench grievance. We
have seen no better example than today at the M āori Affairs Committee, when the
Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill was rushed through the select committee
process with indecent haste and with a full di sregard for democracy. That is saying to
Māori, who absolutely loathe the bill the committee is pushing thr ough, that it does not
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16641
care about their submissions or about their thoughts and opinions on the Marine and
Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. It is saying: “Stuff you! But please do not be angry
with us.”
Another example of the Government ignoring Māori opinions is on exploration rights
and the issuing of permits for oil explor ation off the west coast of Northland.
Exploration permits have been issued for 100,000 square kilometres of seabed in the
Northland Basin. There are 150,000 square kilo metres of seabed off the north-western
tip of Northland in the Reinga  Basin. There are tens of thousands of square kilometres
of seabed in the Rauk ūmara basin. Mā ori have had no say in it. The Government has
said that it does not care that Māori have opinions and interest in the seabed. It is saying
“Get stuffed! But please do not be angry with us.”
The worst grievance that is being perpetrated on the M āori people is that our parents
cannot afford food, cannot afford to pay the rent or the mortgage, and cannot afford to
clothe their kids because the cost of living is  rising so much. That is the real grievance.
That is what is really affecting M āori people these days. So it is a bit rich for the Prime
Minister to mince on up to Waitangi and tell us to put our grievances aside.
He says that Māori should take hold of edu cation. What has the National
Government actually offered in terms of education for Māori? It has offered the national
standards. The national standards will not make a single iota of difference. Bill English
proved that towards the end of last year when he said in this House that over the next 10
years the biggest Government department w ill be the Department of Corrections. I say
to him that if national standards are to make an iota of difference, the Government needs
to address the one child in five who is l eaving school without a qua lification. That will
mean those children will go on to higher e ducation, which means those kids will get
better jobs and will have better social outco mes. We will be locking up fewer kids if
national standards are to make a difference. But Bill English has stood here in this
House and said that over the next 10 years the Department of Corrections will be the
biggest Government department. Bill English has proven that national standards are a
waste of time. He has no confidence in them. They are just another joke perpetrated on
the people of New Zealand by the National Government.
John Key also said that New Zealand n eeds to build up the pool of Kiwi-owned
savings and investment. That is really good, but what happens to all those Māori parents
who are struggling to put food on the table, to pay the rent, and to make the choice
between early childhood education and buying food for their kids? It is an absolute joke,
when Māori are struggling with everyday bills a nd with just buying groceries, for John
Key to say that Māori and New Zealanders need to save. It is an absolute joke.
He went on to say that the G overnment wants to address the drivers of crime. Let me
tell him the drivers of crime: poverty firs t, poverty second, and poverty third. If the
Government wants to address the drivers of crime, then it needs to do something about
addressing poverty. It needs to create jobs. It  needs to come up with a plan that will
actually make a difference for New Zealanders who are out there on Struggle Street and
who are having a hard time just making ends meet. Kia ora.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: That was a wonderful speech from the previous
speaker, Mr Davis, who prior to that speech had a future in the Labour Party. I th
ink Mr
Goff saw that he had a future. But it only goe s to show the one underlying factor I have
picked up from speeches from Labour members in recent days, which is that they
cannot add. I know that Mr Davis was a good te acher in the far north, but his speech
showed me that Labour members cannot add.
In the last 2 days we have seen a whol e lot of choices being presented to New
Zealand—a future of choices. There is a choice between having a balanced, prudent
fiscal position—a sustainable position for my children and gr andchildren to live in in
16642 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
this country in the future—or one where a bank from somewhere overseas comes and
takes us over because we do not have the ability to pay our bills.
Under a Labour Government we would have the situation of another generation of
extreme borrowing, and a crisis would occur.  Under Labour we would have a situation
where we would be borrowing—

items.speaker: Kelvin Davis
items.text: $3,000 a minute you’re borrowing.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: —whatever the amount is that Mr Davis might think is the
right number—another $5 billion a year. Wh at might that mean? Labour members are
telling people not to worry because Labour has a plan. I would like to hear it, and the
public would like to hear it, but we have not heard it. We heard Mr  Darren Hughes talk
earlier tonight about his pla n. He said we should cut Mr Hayes’ Government pension
and that that would save $1 million. That just goes to show us that Labour members
cannot add. The last time I heard, Mr Hayes did not get $1 million a year.
We have heard Labour MPs—and I can talk about the one whom I ran against, Ms
Dalziel—say they would go and get another job if they could but they would not get one
paying what they are being paid now. That shows us the future that the Labour Party
sees in New Zealand.
Today at question time we had a question ab out the decade of deficits that was
coming at the point of the 2008 election. Wh at did Labour members do? They went
quiet, because they knew it was true. They knew that New Zealand was facing a
bankrupt position, which is why New Z ealanders voted in a John Key - led
Government.
Do members know what another $5 billion under Labour would mean to the mums
and dads back home? It would mean a situ ation where interest rates would go up by
about 4 to 5 percent per annum, just like they did in Greece, Ireland, and Portugal. On
the average house mortgage in New Zealand, which is  $150,000-odd, that rise would
shift repayments from $100 to $150 a week, depending on where people live and how
much they borrowed. That is what Phil Go ff will give New Zealand—not 10 bucks a
week from his $5,000 tax-free income but an increase in people’s mortgage that they
cannot afford. That would not be a sustainabl e position. It is not a position that I want,
nor do the majority of New Zealanders, from what we have seen in the polls.
We also heard today the rhetoric about early childhood education. I know a bit about
early childhood education. I have two young kids. I have been through the sector. My
mother was the founder of a playcentre. I went  to a playcentre. I have been involved in
the movement. My children have gone to everything from community-led centres and
parent-led centres through to private centres  with fully trained staff. Do members know
what? Those centres all have positive aspects to them.
In the last 6 months I have visited 16 centres in various parts of Christchurch. What I
heard when I went and talked to those people was that people like choices. They like
having the ability to say that if they are pa rents, they do not care whether they have a
degree, but they want to be able to raise th eir children in some way. That is why we put
in place 20 hours’ early childhood e ducation for playcentres and k ōhanga reos. Under
Labour those centres were discriminated against because they were not run by union
members. If people were running a playcentre or a k ōhanga reo, they did not get the
right amount of money because they were not part of the early childhood education
union. I thought that situation wa s outrageous. That is one of the reasons we are part of
the Government that brought in  equalisation that treated ce ntres across the country the
same. That is what we believe in. We believe that all people are equal.
We have inherited a situation under Labour where 40 percent of the kids in the
country cannot get access to early childhood education—right now it is 40 percent.
There was a meeting 2 or 3 weeks ago in Ch ristchurch that the Labour Party summoned
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16643
me to go along to. I turned up in Christchurch. I had a whole bunch of union people
screaming and yelling at me and saying that we need 100 percent qualified teachers
because that was the right way to do things. I said that that was OK and that was fine,
but I asked who would pay for it. They said  that somebody else co uld pay. That is the
problem with Labour: it is always that somebody else can pay.
The problem we have with the union mentality is that there are not enough people to
pay for all the things it wants them to pay for. I will show members a couple of things.
The wonderful Ministry of Education has this great pamphlet for early childhood
centres about early learning. It states th at young children are r eaders, writers, and
mathematicians. Given the numbers that we have seen from Labour members in recent
times, I think they could do with a bit of ma thematician training. This pamphlet states
that parents, family, and wh ānau are important parts of a child’s learning. It does not
state anything about union members in here . I challenge the Labour  members to look at
this early childhood curriculum for parents at  home and see what it means for early
childhood centres.
We have had record spending in early childhood e ducation this year, more than any
other Government has ever spent. That means 3,500 kids around New Zealand will gain
access to early childhood centres who did not have it previously. I challenge Labour
members to go to those parts of New Zeala nd that are getting money for a new centre
and say that they cannot have that money because a guy down the road wants a better-
quality education and he does not want to pay for it. I do not think that is fair. We will
have 3,500 extra kids accessing early childhood  education in New Zealand because of
this Government, and that is a wonderful thing.
One of the other wonderful things we have talked about is the area of science and
innovation, of which I am a big fan. We have  Dr Mapp in the Chamber. He is a
wonderful proponent of the great work that is being done in this area. We inherited a
ridiculous policy on what was called a tax credit. I will tell members about some of the
stupidity that occu rred under that policy. Every a ccounting firm in New Zealand
thought it was Christmas—every accounting firm. Every senior tax accountant in New
Zealand suddenly ratcheted up his or her rates. They were suddenly making $300,000 or
$400,000 extra in billing, because they were going to anyone who had any form of
research and telling them not to worry about it and that they would fill in the forms and
get them some money and they would take a cu t. That is what we saw. We saw not one
extra dollar of research and innovation, but we saw every accounting firm in the country
make money. I know that that wa s the case, because lots of my friends did it and they
were very open about it.
Under Dr Mapp and our John Key - led Government we have seen a move towards
innovation. We have seen some wonderful move ment in terms of grants to incredibly
innovative companies, a couple of which I have very fond knowledge of. One company
is based on rockets and the other makes jet packs. They are wonderful companies that
have a great future in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: YikeBike.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: And YikeBike. YikeBike is an  innovative biking company in
Canterbury. Those are the sorts of businesse s that will grow Ne w Zealand, create our
wealth, and perhaps give us innovative jobs. The challenge for us is to create real,
sustainable jobs. People will pay taxes, and that will get New Zealand back into a
sustainable position.
I will talk briefly about a series of disast ers that we have enc ountered, particularly
the earthquake in Canterbury. In Christchur ch, where I live, a series of significant
problems has occurred, as members will know. W ith regard to my family, my brother’s
home has been destroyed, my  mum and dad’s home has be en destroyed, and my home
16644 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
has been damaged. Mrs Adams’ house has been damaged. One of the major aspects of
the situation for us is rebuilding the infrastructure of Christchurch. I am looking forward
to the big presentation on Friday, a blessing for the first part of the infrastructure rebuild
in Christchurch.
I will tell members a little thing about so me of the reasons why the people of New
Zealand will re-elect a John Key - led Gove rnment on 26 November. When I was first
elected, a lady called Joan knocked on my door. Joan lives in a State house not far away
from my electorate office—my out-of-Parliame nt office, sorry; I am not allowed to call
it an electorate office—and she had been tryi ng to get her fence fixed for 8 years. She
was a former Labour Party member. She could not get the fence fixed. She had a dog
and a 2-year-old grandchild who kept running through the fence. She could not get it
fixed. I rang the Housing New Zealand Cor poration, which said something about there
being problems, problems, problems and massive  bureaucracy and that it would take all
these forms being filled out before the fence could be fixed. Do members know what we
did? We asked the local people to come down to fix the fence, or we would have fixed it
ourselves. For 9 years Joan had been deali ng with the local Labour MP, trying to get
things fixed. The crazy thing was that we got  it fixed and in 5 mi nutes she went from
being a Labour voter to a National voter becau se we changed a little bit of her life in
some way.
Carol had a different situation. Carol’s heater had gone bung, and she could not work
out how to make her house warmer and better. We arranged to have her house insulated.
She ended up putting an energy-efficient device into her home. The result of that help is
that she thinks the National Government is the greatest thing in the world. For 9 years
she tried to get help from a Labour Governme nt that would not give her help but told
her time and time again that she was not im portant enough and that  she was not of the
right group for it to help in any way.
Those are the reasons why a National-led Government will be re-elected on 26
November. It is all about science and innova tion, investment in infrastructure, smarter
public services, a fairer and better tax system, and smarter regulation. That is why on 26
November we will see a John Key - led Govern ment and a return to prosperity for New
Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: I rise to speak to the Prime Minister’s statement
to Parliament. I listened to the Prime Minister present his speech and I have listened to
the speakers since, and I think I will not be alone in this coun try in asking “Is that it? Is
this the plan? Is this what many New Z ealanders—the overwhelming number of New
Zealanders who are not the rich, and who are struggling with ever-rising prices, with job
losses, and with reductions in income —are going to get from this National
Government?”. Of course, the answer is that, yes, that is what they are going to get—
not much.
There are 265,000 New Zealanders currently jo bless. This document, this so-called
statement, is an insult. It is a document fu ll of platitudes and focus-group-tested spin. I
ask this question of members opposite: does this Government think New Zealanders are
stupid? Well, I can assure those members th at New Zealanders are not stupid and that
they are increasingly seeing through the spin. They are increasingly questioning the
ability of this Government, a Government with no plan, a Government that governs for
the rich and ignores the rest. What does the so-called statement include? It has
privatisation, it has cuts to public services, and it includes bashing beneficiaries—all the
usual things. Maybe they are dressed up in slightly different language, but that is what is
there.
It is outrageous that the Prime Minister and Government speaker after Government
speaker have tried to blame the state of the economy and the ever-burgeoning debt on
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16645
Labour and on the recession. That  is absolutely outrageous coming from a Government
that borrowed to fund tax cuts. It cost $2.5 billion to fund tax cuts for the top 10 percent
of New Zealanders, the very group who did not  need that assistance, and the group who
would not use the money in a way that w ould stimulate our economy. That was from a
Government that has taken a hands-off approach to economic management, and that has
had no plans for jobs or economic growt h. I listened to the Prime Minister on Morning
Report, again spinning the same old line, but the reason there is such huge Government
borrowing is to cover the costs of funding tax cuts for the rich. It is simple; that is what
it is about.
The Prime Minister’s statement will give  no comfort to low and middle income New
Zealanders who are struggling to make ends meet. Some Ne w Zealanders are doing it
harder than others: M āori, Pasifika, young New Zealanders, and women. We will be
making sure we talk to the Minister of Wo men’s Affairs and raise every single issue in
relation to the difficulties that people are fa cing in the job market, in trying to make
ends meet, and in trying to ensure their kids  have uniforms to go to school in and food
in their bellies. There are many, many people like that.
There is no plan in the Prime Minister’s  statement. There are no ideas to deliver
growth and jobs. In fact, there is quite  the contrary. This statement provides a
prescription for job losses in the public sect or, job losses for New Zealanders who work
as public servants. As a consequence, there will be reductions in the services for New
Zealanders that those public servants prov ide. Those losses will be on top of the
265,000 New Zealanders who are already jobless. That is a disgrace.
But what is truly disgusting is that the Government is so obviously twisting the facts.
No matter how many times it is denied, the Go vernment’s own actions have led to the
need to borrow $300 million per week. The Gove rnment’s own actions have led to that,
and the public are getting that message. This  is about priorities; it is about choosing.
The Government chose to make unaffordable tax cuts that benefit a small minority of
New Zealanders, rather than investing in  our people—in skills development, job
creation, and economic development. In other words, that was the choice the
Government made. It was the Government’s priority to give tax cuts to the top 10
percent of earners. It was a choice.
The Prime Minister and all of the Na tional members who have stood up have
asserted that the problem of Government debt is because of the previous Labour
Government or the recession, but they cannot really believe what they are saying. I do
not believe that those members opposite really  believe that. Similarly, I cannot believe
that they can stand up over there and talk  about a tax switch, and claim that New
Zealanders are no worse off under a Nationa l Government. If members opposite believe
that, then clearly they are not talking or listening to low and middle income New
Zealanders. Members across the House must spend their time with the top 10 percent of
earners, who are better off under this Government—the rich rather than the rest.
I see people in my office, I see people out  and about in the Ma ungakiekie electorate,
and I consistently hear their concerns about how hard it is to make ends meet. I was
talking to staff of one of the budgeting services  near my office, and they said that if
people rang up and said their electricity was going to be cut off that day, they would say
to those people that they could see them in 2½ weeks, because that is how busy they
are. I spoke to staff of a chur ch in the electorate, and they said they have just had the
busiest January ever with their food bank. People are hurting, but members opposite
seem not to care about that. That was a choice; it was a choice  to put resources
elsewhere.
Housing is also a huge issue, certainly in Auckland. The New Zealand Herald has
recently provided some pretty good covera ge of what is going on with the rental
16646 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
housing market in Auckland. Housing is the issue that people most often come to my
office about. They have difficulties in getting into a State house. There are big waiting
lists for State houses because people do not have  the income to pay for private rentals.
What is the Housing New Zealand Corporatio n doing? It is referr ing those people back
out into the private housing market. There are people sleeping in garages throughout
Auckland. This week the Salvation Army w ill be making its annual state of the nation
report, and it is my expectation that it will say that the problem has become even worse
since it identified it last year.
Why was the choice not made to spend mone y on housing instead of tax cuts for the
rich? Why was the Government not looking at building more houses as part of a
stimulus package—more Housing New Zealand Corporation houses or affordable
housing options in partnership with other organisations? That  could have been used as
an opportunity to build our ski lls base, to train people in bu ilding skills—skills that we
are no doubt losing to Australia, and will lose  at an ever-increasing rate with wages
being 30 percent higher there and with the demand in Australia for a whole lot of
rebuilding to be done.
I will move on and talk about skills. The previous speaker mentioned skills in
passing, as he was sitting down. Well, the refe rence to skills in the statement of the
Prime Minister was bland rhetoric. That is what  was in there. In response to a real skills
shortage and crisis in New Zealand we have bland rhetoric. Despite the needs of many
who have lost their jobs or who are worki ng in struggling businesses, and the need we
have in our country to lift our skill base , to improve workplace productivity, and to
strengthen our economic performance, Na tional continues to take a limited and
unambitious approach to the issue of skills development. Investing in upskilling our
people would pay huge dividends for people in dividually, for their families, for their
communities, for their workplaces, and for our economy. Significant investment needs
to be made in those who are already in work or who have recently been in work.
National cut over $50 million from industry tr aining in 2010, and in 2011 it is clear that
there will not be bold initiatives in this area. That $50 million could have funded 55,000
more students in industry training.
What does the Prime Minister’s statement say about skills? Well, it makes reference
to examining and improving existing provisions. Although no one would argue with the
need to improve the quality of what is already in place, the magnitude of the skills
shortages and the increasing number of pe ople becoming unemployed require a great
deal more than that. This Government continues to support a low-wage economy, and
continues to support workplaces competing in reducing wages and conditions. That will
not provide the framework necessary to lift bo th skills acquisition and skills utilisation.
In fact, there is just about more about th e 90-day fire-at-will provisions in the Prime
Minister’s statement than there is about the issue of skills development. Of course, hand
in hand, we have seen the recent announcem ent of a 25c per hour  increase in the
minimum wage.
I just want to say there has to be a co mmitment to provide more opportunities to
retrain those affected by the current economic situation, but they will not get that from
this National Government.

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: Yesterday I sat here in this House and listened
to the Prime Minister deliver one of the probab ly rarest things in politics, which was an
honest and very upfront assessment of where New Zealand is and what we actually need
to do if we are going to get ahead. I think th at is one of the reasons New Zealand is
coming so strongly behind John Key and his Government, because it is such a breath of
fresh air to have a Prime Mini ster who does not play games and try to score points. He
stood here and said very clearly to New Zeala nd: “This is what we need to do if we are
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16647
going to build the sort of country that  New Zealanders should have, that New
Zealanders want, and that New Zealanders are looking forward to us delivering.”
We could see that, could we not, when he stood up at our first caucus of the year, and
in front of the media, and said: “Elect ion: 26 November.” There was no mucking
around, hanging on until the last minute, game playing, or trying to give the other side a
bit of an advantage. He said: “Look, New Zealand need s to know. We’ve got a busy
year. Let us make sure that everyone knows early on where they’re going.” I think New

items.speaker: Zealand likes that. He stood up and said
items.text: “If you vote for me, you won’t get Winston
Peters in our Government.” He said: “A vote for Winston Peters is a vote for Phil Goff.”
Why would he not? New Zealanders want to  know what they are going to get. New
Zealanders want to know what their vote will give them. New Zealanders can make that
choice, they can make a decisi on, but at least they  know with us what  they will get.
They will not get a whole lot of smoke, mirrors, game playing, and desperate clinging to
power. We will put out what we are doing. If  New Zealanders want us to get this
country back on track, they will continue to back us as they have since November 2008.
What is really interesting to me, though, is that if Labour members cannot debate
with us on the merit of our pol icies, which clearly they cannot, they simply resort to
misleading the public. They mislead the public on the grounds that if they say it often
enough, maybe people will forget that it is not true. Let us go through it—let us go
through it. What have we heard over and over in this deba te? We have heard about tax
cuts for the rich. Let us look at that, sh all we? There were tax cuts for everyone,
actually. [ Interruption] I ask Mrs Chadwick to listen;  she might learn something.
Seventy-five percent of taxpayers in this country now pay half the tax, and have half the
top tax rate, that they had under Labour. Seve nty-five percent of all taxpayers pay at
that rate.
Then Labour members said that the tax cu ts were funded by borrowing. They said
the tax cuts were funded by borrowing. Let us look at the truth there. The tax cuts are
fiscally neutral because they were paid for by putting up GST. Do members remember
that, or remember the “Axe the Tax” bus th at they have conveniently forgotten about
now because they will actually keep that new GST rate?

items.speaker: Aaron Gilmore
items.text: What are they going to do about that?

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: Oh, well, they will be keeping that now, because they need that.
They need that, plus a whole lot more tax. So rather than debate with us on what we are
actually doing, they mislead th e public and hope that if they say words like “cuts”
enough, it will sink in. But, you know, I have mo re respect for New Zealand than that. I
think New Zealanders know they are paying less tax now than they ever did. I think
they know that when we lowered their tax, we funded it through increasing GST to
discourage consumption. I think they know that New Zealand cannot afford the sorts of
reckless borrow-and-spend policies that are all Labour has. All Labour knows to do is to
throw the money around and never mind about the debt. That will be someone else’s
problem: “Let us just get back into power.  We will deal with anybody, we will get into
bed with anybody, and we will promise anything; we just have to get back into power.”
That is not what National is going to do. That is not what  this Government is going
to do. The nice thing about this election cam paign is that already we have a clear
distinction between the two parties. We have a clear distinction between the two parties.
If New Zealand backs National it will get so und financial management. It will get a
Government that prioritises the spending of taxpayers’ money—because that is what it
is: it is not our money; it is taxpayers’ money—as if  it were our own. We will not throw
it around; we will make sure we get value for every dollar.
We will create productive jobs—productive jo bs, not jobs in the public sector and
jobs the unions want. We will get jobs that actually add to the wealth of this country and
16648 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
raise incomes. Do members know how we w ill do that? We will do it by having an
environment that encourages investment in New Zealand businesses. It is not rocket
science, but that is what we will do and what the other side has failed to do. Actually, on
that point, one of the statistics that jumped out at me was the fact that thanks to the
labour law changes that Kate Wilkinson has brought in, and thanks to the 90-day trial
periods, 13,000 new jobs have been created—13,000 new jobs—because we are
creating an environment that makes businesses have confidence to invest in New
Zealand. What is Labour’s answer? Thos e members will put up the minimum wage.
What will that do? It will cost 6,000 jobs. Six thousand jobs will be lost, but that is their
policy for job creation.
This National Government fundamentally gets  the point that money has to be earned
before it can be spent. It has to be in the bank. It is only when we get back to surplus
that we will have any sorts of choices, and any ability to start spending and looking at
the wish list. If we cannot get back into su rplus, this country w ill be on a downward
spiral. That is why we are working so hard to get us back there.
Labour has promised to borrow and spe nd—borrow and spend. Already it is only
early February, and it has promised $5 billion more in spending than this Government.
We are borrowing $300 million a week. I hate tha t; I hate that we need to do that. But
we have a party over there that wants to borrow $5 billion more, and it has not even
started its campaign promises. Those member s are clearly going to promise everything
to everyone. The most amazing thing is th at they obviously have a good source of
magic beans to pay for it all. That is the fun bit—the pixies at the bottom of the garden
making the money. But do members know what that  really is? It is irresponsible, it is
self-serving, and it is shallow, petty politics at its worst. That is the message Labour has
given to New Zealand: “Don’t worry about whether you can afford it; just keep
spending. Just keep spending it. You want it? Go and get it.  Don’t worry about whether
you can pay for it. Live beyond your means. Get into debt. Keep spending, and don’t
spend it on assets. Don’t sp end it on infrastructure and stuff we need. Spend it on
consumables. Spend it on stuff that won’t work.”
Do members know what Labour left this c ountry with after 9 of  the best economic
years we have ever had? A decade of deficits —a decade of deficits! It left us with 5
years of recession in the productive sector and a devastated export sector. My electorate
of Selwyn relies on exports, tourism, farming, and manufacturing, but Labour
devastated those industries. It devastated them . It left us with an appalling shortage of
infrastructure. My communities cannot get ahead with the poor state of roading,
broadband, and cellphone coverage in our area. What do we ha ve now under Steven
Joyce’s Rural Broadband Initiative? Some 86 percent of rural house holds will shortly
have high-speed broadband and cellphone covera ge. That is the sort of infrastructure
spending we need in order to get ahead.
Labour’s management left families vulnerable, it put workers at risk, and it did just
what it needed to do to cling to power. Everything Labour members have said since
then makes it very clear that they have no intention of running things any other way.
The external indebtedness of this country pu ts us on a par with Spain, with Portugal,
with Greece—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: Kris Faafoi is laughing. He has clearly never looked at the numbers.
I invite Mr Faafoi to come along to th e Finance and Expenditure Committee one day
and learn how perilous the situation is; La bour members could not care less. Are they
really incapable of seeing the damage that their prom ises would do to this country? Are
they really incapable of seei ng it or do they just not care ? That is what I wonder—do
they just not care or can they really not se e it? I find it interes ting, though, that Labour
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16649
is so focused on how much money we are spending on something: “How much money
are you spending?”—as if how much we spend is the only good measure.

items.speaker: Aaron Gilmore
items.text: They don’t care about the outcomes.

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is right. Do members know wh at I care about? I care about the
fact that every year we now have 20,000 more  elective surgeries than there were under
Labour.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: People are getting sicker!

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: I care about the fact that 20 percent of our children leave school
with no future, I tell Mrs Chadwick, because her Government was happy to sit back and
let the unions run the education system rath er than having a system that prioritised
children learning to read and wr ite, which is what this Go vernment will give. Labour
members can talk about cuts if they like; they are not happening. We are spending more
on early childhood education than ever before, and we will make sure the children of
this country can read, write, and get ahead. We will not preside over wasted
opportunities. First we will fix Labour’s mess, and then we will turn this country into
the best it can be.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: All I have to say to Amy Adams is this: no plan,
no progress, no ideas, no ability to control what is going on, no vision for this country,
and no way this Government should be re-el ected in 2011. That side of the House had 9
years—9 long years—to think about how those members might run this country, yet
here they are, 2 years into their term, and they still have no plan. They still do not know
what they are doing.
I have only 10 minutes to comment on the very uninspiring speech that was delivered
by John Key yesterday, and from the get-go it is impossible to know where to start and
how to cover everything that needs to be sa id. We could start with the rising cost of
living and the impact that is having on ordina ry Kiwis. We could add to that the fact
that wages are not going up despite the cost  of living going through the roof. We could
start by reminding everyone that the Govern ment pulled millions of dollars out of
research and development—money that coul d have gone towards investing in clean
technology, which is something New Zealand should lead the world in. We could talk
about the State assets that that side of the House intends to sell off. We could talk about
the fact that National intends to eventually sell off the assets to foreign investors with no
regard for the real mums and dads who cu rrently own them. We could talk about the
fact that National has continually bashed beneficiaries over the course of its time in
Government to try to shift the attention away  from the fact that it has been unable to
create jobs and the fact that the real problem is there are no jobs for New Zealanders to
go into. We could talk about the fact that last month alone 1,000 more people joined the
other 68,000 people who are on the unemployment benefit.
Where do we start? There are so many exam ples of why the National Government is
not fit to govern this country. But I do thi nk that a good place to st art is its tinkering
with our education system and the damage it has caused. I visited a number of early
childhood education centres in the Waitakere electorate over the last 2 weeks—most of
them were second visits; I had visited most of them last year. All of them stand to lose
because of the Minister of Education’s decision to cut $400 million out of early
childhood education, yet we have to listen to  just about each and every National MP
telling us that no money has been taken out of the early childhood education sector and
that $91 million of additional funding has been added to it. We on this side of the House
know that is not true, and every single educator  working in that sector knows that it is
untrue, as well.
I have been to public meetings and I have  listened to the co mmentary from MPs on
the National side about the positive benefits that our Pacific community can look
16650 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
forward to because of the cuts made to early childhood education, or, as they like to say,
the additional funding that has been put i n. National MPs like to go out there and say
that no gains were made for M āori and Pacific early childhood education under Labour,
and right here I have inform ation that tells me straight away that not only did the
participation of Māori and Pacific children go up but  also, from 2001 to 2008, qualified
Pacific early childhood educators increase d by 534. That came directly from an
investment by the previous Labour Government. Also an additional 479 Pacific early
childhood education centres opened during th e Labour Government’s term. That was
because the Labour Government saw it as a prio rity. We have to sit here and listen to
Anne Tolley tell us that Nati onal plans to build an additional five centres—five centres
after 2 years. Under the previous Labour Government 479 centres were built for the
Pacific community alone. That side of the House has its prioritie s in the wrong place.
The early childhood education sector knows, a nd very soon every single parent and
grandparent who has children in those early childhood centres will also know, that that
is the case.
When we look at the early childhood educat ion sector, we see the Government does
not understand there was not just an i nvestment by Labour but an exceptional
commitment by the Pacific community to ensure that Pacific children have the same
start as anybody else. The Pacific populati on is one of the fastest-growing—and the
youngest—populations in New Zealand. Any adve rse changes to the accessibility of
educational resources, like National’s slas h and burn of early childhood education
funding, will have a disproportionately negative impact on Pacific communities.
Let us go from education to welfare. Last year the Social Services Committee had to
sit painfully through the changes that the Na tional Government’s Minister for Social
Development and Employment pushed through, yet it seems that we have even more to
not look forward to. John Key has revealed plans for radical welfare reform, including
pushing people off the domestic purposes, sickness, and invalids benefits. He said that it
is a source of shame that people remain on a benefit for years, even though work is
available to them. The Government says it will provide more detail about its changes
when a welfare reform working-group reports back later this month, but the areas that
we know are likely to be target ed include getting beneficiaries with children  back into
work, along with invalids and sickness beneficiaries, and tackling youth skills.
We believe, even on this side, in welfare reform. But the best reform we can possibly
aim for is the type of reform that creates jobs for people to  go into. We cannot tackle a
welfare problem if we are not creating jobs  for people and growing the economy. That
has been the failure of that side of the House. It has done nothing to create jobs, and
nothing to build the economy in this c ountry post-recession. In fact, John Key has
admitted that we are slipping back into a recession, when countries like Australia do not
seem to have gone through one at all, and other OECD countries seem to have come out
unscathed, unlike us. The only plan that we have seen from John Key and his National
Government is to borrow billions of dollars in order to give tax cuts to the top earners,
to hock off our valuable Stat e assets to foreign buyers, and to slash and burn essential
public services like hospitals and schools. La bour does have a plan. We stated it very
clearly. We will stop the asset sales, we will introduce a tax -free zone to help all New
Zealanders cope with the rising cost of living, and we will create a stronger export
economy, a fairer tax system, and strong public services. Those are all things that the
National Government is unable to promise New Zealande rs at this time.
The Prime Minister’s statement to Parl iament—this is some thing I found really
interesting—included a claim that his Government had placed a special emphasis on the
rights of victims. He failed to state that th at emphasis has been negative and detrimental
to the rights of victims. One example of that  is National’s refusal to enact the Domestic
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16651
Violence Reform Bill, which was introduced  by Labour during its previous term of
Government. We know, and National knows, b ecause the bill has b een through a select
committee, that it was a culmination of ex tensive consultation with organisations and
key stakeholders who support victims of do mestic violence. Instead, whilst our bill,
which was very thoroughly consulted on, languishes on the Government’s Order
Paper—National passed its own watered-dow n version—the National Government has
done nothing to give domestic violence vi ctims the protection an d support they need
moving forward.
In the last year, the National Government  added insult to injury by slashing
counselling and support for victims and surviv ors of sexual assault.  Previously they
were able to access counselling support vi a ACC on the recommendation of their
counsellors or therapists. The National Government imposed more stringent measures,
which included the requirement that victims/ survivors be subject to multiple interviews
with different health professionals. The Mi nister for ACC on that side of the House
knows very well that when an independent  report was release d, it criticised the
Government and the actions that it had taken. The Government was then forced to do a
turn-round and cut back on some of the more ru thless aspects of what it tried to do, but
by that time it was too late and the damage that had been done was immeasurable.
Over the past 2 years that side of the House has caused New Zealand a lot of pain
unnecessarily and it will only get worse. New Ze alanders recognise that that is the case.
Labour does have a plan, Labour is progre ssive, and Labour has a vision for the
country. Watch this space, I say to Ms Goudie, because Labour will be re-elected to
Government in 2011.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: As I came to the Chamber, I
passed an exhibition about Anne Frank. I am sure  that many of us he re in this Chamber
will recall studying her or hearing about her life. She said that everyone has inside them
a piece of good news and that good news is that we do not know how great we can be,
what we can accomplish, and what our potential is. That remarkable young girl lived
and experienced utter hardship yet prevailed to be one of the great examples of courage,
as seen through her writing. She died of t yphus in a concentration camp in 1945 at the
age of 16. She said: “I finally realised that I must do my schoolwork to keep from being
ignorant, to get on in life, to become a journalist because that’s what I want! I know I
can write. … but it remains to be seen whether I really have talent. … When I write I
can shake off all my cares. My sorrow disa ppears, my spirits are revived! But, and
that’s a big question, will I ever be able to write something great, will I ever become a
journalist or a writer?”.
I tell members this story because no doubt  many of us have walked past her
exhibition on display here in our Parliament  this week. She has become great, and the
greatness we celebrate was already there in the words she was writing as a teenaged girl.
The education of our young people is incred ibly important not only for their success
but also, I think, for the success of our country and its future. We are very committed to
the education of young New Zealanders, w ho burgeon with the same promise and
potential. The tragedy for many of those young pe ople is that their pot ential gets buried
by a lack of achievement at an early age, and they carry through with  them that lack of
achievement into every following year and level of their education.
Our Minister of Education, the Hon Anne Tolley, says that the findings of an
international study by the OECD show that more needs to be  done in our nation to lift
achievement for all New Zealand students.  The 2009 results from the Programme for
International Student Assessment compared the performance of 15-year-olds in reading,
literacy, maths, and science. New Zealand continues to have a disproportionate number
of lower achievers, and that ha s not changed in the past 9 ye ars. Further,  there has been
16652 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
no change in our reading performance sin ce 2000, and no change in maths since 2003.
That is grim news, and it is what has empowered National’s education policy.
There is some good news as well. Our top stud ents are some of the best in the world.
In reading, maths, and science we pe rformed well above the average for OECD
countries. This is a credit to our teachers, students, parents, and our education system.
However, we are faced with this challenge to work together to address the issues raised
in this report. It is why our Government  introduced national standards in education,
which is not a test but an assessment to discover difficulty early on so it does not
become entrenched, and so we can see a shif t in the disproportionate number of lower
achievers.
I speak to educationalists all the time. They tell me they already know who the
people are who are in that failing tail. My  answer, then, is th at, obviously, identifying
them has not brought the solution. The solu tion is to ask what we do next. National
standards are a tool to assess where a child is on their educational journey, compared
with where they could be or ought to be. It  is a measure of progress against potential.
That is the point. Educational achieveme nt is built upon the foundation of previous
learning, but if previous learning does not ex ist or is deficient, and if no rungs are
climbed on that educational ladder, it leav es our young people aspiring for things they
cannot reach. We have discovered that one in five students is leaving school without the
literacy and the numeracy achievements to ta ke them on to an apprenticeship or to
further training in order that they may engage in the modern economy.
We have also discovered that one in five  15 to 19-year-olds cannot find employment
at present. It is an interesting correla tion. Twenty percent of young New Zealanders are
struggling to learn and struggling to find em ployment. As the OECD report stated, and
Opposition members are usually so keen to quote the OECD, we have a
disproportionate number of low-achiev ing young people—young children who have
intelligence and potential but who, for ma ny reasons, have been disconnected from
learning. It is because we believe that they ha ve intelligence and potential that we have
put national standards in place, which has relevance in diagnosing those disconnects,
and which then assists educators to determ ine the next step in those young people’s
educational journeys.
Our policy regarding early childhood education is very much part of discovering and
releasing the potential of young children. We  value early childhood education because
we know it helps to prepare children for future learning and assists parents to participate
in the workforce. Our policy is to broaden our reach to those who are disconnected from
learning. In some parts of the country, up to  40 percent of our ch ildren are missing out
on attending early childhood edu cation centres. As proud as members of the previous
Government have sounded on this, the statistics from both the Education Review Office
and the OECD tell us that there are and have been gaps that children have been falling
through for some time—for 9 years, up to  a decade. Under the previous Labour
Government’s watch, no significant progre ss was made with those young people who
were disconnected from learning. It starts  with early childhood education. There are
masses of young children missing out on taxpay er investment in their future. This
Government is making a significant investme nt. There is more invested per child in
early childhood education th an in primary school educ ation or secondary school
education. We are now at the stage where the taxpayer is subsidising early childhood
education centres at an average of $7,600 per child per year. This compares with an
average of $5,528 for a primary school stud ent and $6,733 for a student at a secondary
school. Investment in early childhood educati on has never been higher before. This is
the big news: it is reaching more children than ev er before. We on this side of the House
are proud of that.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16653

items.speaker: Earlier this year John Key said
items.text: “This G overnment views our e ducation system as
one of the fundamental tools for creati ng an egalitarian society where all New
Zealanders have an opportunity to succeed.” That statement was made at the beginning
of the year. We are creating greater educational opportunities for more young New
Zealanders than ever before, to give them th e best possible start in life so that they do
not end up being a sad statis tic in the bottom 20 percent.  Under the early childhood
education system we inherited from Labour , the Government will this year spend a
record $1.4 billion, up from less than $400 million a decade ago. Despite this, the
number of children starting school with so me form of early childhood education has
barely increased at all, and in some parts of the country up to 40 percent of children are
missing out altogether.
We have prioritised building a stronger economy and building skills and knowledge
in our young people so that children can be fu ture-proofed as they look to their working
futures. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Sir ROGER DOUGLAS
items.text: The new year is an opportunity for a fresh
start. Traditionally, people make resolutions that seek to cut back on the excesses they
indulged in the year before. It seems that the National Government has yet to decide on
its New Year’s resolutions. I de cided that maybe I could save  them the hassle, so I put
together a list of resolutions that National could adopt, which would help New Zealand.
The first resolution should be to slim down. The National Government, after 2 years
of bingeing, has made government bigger th an ever. Total Government expenditure
reached just over $81 billion in 2010. That is  almost 43c in every dollar earned. Such
expenditure is financed by borrowing ar ound $300 million every week, simply because
the amount of tax that goes in to the Government coffers is  less than it spends. With
government so big, is it any surprise that our economy is not getting off the ground?
Growth in the New Zealand economy re mains at around 1 percent. When the
economy is leashed to a weight that spends over 40c in every dollar, it is easy to see
why we are going nowhere. In the meantime, we see other countries such as Singapore
float away, with average annual growth ra tes of 4 percent or more. The Singapore
Government spends a mere 17 percent—17c in every dollar. That might be all right if
we were getting better services than Singapore. The reality, however , is that not only
does our spending make us poorer than Singapore but across the board we also have
worse poverty, worse education, worse health care, and more crime—and the list goes
on.
Forecasts show that Austra lia will be 42 percent weal thier than New Zealand by
2025. Because of this, 412,000 New Zealanders, the equivalent of all the residents in the
Wellington region, are likely to leave New Zealand for Australia over the next 15 years.
The first New Zealand resolution that we should have is clear: slim down.
I find it unbelievable that Nati onal, which rightly complained so bitterly about the
years of wasteful spending by the Labour Government, suddenly, when it gets into
power, cannot find any wasteful expenditure to cut. To the contrary, National seems to
have borrowed more money to spend. The simp le truth is we will never spend or tax
ourselves to prosperity. It is a shame that National still needs to learn that basic lesson.
The second resolution should be to focus on wh at really matters. Core services, such
as education, health, and welfare—65 percent of core G overnment expenditure—are
very important Government services. However, the Government has been increasingly
bad at providing them. Our education system is failing our young people. A third of
school-leavers fail to achieve National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA)
level 2 or higher. For M āori, 56 percent will not gain NCEA level 1 or above before
they leave school. Some of our schools are so unsafe that the police are stationed within
them
. A classroom surrounded by police officers  is not a proper learning environment.
16654 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
It is hardly surprising that 30,000 schoolchildren cut class every day. Children are
voting with their feet and ar e choosing to be away from dilapidated classrooms, rigid
curricula, violence, and the monotony of the classroom environment. In education, the
Government should resolve to empower parents.
In welfare, 13 percent of the adult popula tion are receiving a benefit. That is
compared with 2 percent in 1960. Approximately one in five Kiwi children will live in a
benefit-dependent household. Recent figures show over 350,000 people are on some
type of benefit. For every six worker s, one person is on a benefit. Add in
superannuation and the ageing population and it is  likely that our children will live in a
world where every one person receiving a Government handout will be supported by
just two workers. This is simply not sustainable.
In health, the number of pract ising physicians is 2.3 per 1,00 0 people. This is almost
one fewer per 1,000 people than the OECD aver age. The number of hospital beds per
1,000 people is 6.2. This is over one hospital bed fewer than the world average. Every
year hundreds of people continue to die while on waiting lists because our health system
is overstretched.
If Government tax-funded money could solve all these problems, New Zealand
would have solved them already. We spend vast amounts on all these areas, but get
substandard service in return. We have made ourselves poorer to afford all this. But do
we get the kinds of services we want? We n eed to rethink the approach in all of these
areas.
In welfare, the Government should resolve to get two-thirds of the people on benefits
back to work. Despite unemployment re ducing sharply between 1999 and 2008,
expenditure on welfare soared. Part of this  was done by transferring people on to
sickness and invalids benefits. We will never solve the problem by just moving people
around. The number of people on sickness and invalids benefits has increased by almost
70 percent in the last decade. In that pe riod the population increased by 12 percent, and
spending on health almost doubled. It is ve ry difficult to argue that these figures
represent a declining level of health in the population. Rather, it seems that for some it
has become a lifestyle, rather than a transition.
In health, the Government should resolve to restore the right incentives. If we look at
other places around the world we can find practical templates to model our health care
system on. Singapore has one of the best health-care systems in the world. Its infant
mortality and life expectancy rates are amongs t the best in the world. However, what
makes it amazing is its cost-effectiveness. It s Government spends very little money on
making it a good system. It spends between 1 and 3 percent of GD P annually on health
care. In contrast, New Zealand spends between 8 and 9 percent of GDP. Singapore
makes it compulsory to have health savings accounts in which individuals pre-save for
medical conditions, and they have a catastrophic insurance on top of that.
New Zealand’s outlook is bleak. Today we sit in a position similar to the one we had
in 1984. The difference, though, is that in 1984  we made tough decisions. We outlined
the goal we wanted to achieve, and moved swiftly to attain it. The public were
supportive because they were able to see what  we wanted to achieve, and returned the
Government with an increased  majority in 1987. The point  is that we did this by
pursuing the right policies, not by doing what might be popular in the short term.
If members cast their minds back over the last 2 years of the National Government,
can they think of one piece of quality reform  that has made New Zealand better off and
will be remembered by anyone in 10 years’ time? I find it somewhat amusing that a
party that has spent 9 years in Opposition ar guing against most of the changes brought
about by Labour, such as Working for Families, the lack of privatisation, the abolition
of youth rates, the freezing of tariffs, and the re-regul ation of the labour market,
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16655
amongst others, then does not hing about them when in power. National does not seem
to get it, and until it tries to set the age nda, rather than follow blindly what Labour
leaves in its wake, National will continue to fail New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Sir Roger Douglas is absolutely
correct in quoting Singapore in terms of the remarkable results that it gets from its
health system. As he said, Singapore’s curren t expenditure is in the order of 3.5 percent
of GDP, compared with New Zealand’s at 8 percent, Australia’s at 9 percent, and the
USA’s at 15.5 percent, yet Singaporeans live long er and the infant mortality rate is less
than half of ours. It is underpinned by a va riety of very clear principles that were
worked out in a white paper in the 1990s. But I must add to that. I do not believe that
the New Zealand ethos would quite accept the autocratic way that Singapore works. But
we certainly have lessons to learn, and we can learn enormously from the remarkable
outcomes that Singapore has achieved.
Yesterday Prime Minister John Key was clear and concise in his speech. National
will focus on building a strong economy, which is vital for an excellent health, welfare,
and education system. National will focus on building better results from our public
services, and, goodness me, it needs to. We have Labour’s record over 9 years of
spending double the amount of money, for absolutely no increase in productivity.
John Key’s speech was in sharp contrast to  that of Phil Goff, who presented a
