somewhat vein-popping, shaking-hand charad e that proposed everything that was the
reverse of what he said he believed in b ack in the 1980s. He faile d to acknowledge that
the last Labour Government had built up the Public Service by 50 percent, over 9 years,
into a creaking bureaucracy with very poor productivity. As I said earlier, that was
particularly the case in the health sector. C ontrary to the advice of the Savings Working
Group, Mr Goff wishes to spend, spend, spend, and so far the cost has been tallied up to
over $5 billion, and there is still much of the year left. He has not explained how he will
get the money to pay for his promises—all in an environment in which the Savings
Working Group says New Zealand’s level of de bt is too high. Net fo reign liabilities,
public and private, amount to 85 percent, leaving New Zealand vulnerable to economic
shocks. According to the group, it is absolute ly vital that we increase savings as an
essential component to reducing our vulnerability.
National is taking a prudential and measured approach to the economy, in stark
contrast to Labour’s somewhat reckless and irresponsible policy to spend and bribe the
vulnerable, just as it did b ack in the 1980s and repeated ov er the last 9 years. I was
astounded but not surprised to listen this afternoon to that vete ran shroud-waver, the
Hon Annette King. She was complaining that the Prime Minister should have talked
about growing the economy. I tell the Hon A nnette King that she was given a copy of
his statement. She could have read it, but she continues to be in denial about what has
happened over the last few decades. I am very happy to present her with another copy.
Why did I call her a shroud-waver? In 1998, when she was the Opposition
spokesperson on health, she said it was criminal that the then Mini ster of Health had
allowed waiting lists to expand out to 86,000, yet 2 years later she had presided over the
building of one of the most complex, cumbersome, and lowly productive health systems
in the history of New Zealand. Waiting lists had blown out to 140,000, and she was
culling the waiting lists in lots  of 10,000 at a time. In very sharp contrast to that, over
the last 2 years Minister of Health Tony Ryall has achieved some very remarkable
results, which are shown up in the health targ e ts. They include shorter waiting times in
emergency departments and improved access to elective surgery, with something like
400 extra elective surgeries per week. We have shorter waits for cancer treatment, with
99 percent of people who were referred for radiation starting treatment within 6 weeks. I
can vividly recall under Labour literally planeloads of patients going across to Australia
16656 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
for radiation therapy. We have increased im munisation, with 87 percent of 2-year-olds
now fully immunised. In the Lakes District He alth Board there has been an increase in
immunisation of 22 percent in just the last year. There is better help for smokers to quit,
and better services for people with diabetes and cardiovascular problems.
Those are objective advances that have occu rred in the last 2 years, and they are
quite remarkable. It is a good thing that, at least, Labour voted with the Government on
the recent New Zealand Public Health a nd Disability Amendment Bill, which has
allowed for greater national and regional c oordination of our health system, and the
introduction of the very important Health Quality and Safety Commission.
I was also very glad that the Hon Annette King said in a speech in October 2010 that
she had been “thinking and re-examining all of  Labour’s policies.” I believe it will be
very good for New Zealand if she stays in O pposition and continues to think for a very,
very long time. I was also glad that she had decided to work on a policy she called
“Putting Children First”. There is no doubt in my mind that over the last few decades, or
even longer, New Zealand’s record at putting children first has failed miserably.
Successive Governments have failed them, and it is hugely important that that situation
is reversed.
I sincerely ask Mrs King to look carefully at the excellent policies the Government is
evolving. They have to be cross-sectoral, they need to be evidence-based, as is so
strongly advocated by Sir Peter Gluckman  and people such as Professor David
Fergusson, and they need to operate from pre-conception onwards. I note that Annette
King talks about the child from the age of nought to 2, but she must think prior to that. I
am sure the Hon Stevie Chadwick would agre e with me, because, after all, the toll on
foetuses in New Zealand from alcohol, drugs, and tobacco is hugely profound and
substantial. National will very shortly bri ng through yet more legislation to progress
measures reducing tobacco and alcohol, along with our coalition partner the M āori
Party, in this country. That has to make a huge difference.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Not alcohol labelling? Oh great!

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I am very sad to see Stevie Chadwick not taking this
issue extremely seriously.
Annette King must be realistic. I note that in the beginning of her October speech she
said detailed announcements, including costings, would be made in due course. Once
again, we see from the Hon Annette King a situ ation where she talks, and her rhetoric is
extraordinarily voluble, but we do not see the record. In stark contrast we have a
National Government that has a proud record of evidence-based improvement in the
health system.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: That speech from Dr Paul Hutchison
was 10 minutes of my life that I will not get back. It is not often that I agree with Sir
Roger Douglas, but his analysis of this economy as bleak was exactly on the button. His
leader’s belief that the economy is broke is  exactly right as well.  Rodney Hide agreed
that he needed to be with a National-le d Government, even though the Government had
broken the economy, for his own political survival and that  of his party. His party
agreed with him so wholehear tedly that one of them even stood up afterwards and gave
him some applause.
This country is going backwards, and it is not good enough. We deserve a lot better. I
remember that last year—and this has been said before in this House—John Key said
we were aggressively coming out of rece ssion. In the Budget John Key talked about a
step change, but this time he said that there could be days when it is a step forward and
half a step backward. That is a step change John Key - style. He got it round the wrong
way. W
hat he really meant to say was that so me days there will be half a step forward
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16657
and a full step backwards, because that is where the economy is going. That is what a
step change means to this Government.
We are an increasingly unequal society. I was amazed in the House today when the
Minister of Finance said that somehow, as a result of his tax switch, we were not a more
unequal society. Those people earning $1 m illion a year get a $1,000 a week wage
increase and those people on the median wage get $15 a week. That means that the
person earning $1 million gets $52,000 a year  and the other pers on gets $850 a year—
not even 1 week’s increase—and somehow that will not make us a more unequal
society.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: How much are you going to put up tax?

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The analysis, I say to Dr Smit h, is fine, but people listening to
it will say that that analysis is simply mumbo-jumbo. Qu ite frankly, it is simply
mumbo-jumbo. We are becoming a more unequal society. The policies of this
Government are making it that, and inequality is an unhealthy situation for this country.
We deserve better, but this country is going backwards.
Then we talk about the aspiration to catch up with Australia. It used to be a goal, then
it became an aspiration, but it was not mentioned in John Key’s speech this time around.
It is not really an aspiration; it is more an aspirator—a machine that sucks fluid out of
the body, only this time it is Australia sucking ou r best brains and our best talent out of
New Zealand. That is what aspirational m eans for the National Government. That is
what aspirational means. Then the Government has the audacity to  turn round and tell
Labour members that somehow our economic policies are all wrong.
Let us look at some of the economic polic ies that Australia has put in place. In
Australia the upper tax limit kicks in for those on $180,000 at 45 percent. We are
talking about raising the upper tax limit. Is th at radical? The Aust ralians have exactly
the same thing; Australia has no tax under $6,000. We are talking a bout bringing it in
under $5,000—is that radical? We are aspiring to be as rich as Australia, but we do not
want to take on any of its policies. Here is another one: Australia has a capital gains tax.
This Government ruled out capital gains fo r the Tax Working Group when it came to
put provisions into its report. So what ar e we going to do? We are looking at ring-
fencing the losses on property. Then the big kicker of the lot—and the Minister of
Science and Innovation, as the portfolio is now called, is in the House—scrapped the 15
percent tax credit on research and development.

items.speaker: I will tell members what happened
items.text: we put the tax credit in place here. What did the
Australians do? As soon as the Labor Gove rnment got into power in Australia it came
over here, copied the tax credit in its entiret y, and put it in place in Australia. What did
we do? I will tell members what we did: we put in vouchers and grants to replace it. Dr
Mapp and even his adviser Professor Gluckm an—the real Minister of Science and
Innovation—told me that the policy is gros sly oversubscribed; ther e has been such a
great take-up. Of course there is a great  take-up. There is $2 million for those
companies out there to get from the Governme nt. What company is going to be stupid
enough to say no? The big question is how ma ny of those companies out there did not
get the grants and vouchers that they would have been eligible for under the tax credit.
That is stifling the very growth accelerators that this country needs.
I tell members that all of those things are in place in Australia and are working well,
and this country wants to  be like Australia. The New Zealand Herald noted in its
editorial yesterday morning that there was a 16 percent increase in people going to
Australia. This Government campaigned in 2008 on stopping that flow, and last year it
was 16 percent higher than in 2009. That is  a testimonial of th e failure of this
Government in respect of the economy. People are going over because Australia is
sucking them there because of the things it can provide. Their policies are the very
16658 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
economic policies being proposed by this side  of the House for when we come into
Government later this year.
This country is going backwards, it is st uffed, and we are not going anywhere. What
is the answer? When Kathryn Ryan inte rviewed John Key on Radio New Zealand he
gave the example of Asia—a high tech, high-growth econo my roaring ahead, and with
manufacturing and all of those things roaring ahead. He said  that we could supply them
with food. Is that not visionary! Is it not extraordinarily visi onary that, after all of this
time, after 9 years in Opposition, and in 2 years in Government, the only vision we have
for New Zealand’s future is to supply Asia, which used to be  behind us—well behind
us—with food? That is extraordinary.
We need, in addition to our primary pr oducts, a high-growth, a high-value, a high-
tech, and a green economy that will keep  our children and our young people here and
stop them moving to Australia. That is no t to say that our pr imary products are not
important, but we have to do a lot more to make sure that that happens. That means
changing many things in the science and innovation area. Dr Mapp knows that although
he changed the name from the Ministry of Research, Science and Technology to the
Ministry of Science and Innovation, it is only a name. It was heralded as a step change
in science and innovation, when it is simply  a 5 percent increase and a whole lot of
welfare to corporates who are just shifting—a nd I know this because some of them told
me—a lot of their expenditure from the research and development that they are doing to
buy all the other bits and pieces. Then they  go along to Dr Mapp and apply for the
vouchers and grants that will give them the money to replace them. That is exactly what
they are doing. Talk about rorting! My God, I cannot believe that this Government is so
naive not to see what is happening.
If Dr Mapp wants to see real step change, I tell him to have a look at Finland, or
Denmark, which he quotes prolifically in every single speech he gives. But this
Government is not doing anything like Denm ark did. I say to Dr Mapp that if he is
going to quote Denmark, then how about backi ng it up with a bit of action? He is not
getting anywhere close to what the Scandinavian countries are doing. They have 3
percent of GDP expenditure on research and development and we have something like
1.25 percent.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: The simple fact is that th is country is broke. It ain’t
got any money. We cannot keep on borrowi ng $300 million each week; it is just not
sustainable. That is why John Key has outlined a plan for building on the recovery. The
Government makes no apology for that—for c ontinuing to build a brighter future for
New Zealand. The Government’s 2011 programme will focus on building the
foundations for a stronger economy and building better results from the Public Service.
Building a strong and solid economy will be absolutely critical going forward, and a
strong economy will give New Zealanders jobs, increased incomes, and a better
standard of living. Compared with other coun tries, our Public Service is bloated. New
Zealand needs and deserves an efficient and responsive Public Service that will
ultimately improve the lives and the well-being of New Zealanders.
At this stage, I congratulate the Minister Tony Ryall on the fantastic leadership he is
showing in the health  sector. The immunisation targets were well ahead of schedule,
and the district health boards are achieving the cancer waiting list targets. Under Labour
there were terrible stories of women having to go to Australia to get radiotherapy, which
was devastating to them and their families at a very vulnerable time. The emergency
department targets are being achieved by di strict health boards around the country. The
voluntary bonding scheme has been unpreceden tedly welcomed by doctors, nurses, and
midwives. The voluntary bonding scheme will be one solid way we will keep our
professionals in New Zealand. It has been fantastic.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16659
In electives, again, unprecedented numbers have been achieved by district health
boards around the country. We heard today in the Health Committee from Lester Levy,
who is now the chair of the Waitematā  District Health Board and also, more recently,
the Auckland District Health Board. When  Lester became the chair of the Waitemat ā
District Health Board, it had terrible problems. There was a deficit, morale was low, and
the culture needed changing. There were terrible problems with the emergency
department, with long waiting times. The Waitakere emergency department had
problems opening 24/7 for both children and adults. That has all changed. There was
daily bad press in the newspaper of patients having bad experiences. We were delighted
to hear that that has changed, and that is all due to leadership by Lester Levy. He is
doing a wonderful job, and I congratulate him on that.

items.speaker: But it goes back to the economy
items.text: if we ar e to get the money to buy the medicines,
and to invest in new technologies to help New Zealanders stay healthy and to keep them
well, we will need a strong economy. The fact  is that that is really what this
Government is about. A key cornerstone of where we need to go is a solid economy to
build for a brighter future.
The simple fact is that when the Government came into power after the 2008 election
the economy was in recession, and had been so for almost a year. That was with the
backdrop of a worsening inte rnational economic crisis. So the most immediate focus
this Government had after the election was to  steady the economy and pull it back on to
a growth path. That is why building the foundations now for a stronger future is so
critical. It is the only way we will get peopl e jobs, higher incomes, a better standard of
living, and the New Zealand that they deserve.
We are rebalancing the economy away  from debt-fuelled consumption and
Government spending, and towards savings, in vestments, and exports. We are reducing
new spending in Budget 2011 so we can return to surplus sooner. We are getting better
value for taxpayer money, including consider ing ways to streamline and improve the
performance of the bureaucracy. Our other priorities include building world-class
infrastructure to help businesses compete,  building skills and knowledge for future-
proofed jobs, helping exporters to sell more of their goods to the world at a better price,
and giving businesses confidence and certainty to invest in  and create new businesses,
to take on more workers, and to pay them more. That is so important.
We know we have made progress. The ec onomy is forecast in  2011 to grow in
excess of 3 percent, which will result in better job prospects and higher incomes for
many New Zealanders. Although th e immediate crisis is ov er, our focus is now on
repairing the systemic imbalances, and that is  why it is so important that we keep on
steering that economy away from consum ption and spending, and towards savings,
investments, and exports.
The extension of the 90-day tr ial period is part of buildi ng the economy. It will give,
and is giving, businesses the confidence to hi re, and will give job opportunities to those
who do not have a track reco rd or work history, such as migrants, youth, and women
returning to the workforce. National is a pa rty that backs businesses and backs workers,
because we know that without jobs New Z ealand and New Zealanders will not get
ahead. Having a job is crucial for self-estee m, giving people choices and independence.
That is why the Government has an unrelen ting focus on getting people into jobs, and
we make no apology for that. Increasing the number of jobs, when they are not
available, does not magically happen out of thin air. A business needs to see the
opportunity to expand and have the confidence to hire new staff.
Our nation’s backbone, quite frankly, is small to medium sized businesses. The fact
is that 99 percent of New Zealand businesse s, which employ 60 percent of our workers,
are small to medium sized businesses and en terp rises. These businesses generate a big
16660 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
part of our wealth. When they prosper, we all prosper, and our plan for small to medium
sized businesses links with our plan for growing the economy. The 90-day trial period is
an integral part of our 2008 election promis e, and we have followed through with that
promise. Recent research has confirmed that the trial period has been a positive
experience. It has shown that the trial pe riod has a positive imp act on job numbers for
small employers at a time of rising unemp loyment. The analysis by the New Zealand
Institute of Economic Research looked at the impact of the trial period over 6 months
following its introduction in March 2009. The re view was due at a time when the actual
labour market overall was shedding workers due to the recession. Indeed,
unemployment peaked at 7.1 percent that particular year. The research by the New
Zealand Institute of Economic Research show ed that the total job numbers for the firms
reviewed were higher by about 2 percent. Alth ough it is early days fo r this policy, it is
still very encouraging and promising that th is proposed extension is showing this small
benefit quite early on.
Goodness me! The near hysteria when the 90-day trial period was extended was
really quite astonish ing. Anyone would have thought sweatshops had been introduced
and that we had been transported back to the 19 th century. The ill-inf ormed critics who
call this policy “fire at will ” are really ignorant of the commercial facts of life. A
business that wants to compete and get ahead will not be relentlessly hiring and firing.
That is an utterly ridiculous suggestion. It costs money and time to train staff. It is
evident from the research that has been done that employers are now more willing to
take a chance on someone whom they otherwise would not have been. That is where the
trial period is valuable. It is worth noti ng that many other developed countries have
similar policies and go further than we have with our particular 90-day policy.
Under the previous Labour Government the economy got way out of balance and out
of kilter. The National Government is determined to reduce our reliance on foreign
lenders, and build Kiwi-owned savings and investments. We  are considering advice on
extending the mixed public-private owne rship model for our four State-owned
enterprises. That will be a way we can release money that can be reinvested and, in turn,
give the opportunity for New Zealanders to invest. Instead  of money going offshore to
be invested, ACC, the Superannuation Fund, Kiwi Saver, and iwi will be able to invest
in these State-owned enterprise s. It will be a win-win situa tion, and this Government is
determined about building a brighter fu ture for New Zeala nd. That is why the
Government’s focus this year will be on tw o main goals: first, building the foundations
of a stronger economy; and, second, building better  results for the Public Service.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Dr Rajen Prasad, welcome home.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and likewise to
you. The battle-lines for the upcoming November  general election could not be clearer
after the speeches yesterday from the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition.
Mr Key’s Government is asking the country to trust it while it pl ans to sell assets
already owned by New Zealanders to private in vestors and corporates. As sure as night
follows day, that plan will result in overseas  ownership in a relatively short period of
time. That is a fact, and in their speeches  members opposite have not excised that fact
from the debate, at all. Overseas ownership will happen, and it seems that the other side
knows it and is quite happy with it.
National Governments have always been keen on hocking off assets rather than
creating them. When National did try to create some assets once, under Think Big—

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: Most of them were sold under Labour.
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16661

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: The member’s own electorate had some benefits out of it.
Think Big felt flat on its face except for one or  two successes. Most of its projects were
unsuccessful, and it took years for that debt to be paid off.
The Government is asking the country to  trust it when it guts early childhood
education. It believes that costs have in creased so much that the level of support
provided is now unsustainable. That is what members opposite have been saying. The
Government is not telling Ne w Zealanders under what cond itions the subsidies will be
increased. Maybe the next speaker might take up this matter. When will it be OK for us
to support our families with children whose parents have to work and require early
childhood education and childcare for their children? When will that happen? The
Government is not telling New Zealanders  what level of support is acceptable for
working parents with young children requiring ca re. Maybe the next speaker will tell us
that. All the Government is telling New Zealanders is that what was available under
Labour is now unaffordable, so it will cut it.  That is what the Government members
opposite are telling us.
The Government is asking the country to trust it when it scraps home help for
thousands of elderly people. What a mean-s pirited Government. Do es it really care
about these people? For hundreds of them, thousa nds of them, that litt le bit of care and
assistance that made life bearable has been cut. The Government has denied victims of
sexual assault access to counselling, and it has dumped thousands of people from access
to surgical procedures under the accident  compensation scheme. The Government is
asking us to trust it when it makes those kinds of cuts.
The Government is asking New Zealanders to trust it when it cuts over $50 million
from industry training and uses it to f und the shortfall in university places. The
Government effectively has no plans for ups killing New Zealand’s workforce, because
it has dumped the $180 million skills traini ng strategy developed by industry and
institutions together. They should be at the table. They are the workers. They developed
it; they agreed on it. It was funded by the previous Government. That was not good
enough for the anti-worker Government oppos ite, so it cut it. National should be
ashamed that half of all Māori and Pacific teenaged girls leaving school are unemployed
and not in further education or training, and the same is true for more than a third of the
boys.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: How could that happen after 9 years of Labour?

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Well, what is the answer  from members opposite? New
Zealand has seen previously what happens when the Government is prepared to write
off a generation of young people. National has d one this before while in Government. It
is not concerned about young people mi grating from underachievement to
unemployment and to crime. Those members talked about crime a lot in the election
campaign, but when there is an opportunity  to actually ensure that the bedrock
assistance required by our young people and our children is there, they are not
interested. When National cut assistance fr om a previous genera tion of youth, it took a
long time for those young people to recover and many never recovered, and we may still
be reaping the downside of that. The fact we  are revisiting thos e risks on the present
generation of young people beggars belief.
Sometimes it feels like this Government is playing a game. This is most evident in
health. Day after day, when questions are as ked and the answers are given, it is a game.
The Government has presented its targets fo r elective surgical procedures, emergency
department waiting lists, and cancer treatmen t times as progress, when in many cases
this progress is absolutely manufactured. What happens is cuts are made in one area of
the hospital and the resource is moved to another area to increase performance there,
and the Governm
ent says: “Look how well we have done.” But the Government is not
16662 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011
intellectually honest enough to show us the full picture. No, that would be too difficult.
After National’s 2¼ years in Government, people are beginning to suspect that it has no
plans for increasing the workforce to address these issues, and it is  becoming very, very
hard to trust. Why should people believe th is Government, which already has a track
record of a long and growing list of broken promises?
Many will remember that State services were not going to be cut. John Key said that
he would cap the number of State servants, but it has already been cut. In the next
period, National intends to drive it down further. Now, all of a sudden, the Public
Service has become bloated, inefficient, etc ., etc. Well, National has cut it before, and
subsequent Labour Governments have had to  rebuild the Public Service. National
promised not to do it, but that is what it will do.
This Government promised that GST w ould not be increased. No matter how the
Government tries to resile from that promise by circumscribing the context in which it
was made, no one believes the Government. Hi gher GST is disproportionately affecting
the less well-off and those on limited incomes. That is the group that  this Government
does not care about.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Show some courage and promise to reverse it.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Dr Smith has seen plenty of  figures. He knows where those
people are. He can talk to them in his el ectorate. He can go and see those who are on a
limited income and ask them what the effects of the tax switch and the GST increase
are, and he will know. If the member keep s on talking to just the wealthy in his
electorate, then maybe he will not see that.
Essentially, this Government does not have a plan that the country can identify with
and accept at all. Perhaps what is most alarming is that this Government does not have a
heart. No one believes that  the Government has an intim ate understanding of the pain
that many New Zealanders are feeling, and that  many more will feel as these cu ts bite
deeper. The plan that has been presented is  formulaic, predictable. That is what
conservatives do; they do not create but cut,  slash, and burn, give tax cuts, and expect
the market to perform. It never performs, and somebody else has to come back and fix
it.
Labour’s vision is for a society where ever yone has the potential to achieve to their
fullest. Labour believes in i nvesting in people. Labour believ es that it is our families
who produce our workers, and they must be factored into everyt hing we do. We believe
that focusing on just the economic side of the argument, the investment side of the
argument, is not enough. It has happened before and in the end our people suffer,
difficulties emerge, and our society is less sa fe in the long run. We believe in a strong
economy, we believe in creating jobs, but we also believe in supporting our families and
our communities that partner capital to develop a great so ciety. Let the speakers from
the Government side balance th at equation. At the moment th ey are talking about just a
few factors in the economic ar ea. Labour believes that we  should all contribute in a
manner consistent with our means, and accepts that in many cases we need to invest in
our human capital to ge t a return as a society. Our policie s will be fair. They will not
ask some people to wait until good times retu rn to get attention. We will use all our
resources for all our people.
The battle lines have been drawn; the battle will unfold this ye ar, the unbalanced
approach of this Government will be e xposed, and we will see what happens on 26
November. Thank you.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is always a privilege
to follow the previous speaker, Dr Prasad.
We are here today because 70 percent of New Zealanders  support the direction that
the John Key Government has taken. So for the 30 percent of the House who have been
9 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16663
putting up a debate against that direction tonight, I say that this is what the John Key
Government has proposed for its work programme going forward. [ Interruption]
Seventy percent support the current economic direction of the John Key Government.
In 2011 the Government will focus on two key areas. We will build foundations for a
stronger economy and build better results from  the Public Service sector. I think those
comments just strike fear in to the hearts of Labour members. We will build better
results from within the public sector. Th eir mates, the guys they employed, the
thousands of people who were put on the payroll under the Labour Government will be
asked for the first time in a number of years to front up and say how they will do better
without coming back to the Government for more money.
We listened to a number of speakers from the other side of the House, and it is
interesting to note that one in particular ga ve a life story of hardship and oppression in
her childhood. She rounded it off by saying th at the National Government intended to
make things worse for people like her. Memb ers make those comments in a way that
suggests they are unique and have the to tal franchise on growing up poor. They make
comments about those kinds of  things as thou gh they are the only ones who have
knowledge of what it is like to come up on th e lower socio-economic side of the track. I
just inform the House that one or two of  us on this side have been in those
circumstances ourselves.
I have not heard, but I have waited throughou t this debate to hear it, what those
members are going to do about those circumstances going forward, and how they will
fund the social policies that everybody in this House wants to see: more social policy in
the low socio-economic area. How will they do that? The only answer I have heard from
speaker after speaker is that they will charge more taxes. A number of those members
have been school teachers; thank goodness they were not mathematics teachers, because
they certainly cannot count. When they do th e sums on those figures, they will find out
that there is no way they can fund the type of social spending they are talking about
without growing the economy.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 9 FEBRUARY 2011 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE 
Hon SIMON POWER (Deputy Leader of the House) : Following agreement in the 
Business Committee, I seek leave for the House to sit on the ringing of the bell on 
Wednesday, 16 February 2011, following the State luncheon in honour of the Prime 
Minister of Australia. Prime Minister Gillard will address members at 11 a.m. that day, 
and, in this regard, I also seek leave for se lect committee meetings to adjourn at 10.45 
a.m. until the conclusion of questions for oral answer. I further seek leave for the bell to 
be rung at 10.50 a.m. for 2 mi nutes to summon members to the address to be given by 
the Prime Minister of Australia in the Chamber. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none.  
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
State-owned Assets, Sales—New Zealand Investors 
1. Hon PHIL GOFF (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement on the sale  of State assets that “we do  want to sell to Kiwi mums 
and dads as a priority”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. If we were to go ahead with a mixed-
ownership model in some Crown-owned compan ies, we would want to sell shares to 
Kiwi mums and dads as a priority. There would, no doubt, also be demand from 
KiwiSaver accounts and other New Zealand ma naged funds, as well as from iwi, the 
New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and other Crown financial institutions. 
Hon Phil Goff : Will the mums and dads be free to onsell their shares to foreign 
investors? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes, but history indicates that they are less likely to do that. 
Hon Phil Goff: Actually, does history not indicate that when National sold Contact 
Energy, the shares to the so-called mum and dad investors that it talked about then 
quickly flowed to the corporates and to foreign investors, and that most of the dividends 
from that company now flow out of this country? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Unfortunately for Mr Goff, no. The proportion that was 
originally sold was 31 percent to retail investors. It will be remembered that 51 percent 
was sold to Edison Mission Energy. That has now fallen to 22 percent in 12 years. But 
interestingly enough, the member might be in terested in the report that I am holding, 
and I suggest he takes it away and reads it. It is by Pattri ck Smellie. Let me just quote a 
little bit from the report: “One of the least defensible criticisms of the Key 
Government’s partial privatisation plans have been regular references to Contact Energy 
as an example of a privatised company which lost control to foreigners. Yet nothing 
could be further from the truth. The reality of the Contact share register is it remains 
possibly the most widely held share by domestic New Zealand investors. What it shows 
is that many small-scale investors have piled into privatised companies like Contact 
precisely because they want to retain cont rol and as much New Zealand ownership as 
possible.” 
16578 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2011 
Hon Phil Goff : When the Prime Minister said “ no” to my last question, was he 
denying that the majority of shares are now owned by foreign owners, and that the 
majority of dividends that are paid back therefore go out of the country? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No. What I was saying was that  initial public offering started 
with a 51 percent offering to an offshore party. Any initial public offering that we might 
do would have 51 percent control by the Cr own. On top of that would be the New 
Zealand Superannuation Fund with its $17 billion, ACC, 1.6 million KiwiSaver 
accounts, many New Zealand mums and dads up and down the country, and iwi who are 
interested in buying in. It will not be forei gners who will own those companies; it will 
be New Zealanders. 
Hon Phil Goff: Is it not dishonest to talk about sale to mum and dad investors when 
in fact all Kiwi mums and dads currently own those companies and the result of his sale 
will be that those shares go only to those who can afford them and to foreign 
corporates? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No, because 51 percent will be controlled by the Government. 
There are 1.6 million KiwiSaver accounts. Wh at is interesting about those KiwiSaver 
accounts is that, firstly, they  need investments for the long haul, because they are 
largely dominated by younger people; secondly,  the economic distri bution of those 1.6 
million accounts is very much skewed to lo w and middle income New Zealanders; and, 
thirdly, the New Zealand Superannuation F und will be buying on their behalf, along 
with ACC. I think the member should give up and try another question. 
Hon Phil Goff: I will, if I get a better answer th an that one. Can the Prime Minister 
guarantee to mum and dad consumers that prices for electricity will not go up at an even 
faster rate, as the private shareholders seek to maximise their dividends and increase the 
directors’ fees, as in fact happened with Contact Energy when it was privatised, and as 
happened in Australia with privatisation?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I am pretty sure I can guarant ee that they will not go up by 72 
percent, as they did under the previous Labour Governme nt in 9 years. Secondly, 
members need not take my word for it. We can check out the statements of Consumer 
New Zealand, which is an independent body. It s chief executive, Sue Chetwin, stated 
that she “agreed with Mr Key’s assessment that electricity pric es would not increase 
with partial privatisation.” 
Hon Phil Goff : If it is demonstrated that a cl ear majority of New Zealanders are 
opposed to these sales, will the Prime Minister  ignore their views and go ahead and sell 
the assets off anyway?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : On 26 November we are having an election. I think we will 
find that their views will be demonstrated through the ballot box.  
Budget 2011 and Wider Economic Programme—Focus 
2. CRAIG FOSS (National—Tukituki)  to the Minister of Finance : What will be 
the focus of Budget 2011 and the Government’s wider economic programme this year? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Today I have announced that Budget 
2011 would be presented on Thursday, 19 May. It  will focus square ly on taking further 
measures in the Government’s programme to build New Zealand’s national savings, 
increase investment, create jobs, and lift in comes, as well as reducing our vulnerability 
to foreign debt.  
Craig Foss: How will Budget 2011 build on the National-led Government’s first two 
Budgets?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : In Budget 2009 we had to get on top of spiralling debt, 
which was out of control as a result of a recession and very poor management by the 
previous Government. In Budget 2010 the G overnm ent changed the incentives in the 
9 Feb 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 16579 
tax system to reduce the incentive for excessive spending and borrowing, and to 
increase the incentive for savings, and we will continue along that line in Budget 2011.  
Rahui Katene : Is the Minister aware that in 2008 Treasury observed that the last 
recession, from 1988 to 1993, had had adve rse social and economic effects on M āori 
that lasted for at least a decade, and what will he be doing in Budget 2011 to prevent the 
same scenario from reoccurring?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government has moved to prevent that scenario from 
occurring again by supporting the economy thr ough this last recession, and this year we 
are borrowing $300 million a week to pump into  the economy to maintain transfer 
payments and income support, as well as to  underpin publicly funded jobs. In Budget 
2011 we will have a strong focus on investment —that is, getting businesses to invest 
their money so that they can create new jobs and lift incomes, and that will certainly 
benefit Māori. 
Craig Foss: What specific measures will the Govern ment consider to ensure that it 
contributes to improving New Zealand’s national savings?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government needs to ca rry some of the weight of 
improving national savings. Households are do ing their bit, because they are being 
careful with their spending, payi ng off debt, and increasing their savings—in fact, they 
are doing that faster than we expected. However, at th e moment the Government is 
driving up our external debt. We need to get hold of Government spending in the first 
place, to improve its effectiveness and focus,  and we need to get back to surplus as 
quickly as we can, so that the Government is not driving up New Zealand’s already very 
high level of foreign debt.  
Hon David Cunliffe : Given that the Government’s books have deteriorated on the 
Minister’s watch from a surplus of $8 billi on as at election day to a debt now of $40 
billion, and given that he has just admitte d that the Government may be taking the 
country into a double-dip recession, will he now admit that his programme has failed 
and he has no new ideas for jobs and growth?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: No. 
Metiria Turei: Why will the Minister not increase the minimum wage to at least $15 
an hour, saving around $1 billion in Government social services spending? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government has made a balanced decision about the 
minimum wage. On the one hand we do not want  to take measures that will lock young 
people, particularly, out of the labour market. On the other hand people on the minimum 
wage need to be able to deal with the ri sing cost of living. So the Government has 
announced about a 2 percent increase in the minimum wage. 
Craig Foss: What Budget measures has the Government already rejected and why? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : A number of measures have been proposed that would 
significantly increase the need for New Zeala nd to borrow in financ ial markets that are 
increasingly reluctant to lend, pa rticularly to countries with already high levels of total 
debt. So we have rejected the $1.3 billion cost of a tax-free threshold of $5,000, we have 
rejected the idea of taking GST off fruit and ve getables at a cost of a quarter of a billion 
dollars, and we are not going to be borrowing another $400 million to add to early 
childhood education spending. 
Metiria Turei: Is the Minister of Finance, like John Key, proud of the 5 percent cut 
in full-time public sector jobs, given hi s concern about young people and jobs; if so, 
why? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Prime Minister has outlined his concern to ensure that 
we provide better public servic es and do so with fewer re sources. Every other business 
in New Zea
land has gone through that proces s, and most households in New Zealand 
have gone through that process; the Govern ment has not. We will be investing in 
16580 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2011 
improved public services. In some cases that may mean there are fewer jobs but in many 
cases it will mean a better service. 
Grant Robertson : Can the Minister confirm that the grand plan for lifting New 
Zealand out of economic recession is based on the merger of the Ministry of Fisheries 
into the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry ; if so, will it generate more savings than 
the $165,000 a year being saved by merging Archives New Zealand and the National 
Library into the Department of Internal Affairs? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government is focusing on considering on a case by 
case basis how to provide better public services  for less cost. In that case, the industry 
has suggested that such a merger would reduc e the levy on the fi shing industry. That 
would help it employ more people, grow mo re exports, and lift incomes across the New 
Zealand economy. So the Government is going to play its part. 
Metiria Turei: Why is the Minister of Finance e ffectively subsidising the wage bills 
of large corporates like Foodstuffs and Bu rger King, rather than supporting families 
who need just a decent job with a living wage? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : When the Government came i n, despite the fact that we 
faced significant deficits for a long time we maintained the Working for Families 
programme with only minor changes because we believe that those families need the 
certainty of the income support, particularly through a recession. Whether or not income 
support is a subsidy on wages is an old argum ent, but we believe that, regardless of 
what one thinks of that issue, those families need cash support, and this Government is 
borrowing $300 million a week to help ensure they get it. 
Education Outcomes, Māori Children—Impact on Māori Unemployment 
3. Hon CHRIS CARTER (Independent—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of 
Education: Does she agree with the Rt Hon John  Key’s comment at Waitangi’s Te Tii 
Marae last year that improvi ng education outcomes for M āori children would help 
address rising Māori unemployment? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Minister of Education): Of course. 
Hon Chris Carter : Can she explain, then, to the House how cutting Government 
funding to over 2,000 early childhood centres by some $285 million improves the 
educational outcome for Māori students? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : First of all, I say that this Government is investing more in 
early childhood education than any other Government has ever done: $1.4 billion, 
which is up now over 10 percen t of the education budget. The second thing I say is that 
under the previous Government, which that  member used to be a member of, a 
considerable number of children, particularly M āori, did not access early childhood 
education. In some areas, up to 20 percent of Māori children were unable to access early 
childhood education. This Government is  putting almost $100 million into early 
childhood education participation projects aimed at lifting Māori participation. 
Colin King: What initiatives has she taken to improve M āori education outcomes, 
since becoming Minister of Education? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : We are taking this issue extremely seriously. It is why we 
have introduced national sta ndards and now whanaketanga r ūmaki M āori to pick up 
struggling kids before it is too late and help  them to read, write, and do m
aths. We are 
introducing the Youth Guarantee to help address the fact that more than half of M āori 
students are dropping out of school without a worthwhile qualification. We also have a 
number of M āori-focused initiatives—it is a long list; I will keep it as brief as 
possible—early childhood edu cation participation projec ts and extending 20 free hours 
to k ōhanga reo; $36 million to support schools with national standards and now 
whanaketanga r ūmaki Mā ori; $45 million in this financial year alone on kura 
9 Feb 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 16581 
developments; extending Te Kotahitanga and He K ākano; helping to better manage 
Māori learner engagement and attendance of students; the parents, families, and wh ānau 
programme; the 43 iwi relationships; and more te reo teachers. This list compares with 
the Labour Government’s great  initiative to improve M āori learning: the “Wassup!” 
badges. Do members remember them? That was Labour’s answer to Māori— 
Mr SPEAKER: I allowed the Minister to go on for quite a while on that answer. I 
think we have heard sufficient. 
Hon Chris Carter: Mr Speaker— 
Hon Members: Wassup! 
Hon Chris Carter: What is up is that education is being wrecked— 
Mr SPEAKER: I intend to make sure that we start this year as we are going to carry 
on. I have just reminded the Minister that answers are not time for a speech. I listened 
while the Minister was giving informati on, but once she went on to attack the 
Opposition in response to a question from her own colleague, I interrupted her. I ask the 
member, when I have called him, to just ask his question, please.  
Hon Chris Carter : Is she aware of Ministry of E ducation statistics that clearly 
demonstrate that increased early childhood education funding by the Labour 
Government between 2000 and 2007 led to  an increase in participation of M āori 
preschoolers from 84 percent to 90.6 percent,  and Pasifika preschoolers from 76.1 
percent to 84 percent, and does that not ju st prove that educational success happens 
when we put in more resources, not cut them? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : Yes, the Labour Government increased funding 
dramatically—in fact, three times. It tr ebled the money that was going to early 
childhood education. Unfortunate ly, across the board  the children turning up at school 
having had early childhood education experi ence grew by less than 1 percent. So 
throwing money at something does not get good results. All it gets is an out-of-control 
education system. 
Hon Chris Carter: I seek leave to table some statistics prepared by the Ministry of 
Education showing increased  participation through the period that the Labour 
Government spent extra on early childhood education funding. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : I seek leave to table a report in which the Swannanoa 
Preschool makes two points: one, that they are losing $100,000— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove: —a year in their budget. 
Mr SPEAKER: The member will resume his seat  immediately. He will not go on to 
make a statement like that without making ve ry clear what the report or document is 
that he is seeking to table.  He did not make the source of  the document clear. Before he 
says what is in it, he will make the source clear. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : Sure. The $100,000 cut is noted in the Northern Outlook 
community newspaper. 
Hon Trevor Mallard: Widely read! 
Mr SPEAKER : I am on my feet. That is exac tly why the member should have 
identified what the document was before he sought to m ake his political point. I will not 
tolerate that kind of thing. 
Sue Moroney: I seek leave to table a letter from the Minister of Education to the 
Matua Plunket Kindergarten, pr oposing that it increase fees  for 20 hours’ free early 
childhood education to make up for her funding cuts to the kindergarten. 
16582 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2011 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Egypt, Protests—Government’s Position on Presidential Resignation 
4. KEITH LOCKE (Green)  to the Minister of Foreign Affairs : Why is he not 
calling for the immediate resignation of Hosni Mubarak as Egypt’s President? 
Hon MURRAY McCULLY (Minister of Foreign Affairs) : Decisions about the 
future of Egypt are for the people of Egypt to determine. President Mubarak has 
announced he will stand down in September, a nd it is clear that a transition in Egypt’s 
leadership is under way. Along with Govern ments of many other countries, the New 
Zealand Government has called for that transition to be orderly and non-violent, and for 
the end result to reflect the democratic wishes of the people of Egypt.  
Keith Locke : Does the Minister agree with  the Nobel Peace Prize winner and 
democracy leader Mohammed ElBaradei that  “Mubarak is a symbol of an outgoing 
regime … If he doesn’t leave, the regime w ould retrench and then come back … with 
vengeance.”? 
Hon MURRAY McCULLY : The Government of New Zealand believes that 
decisions about the future of Egypt are for the people of Egypt to make. As I noted in 
my primary answer, President Mubarak has announced his intention to stand down in 
September of this year, commencing a transition process that the New Zealand 
Government hopes will be orderly and non-viol ent and will result in a situation that 
reflects the wishes of the people of Egypt.  
Keith Locke: If, as the Minister says, the decisi ons are to be made by the people of 
Egypt, why is the Government not list ening to the people of Egypt who are 
demonstrating in their hundreds of thousands—for example, today? Is the 
Government’s reluctance to say that Mubarak should stand down now because the 
Government is reluctant to take a different foreign polic y position from that of the 
United States Government? 
Hon MURRAY McCULLY: The Government of New Zealand is aware that Egypt 
is a Sovereign nation. Therefore, it is for the people of Egypt to determine their future. I 
note the demonstrations that the member refers to. I also note that a transition has 
commenced, which the New Zealand Government welcomes. 
Keith Locke : Does the Minister agree with John Key, who said on Breakfast that 
Mubarak had provided stability for Egypt, and should a New Zealand Prime Minister be 
supporting a stability enforced by 30 years of suppressing all dissent?  
Hon MURRAY McCULLY : I have read the Prime Minister’s comments very 
carefully. Clearly, he was reflecting on the long history of conflict in the Middle East 
and the constant risk of that conflict sparking other tensio ns around the world. The 
Prime Minister gave appropriate credit to President Mubarak for his role in achieving 
and maintaining peace between Egypt and Israel . The fact that that peace has held for 
over 30 years is indeed a significant achieve ment for which the Prime Minister quite 
rightly gave President Mubarak credit. 
Keith Locke : I seek leave to table a document from the Hindu newspaper of 8 
February 2011 quoting the Nobel Peace Priz e winner Mohammed ElBaradei calling for 
Mubarak to go. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?

Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister): In the House yesterday the Prime 
Minister outlined the next steps in the Government’s programme to get the economy on 
track, to strengthen it, and to raise income s. All of us need reminding every now and 
again of the scale of the change and adjustment that the New Zealand economy needs to

I will use for example the discussion about debt levels, because there will clearly be 
an important public debate this year between  the Government’s interest in getting New 
Zealand’s debt— 
Hon Lianne Dalziel: Talk about public debt. 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: —and Government debt down, and the Labour Party, which 
takes a different view. Labour se ems to think that if debt is cheap, then we should have 
endless amounts of it.  
The average household in New Zealand owed $61,000 in 2003. That amount is an 
average, and it includes all types of credit, of which mortgages are obviously the largest, 
but it also includes credit card debt, consumer debt, and overdrafts. Of course, debt is 
not distributed evenly acros s households. Some househol ds are debt-free. Older 
households tend to be debt-free; younger households tend to have a lot of debt. But in 
2003, on average, household debt was $61,000. By 2008, just 5 short ye ars later, it was 
$107,000. That is by far the fastest rise in debt burden that New Zealand has seen over 
any reasonable period. The average household now owes $107,000.  
New Zealanders have, fortunately, understood the risks of that debt. They understand 
that if interest rates are rising, it will eat into their standard of living, because they will 
have to pay more interest on what is now a much larger stock of debt than they had 
before. Much of that debt has been incurred in buying houses from each other or buying 
consumer goods, none of which generates a re turn to the econom y. New Zealanders are 
now being careful with their spending and are trying to pay off debt, but we have barely 
16598 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9 Feb 2011 
made a dent in that $107,000. In the meantime, the people who lent the money to us still 
want us to pay interest, and we have to keep going back to them through the banks to 
roll over that debt.  
If we thought that $61,000 was enough debt per household, then every household in 
New Zealand would have to pay off $40,000 of  debt. That would have an enormous 
impact on this economy, because it is money that would not be going into the job-rich 
areas such as the retail sector, or into building new houses. Even if we think $107,000 is 
about the right amount of debt, that figure sti ll represents a lot of constraint in this 
economy. The burden of debt that households  have built up has now become quite a 
considerable drag on economic growth. Until households believe that they have their 
debt at the right level and th at they can cover the risks of interest rates rising on that 
debt as the economy recovers, they will not go out and spend up.  
In the agricultural sector it is worse. The ag ricultural sector debt per farm more than 
doubled over the period from 2003 to 2008. De spite the fact that we have record 
commodity prices, we are not seeing that money flowing into the shops in Hamilton and 
Invercargill, because people in the farming community have to pay down the debt that 
they ran up, some on productive investment , but mostly on bidding up the prices of 
farms and buying them from each other.  Again, although conditions are favourable, 
with very high commodity pric es, it will take some time for those conditions to filter 
back into the economy because the debt hole on our farms is so large. They will be 
pouring their profits into that hole for some time yet.  
The same kind of scale of rebalancing is evident when it comes to job growth. We 
can think of the economy as being 80 percen t non-tradable—that is, domestic, which is 
not competing with the rest of the world—and about 20 percent making up the export

generated all the jobs, is now heavily constrained by debt and will not be growing 
nearly as many jobs as it used to grow. There is a long road ahead of us to get a vibrant,

RAHUI KATENE (Māori Party—Te Tai Tonga): For the average New Zealander 
the world of politics must be really hard to fathom. Over recent months the news that 
has captivated the headlines has been about whether particular politicians have dyed 
their hair, whether the Prime Minister shoul d have minced on the catwalk or admitted 
that Liz Hurley is “hot”, and what sort of behaviour is befitting of MPs.  
What seems to have slipped below the radar is the fact that a crisis is occurring in our 
hospital admissions. It is a fact that medical conditions, which occur more frequently for 
tamariki living in poverty, have been increas ing over recent years, particularly for our 
Māori and Pasifika mokopuna. Close to 250,000 ta mariki are living in homes reliant on 
the benefit for their income.  
My colleague Te Ururoa Flavell last night  sp elt out some of the consequences for 
families living in severe or significant ha rdship: families who go without fruit and 
vegetables, put up with the cold to save on heating costs, delay going to the doctor or

the dentist, live in cramped conditions, or tell their children that the opportunity to go on 
a school trip or play sport is a privilege that they can ill afford. Is this a nation fit for our 
tamariki? We need to heed the research that  shows us there can be a different life for 
our babies, if we make it a priority.  
Last year I spoke at the launch in Dunedin of The New Zealand Children’s Social 
Health Monitor Report 2010 . That report revealed th e inevitable, showing that 
economic recessions have affected children’s health in other countries. We have seen 
research showing the close correlation be tween recessions and high hospital admissions 
for children here in New Zealand. However, the report also reported on the experience 
of Sweden in the 1990s when, despite large numbers of children living in low-income 
families, there were no significant increas es in childhood hospitalisations for poverty-
related illnesses.  
I remind the House of the question I asked th e Minister of Health earlier today. In 
question time I noted that in 2010, 2,000 more children were admitted to hospital with 
poverty-related illnesses th an during 2007-08. We are talking about admissions for 
respiratory problems, infectious diseases, and other conditions with links to poor 
housing and economic hardship. Those are a ll diseases of poverty, which could have 
been prevented if children had been taken to see a doctor earlier. The Prime Minister 
said earlier in this debate , when talking about those ve ry children, the children who 
suffer the consequences of long-term dependency, that the “Government is not prepared 
to leave those people behind.” Th at was welcome news for the M āori Party, but 
statements are at risk of becoming platitude s without a plan being put in place. Slogans 
and placards are great for the cameras, but where is the strategy to put the words into 
action?  
I tell the House that it is  in the relationship and in  the confidence and supply 
agreement between National and the M āori Party. In that document we spelt it out in 
black and white: “The Maori Party seeks sign ificant outcomes in whanau ora, through 
eliminating poverty”. Not content with that, we then made child poverty a key platform 
in our economic policy. In our policy appro ach to end child poverty by 2020 we stated 
that successive Governments and their policies have created policy problems in our land 
of plenty. We put the time and effort into investing in the promise of prosperity. We 
called for seven simple solu tions to support children, whānau, and families. We will set 
a deadline to eliminate child poverty by 2020. We will designate an official poverty line 
at 60 percent of the median household dispos able income after housing costs, and set 
net income for those on benefits at this measure to prevent poverty. We will increase the 
minimum wage to at least $15 an hour. We will raise core benefit levels, including 
superannuation and veterans pensions. We  will simplify Working for Families, 
including extending the in-work payment to  all families. We will investigate the 
reintroduction of a universal child benefit. We will esta blish a neighbourhood renewal 
fund, which may include incentives to encour age people to live more collectively by, 
for example, encouraging the use of community gardens, after-school care, and post-
natal support for parents.  
There were other cross-sector priorities that we have brough t to the attention of this 
Government. We have talked about the adop tion of the genuine progress index, rather 
than the continuing reliance on GDP as the onl y measure of the health of a nation. We 
proposed the establishment of an “every chil d matters” fund, which would be a targeted 
and time-limited grant to ensure, among other things, that no child starts school without 
shoes or a raincoat. We have put pressure  on the Government to expand retrofit

minimum wage been raised to $15 an hour it would have resulted in 6,000 job losses. 
When we add to that more than $5 billion worth of promises, under Labour ideology we 
would have increased debt, increased taxes,  and higher unemployment. Is that what 
New Zealanders want? I think not.  
National is taking significant steps to alter the environment in which New Zealand’s 
businesses exist, to allow them, and therefore our economy, to grow. What does it mean 
when the economy grows? It means more money for healt h, more money for welfare, 
more money for education, and more jobs. It also means more money to spend on safety 
and law and order. We are building world-class infrastructure to help businesses 
compete. We are building skills and knowledge  for future-proof jobs. We are helping 
exporters to produce more valu able products more efficien tly, and to sell those goods 
for a higher price. We are giving businesses c onfidence and certainty so they can invest 
in new businesses, take on more workers, and pay them more. What a stark contrast this 
is to the borrow, promise, and hope approach from the spendthrift Labour Party.  
The National Government plans to address all the reasons that New Zealand is not as 
productive, as healthy, as wealthy, or as safe as we aspire to be. We have the guts and 
determination to tackle the hard issues, li ke a bloated Public Service that grew like 
Topsy under Labour at the expense of front-lin e services. New Zealanders instinctively 
know that if the biggest business in town is the Government, we  will never build 
ourselves a brighter future. In Rangitata a nd around the rest of the country the question

only themselves.

me any confidence that John Key, the National Government, its Māori Party supporters, 
or ACT have any plan whatsoever for the future , to create jobs, or to ease the cost of 
living. In fact, in the time it took for Jo Goodhew to finish her speech, the National 
Government borrowed an extra $300,000. It  is borrowing $30,000 a minute. It is 
borrowing $500 a second. The borrowing is all to  pay for the tax cuts that this country 
cannot afford.

One early childhood education centre up in the far north is losing $160,000 a year—
$160,000. That is being taken from the kids of that particular early childhood education 
centre up in Kait āia. We are talking about Tai Toke rau here. We are talking about 
Northland, one of the most socioeconomica lly deprived areas in New Zealand. The 
Government thinks it can cut $160,000 from that early childhood education centre.  
What will happen? That early childhood education centre has two choices. I heard 
the Minister Anne Tolley ta lking today about c hoices; this early childhood education 
centre has two choices. The first choice is to reduce the education op tions it is offering 
the kids. I ask Mr Key how it will improve th e prospects of the ne xt generation if the 
Government reduces the education options of those kids. The second choice is to charge 
the parents to make up the shortfall in the funding. The parents in one of the most 
socioeconomically deprived areas in New Zealand can expect to pay an extra $20 or $40 
a week to have their kids go to an early childhood education centre. 
Those parents also have choices: they can c hoose to pay to have their child attend an 
early childhood education centre, or they can choose to feed their kids that week. Those 
are the choices that parents are being forced to make: food, shelter, and clothing over 
early childhood education. Yet the Prime Minister  said in his speech  that he wants to 
improve the prospects of the next generation.  
It is just ridiculous. The research is adaman t that if we give children the best start in 
the years from birth through to age 6, then  we will see improved outcomes throughout 
their life at 10 years of age, 12 years of age, 16 years of age,  and through into adult life. 
But the Government is cutting the support. Na tional members sit there and defend cuts 
to the kids—the little kids in early ch ildhood education, who are the most vulnerable 
sector of our society.  
The Prime Minister minced up to the marae at Waitangi on the weekend and told 
Māori that they have to set aside grievance and take hold of education. Those are the 
exact sentiments that I have. We as M āori need to set aside grievance and focus on 
education. In my maiden statement I said that  we can achieve more with one generation 
of fully educated M āori than we can from another 171 y ears of grievance. I still hold to 
that view, and I am glad to hear that the Prim e Minister supports my sentiments.  
The problem is that we have seen the Government actually entrench grievance. We 
have seen no better example than today at the M āori Affairs Committee, when the

John Key also said that New Zealand n eeds to build up the pool of Kiwi-owned

He went on to say that the G overnment wants to address the drivers of crime. Let me

Government wants to address the drivers of crime, then it needs to do something about 
addressing poverty. It needs to create jobs. It  needs to come up with a plan that will 
actually make a difference for New Zealanders who are out there on Struggle Street and 
who are having a hard time just making ends meet. Kia ora.

speaker, Mr Davis, who prior to that speech had a future in the Labour Party. I th
ink Mr 
Goff saw that he had a future. But it only goe s to show the one underlying factor I have

In the last 2 days we have seen a whol e lot of choices being presented to New

this country in the future—or one where a bank from somewhere overseas comes and

We also heard today the rhetoric about early childhood education. I know a bit about

In the last 6 months I have visited 16 centres in various parts of Christchurch. What I

the Government that brought in  equalisation that treated ce ntres across the country the

We have inherited a situation under Labour where 40 percent of the kids in the

There was a meeting 2 or 3 weeks ago in Ch ristchurch that the Labour Party summoned

Under Dr Mapp and our John Key - led Government we have seen a move towards

Hon Dr Wayne Mapp: YikeBike. 
AARON GILMORE: And YikeBike. YikeBike is an  innovative biking company in

I will talk briefly about a series of disast ers that we have enc ountered, particularly 
the earthquake in Canterbury. In Christchur ch, where I live, a series of significant

I will tell members a little thing about so me of the reasons why the people of New

Carol had a different situation. Carol’s heater had gone bung, and she could not work
